Two extensions apply only to public companies and companies associated with a public company:

s.198 — quasi-loans (where the company pays a sum for the director, or agrees to reimburse expenditure incurred by the director, on terms that the director will reimburse the company).
s.201 — credit transactions (supplying goods, selling land under a hire-purchase or conditional sale, or otherwise disposing of land or supplying services on deferred payment terms).

Sections 200 and 201 also extend the loan and quasi-loan controls to persons connected with a director, again only for public companies and their associates.
Exceptions — the numbers matter and are examined:








Section
Exception
Limit




s.204
Expenditure on company business
£50,000


s.205
Funding a director’s defence costs in proceedings relating to the company, or a regulatory investigation
No cap; must be repaid if the defence fails


s.207(1)
Minor loans and quasi-loans
£10,000


s.207(2)
Minor credit transactions
£15,000


s.208
Intra-group transactions
—


s.209
Money-lending companies lending in the ordinary course of business on ordinary terms
—



Consequences of contravention (s.213). The transaction is voidable at the instance of the company on the same four conditions as s.195, and the director or connected person, and any director who authorised it, must account for any gain and indemnify the company for any loss. The transaction may be affirmed by the members within a reasonable period (s.214).






Exam trap



Quasi-loans and credit transactions are unrestricted for a stand-alone private company. A question describing a private company paying a director’s personal credit card bill on terms that he will reimburse it is describing a quasi-loan, which needs no approval — unless the company is associated with a public company. Candidates who have learned “all transactions with directors need approval” choose the wrong answer. (Note that there may still be a tax consequence: see the s.455 charge on loans to participators in Chapter 6.)




3.4.4 s.217 — Payments for loss of office
A company may not make a payment for loss of office to a director of the company or of its holding company (and, under ss.218–219, in connection with a transfer of the company’s undertaking or a takeover) unless approved by ordinary resolution, with a memorandum of the proposed payment made available in the same way.
“Payment for loss of office” (s.215) includes payments made in connection with retirement from office or employment, and payments to connected persons or at a director’s direction.
Exceptions (ss.220–221):

Payments made in good faith in discharge of an existing legal obligation (including damages for breach of such an obligation), by way of settlement or compromise of a claim arising in connection with the termination, or by way of pension in respect of past services.
Small payments: where the aggregate does not exceed £200.

Consequences (s.222). An unapproved payment is held on trust for the company, and any director who authorised it is jointly and severally liable to indemnify the company for any resulting loss.






Exam trap



Section 220 does most of the work in practice, and it is the discriminator. Contractual payments in lieu of notice, and genuine damages or settlement payments, are not caught, because they discharge an existing legal obligation. What is caught is the ex gratia golden handshake — the payment the company was not obliged to make. If the question stresses that the board wished to “recognise his long service”, the answer is that members’ approval is required.




3.4.5 s.188 — Long-term service contracts
Covered above with directors’ service contracts. Remember the distinctive sanction: it is the offending term that is void, not the contract, and the contract becomes terminable by the company at any time on reasonable notice.


3.4.6 Check yourself: transactions requiring approval
Q1. A private company’s most recent statutory accounts show net assets of £1.2 million. The board resolves to sell a warehouse, valued at £115,000, to the wife of one of the directors. No members’ resolution is passed.
Which of the following is correct?
A. No members’ approval is required, because £115,000 is less than 10% of the company’s net assets.
B. No members’ approval is required, because the buyer is not a director.
C. Members’ approval by ordinary resolution was required, because the value exceeds £100,000 and the buyer is a person connected with a director; the arrangement is voidable at the company’s instance.
D. Members’ approval by special resolution was required, because the transaction involves land.
E. No members’ approval is required, provided the warehouse is sold at full market value.
Q2. A private company with no connection to any public company pays a director’s personal hotel bill of £6,000, on terms that the director will reimburse the company within three months. The company is not a money-lending company.
Which of the following is correct?
A. Members’ approval by ordinary resolution is required, because this is a loan to a director.
B. Members’ approval by ordinary resolution is required, because this is a quasi-loan and exceeds £5,000.
C. No members’ approval is required, because the quasi-loan provisions in s.198 apply only to public companies and companies associated with a public company.
D. No members’ approval is required, because the amount falls within the £10,000 minor loan exception in s.207.
E. The payment is prohibited outright and cannot be authorised by any resolution.
Q3. A director retires. Her service contract entitles her to six months’ pay in lieu of notice, and the company pays her £45,000 accordingly. The board separately resolves to pay her an additional £25,000 “in recognition of twelve years of loyal service”, to which she has no contractual entitlement. No members’ resolution is passed in relation to either payment.
Which of the following is correct?
A. Both payments require approval by ordinary resolution, and both are held on trust for the company.
B. Neither payment requires approval, because both arise from the director’s employment.
C. The £45,000 does not require approval, because it discharges an existing legal obligation; the £25,000 does require approval, and is held on trust for the company, with the authorising directors jointly and severally liable to indemnify it.
D. Both payments are valid, because payments for loss of office are within the board’s ordinary management powers.
E. The £25,000 requires approval by special resolution, and the £45,000 by ordinary resolution.
Q4. A company proposes to enter into a service contract with its managing director for a fixed term of four years, during which the company cannot terminate except for cause. The board approves it. No members’ resolution is passed.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The whole contract is void.
B. The contract is valid, because a director’s service contract is a matter for the board.
C. The guaranteed term is void, and the contract is deemed to contain a term entitling the company to terminate at any time on reasonable notice.
D. The contract is voidable at the instance of the company, and the director must account for any salary received.
E. The contract is valid, but the company commits a criminal offence.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. A spouse is a member of the director’s family and therefore a connected person (s.253). The asset is substantial because its value exceeds £100,000 — the two limbs of s.191 are alternatives, so it does not matter that £115,000 is under 10% of £1.2 million. Section 195 makes the arrangement voidable at the company’s instance, and the director and connected person are liable to account and indemnify.

A treats the two limbs as cumulative. They are alternatives.
B ignores the extension to connected persons.
D invents a special resolution requirement; s.190 needs only an ordinary resolution.
E is the fairness fallacy. Section 190 applies at full market value; it is about members knowing, not about the company being short-changed.

Q2 — C. This is a quasi-loan: the company pays a sum on the director’s behalf on terms that she will reimburse it. Section 198 applies only to public companies and companies associated with a public company. A stand-alone private company may make a quasi-loan of any size without members’ approval.

A mischaracterises it as a loan; no money was lent to the director.
B applies s.198 to a company outside its scope and invents a £5,000 threshold.
D reaches the right result by the wrong route: the £10,000 exception in s.207 would matter only if s.198 applied in the first place, and the sum here is £6,000 in any event.
E invents an absolute prohibition.

Q3 — C. Section 220(1)(a): a payment made in good faith in discharge of an existing legal obligation is not a payment for loss of office requiring approval, so the contractual £45,000 is outside s.217. The ex gratia £25,000 is not owed and is a payment for loss of office. Without approval, s.222(1) makes it held on trust for the company, and any director who authorised it is jointly and severally liable to indemnify the company for resulting loss.

A sweeps in the contractual payment.
B and D ignore s.217 entirely.
E applies the wrong resolution to the ex gratia payment and wrongly requires approval for the contractual one.

Q4 — C. Section 188 requires an ordinary resolution for a guaranteed term exceeding two years. Section 189 supplies the sanction: the offending term is void, and the contract is deemed to contain a term entitling the company to terminate at any time on reasonable notice.

A over-applies the sanction; only the term is void.
B ignores s.188.
D applies the s.195 / s.213 consequences, which belong to substantial property transactions and loans, not to service contracts.
E invents a criminal offence.

title: 3  Running the business
text:
3.5 Company decision-making

3.5.1 Board meetings
The Model Articles for private companies supply the default procedure:







Article
Rule




MA 3
The directors may exercise all the powers of the company


MA 5
The directors may delegate to committees or individuals


MA 7
Decisions are taken collectively, at a meeting or by unanimous written decision; MA 7(2) allows a sole director to act alone where the company has only one director and the articles require no more


MA 8
A unanimous decision may be taken without a meeting where each eligible director indicates a shared view


MA 9
Any director may call a board meeting; notice must be given to each director but need not be in writing


MA 10
Directors may participate by any means enabling them to communicate


MA 11
Quorum: two, unless the directors fix a different number; if there is only one director, one


MA 12–13
The chair is appointed by the directors and has a casting vote


MA 14
An interested director may not vote or be counted in the quorum, subject to the exceptions and to disapplication by ordinary resolution



Decisions are taken by a simple majority of those voting. There is no concept of a “special” board resolution. Minutes must be kept for 10 years (s.248).






Exam trap



Notice of a board meeting must be reasonable in the circumstances but need not be in writing, need not state the business, and need not be of any fixed length. A question in which a director complains that he was given only two hours’ oral notice is usually testing whether you know there is no statutory notice period for board meetings — the issue is whether the notice was reasonable, judged against the company’s practice and the urgency.




3.5.2 General meetings: calling and notice
Who can call one. The directors may call a general meeting (s.302). The members may require the directors to call one under s.303, and may call one themselves under s.305 if the directors do not. The court may order a meeting under s.306 where it is otherwise impracticable to call one — the provision used where a 50/50 deadlock or a member’s refusal to attend makes a quorum impossible.
The s.303 requisition. Members holding at least 5% of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights may require the directors to call a general meeting. The request must state the general nature of the business and may include the text of a proposed resolution. The directors must then call the meeting within 21 days of the request, and the meeting must be held not more than 28 days after the date of the notice convening it (s.304). If they fail, the requisitioning members (or any of them representing more than half of their total voting rights) may call the meeting themselves within three months, and the company must reimburse their reasonable expenses (s.305).
Notice (ss.307–311):









Private company
Public company




General meeting
14 clear days
14 clear days


AGM
(not required)
21 clear days


Short notice consent
Majority in number holding 90% in nominal value of the shares giving a right to attend and vote (articles may raise this to 95%)
Majority in number holding 95%



“Clear days” excludes the day of service and the day of the meeting; where notice is sent by post the articles typically deem service 48 hours after posting, so two further days must be added.
The notice must state the time, date and place of the meeting and the general nature of the business (s.311), and must include a statement of the member’s right to appoint a proxy (s.325). Notice must go to every member and every director (s.310). Accidental failure to give notice to one member is disregarded if the articles so provide (s.313).






Worked example



A private company wishes to hold a general meeting on Thursday 15 October. Notice is to be posted, and the articles deem service 48 hours after posting.
Work backwards: 14 clear days before 15 October means the notice must be served by 30 September at the latest (excluding both the day of service and the day of the meeting). Deemed service 48 hours after posting means the notice must be posted by 28 September.
If the company cannot meet that deadline, its options are to move the meeting, or to obtain short notice consent from a majority in number of the members holding at least 90% in nominal value of the voting shares.




3.5.3 General meetings: conduct

Quorum (s.318): two qualifying persons, unless the company has only one member, in which case one. A “qualifying person” is a member present in person, a corporate representative, or a proxy. Two proxies for the same member do not make a quorum.
Voting (s.284): on a show of hands, every member present in person or by proxy has one vote; on a poll, every member has one vote per share.
Demanding a poll (s.321): the articles may not exclude the right to demand a poll on any question other than the election of the chair or the adjournment of the meeting, and may not make ineffective a demand by not fewer than five members having the right to vote, or by members representing 10% of the total voting rights, or by members holding shares on which 10% of the total sum paid up has been paid.
Proxies (s.324): every member entitled to attend and vote may appoint a proxy, who need not be a member, to exercise all their rights to attend, speak and vote.
Minutes (s.355): kept for 10 years; minutes signed by the chair are evidence of the proceedings (s.356).



3.5.4 Resolutions








Type
Majority
Where used




Ordinary (s.282)
Simple majority of votes cast
Everything not otherwise specified: appointing and removing directors, approving SPTs, loans, payments for loss of office and service contracts, declaring a final dividend, granting authority to allot under s.551, ratification under s.239


Special (s.283)
75% of votes cast
Amending the articles, changing the name, reducing capital, disapplying pre-emption rights, re-registration, winding up voluntarily, approving a buyback out of capital, directing the board under MA 4



Filing. All special resolutions, and certain ordinary resolutions (notably a s.551 authority to allot), must be filed with the Registrar within 15 days (s.30).


3.5.5 Written resolutions
Available to private companies only (s.288). The mechanics are examined precisely:

The eligible members are those entitled to vote on the circulation date (s.289).
An ordinary written resolution is passed when members representing a simple majority of the total voting rights of eligible members signify agreement; a special written resolution needs 75% of the total voting rights of eligible members (ss.282(2), 283(2)).
Agreement, once signified, cannot be revoked (s.296(3)).
The resolution lapses if not passed within 28 days of the circulation date, unless the articles specify a different period (s.297).
Members holding 5% of the total voting rights may require the company to circulate a written resolution (s.292), together with a statement of up to 1,000 words (s.292(3)).
Two resolutions cannot be passed by written resolution: removal of a director under s.168 and removal of an auditor under s.510 (s.288(2)).







Exam trap



The denominator changes. At a meeting, the majority is of the votes actually cast; on a written resolution, it is of the total voting rights of all eligible members. A member who does not respond to a written resolution is, in effect, voting against it. A question giving you an apathetic 30% shareholder and a 71% shareholder seeking a special resolution is testing exactly this: 71% of the total is not 75%, so the written resolution fails, while a general meeting at which only the 71% holder votes would pass it comfortably.




3.5.6 Informal unanimous consent: the Duomatic principle
Re Duomatic Ltd [1969] 2 Ch 365: where all the members entitled to vote on a matter assent to it, that assent is as binding as a formal resolution, even if no meeting was held and no resolution passed. Section 281(4)(a) preserves the principle by providing that nothing in Chapter 3 affects any rule of law as to things done otherwise than by passing a resolution.
Its limits matter: it requires the assent of all members entitled to vote, given with full knowledge of what is being assented to; it cannot validate something the members themselves could not authorise (an unlawful distribution, or a transaction prejudicing creditors of an insolvent company); and it does not dispense with a statutory requirement of a filed resolution or a written document where the statute demands one.


3.5.7 Check yourself: decision-making
Q1. A private company has two shareholders: one holding 72% and one holding 28%. The 72% shareholder wishes to amend the articles. She circulates a written resolution; the 28% shareholder ignores it and does not respond within 28 days.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The resolution is passed, because 72% of those who responded voted in favour.
B. The resolution is passed, because a special resolution requires 75% of the votes cast and only one member cast a vote.
C. The resolution lapses, because a special written resolution requires 75% of the total voting rights of eligible members, and 72% is insufficient.
D. The resolution is passed, because failure to respond within 28 days is deemed agreement.
E. The resolution is void, because the articles cannot be amended by written resolution.
Q2. Members holding 6% of the paid-up voting capital of a private company deliver a request to the directors requiring them to call a general meeting, stating the general nature of the business and enclosing the text of a proposed resolution. The directors take no action.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The members’ only remedy is to apply to the court under s.306.
B. The directors were not obliged to act, because a request under s.303 requires members holding at least 10% of the voting capital.
C. The directors were required to call the meeting within 21 days of the request, for a date not more than 28 days after the notice convening it; having failed to do so, the members may call the meeting themselves within three months and recover their reasonable expenses from the company.
D. The directors were required to call the meeting within 14 days, and the members’ only remedy for failure is an unfair prejudice petition.
E. The members may pass the resolution by written resolution instead, whatever its subject matter.
Q3. A private company’s articles are the unamended Model Articles. It has three directors. One of them, who is abroad, is given four hours’ oral notice of a board meeting at which a significant contract is approved by the other two. He objects that the meeting was invalid.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The meeting was invalid, because notice of a board meeting must be given in writing.
B. The meeting was invalid, because at least 14 clear days’ notice is required.
C. The meeting was invalid, because a director who is abroad cannot be given valid notice.
D. The meeting was valid if the notice was reasonable in the circumstances; there is no prescribed form or minimum period for notice of a board meeting, the quorum of two was satisfied, and a simple majority approved the contract.
E. The meeting was invalid, because a board decision requires the participation of all directors.
Q4. A private company has four members holding 25% each. Three of them meet informally, without notice, and all four subsequently indicate to each other in an exchange of emails that they agree the company should sell its principal asset. No meeting is held and no resolution is recorded. The transaction is within the board’s powers, and the company is solvent.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The members’ assent is of no effect, because no general meeting was held.
B. The members’ assent is effective under the Duomatic principle, because all the members entitled to vote assented with full knowledge of the matter.
C. The members’ assent is effective only if reduced to a signed written resolution.
D. The members’ assent is effective only if 75% of them assent.
E. The members’ assent is of no effect, because informal assent cannot bind a company in any circumstances.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. Section 283(2): a written resolution is passed as a special resolution if it is passed by members representing not less than 75% of the total voting rights of eligible members. The denominator is the total, not the votes cast. 72% falls short, and under s.297 the resolution lapses after 28 days.

A and B apply the meeting-based “votes cast” denominator, which is the central trap. Had a general meeting been held on proper notice and only the 72% holder attended and voted, the resolution would have passed.
D invents deemed agreement; silence is not assent.
E is wrong: the articles may be amended by written resolution. Only ss.168 and 510 are excluded.

Q2 — C. Section 303 requires members holding at least 5% of the paid-up voting capital; 6% qualifies. Section 304 requires the directors to call the meeting within 21 days, to be held not more than 28 days after the notice convening it. Section 305 gives the requisitionists the right to call the meeting themselves within three months and to be reimbursed their reasonable expenses.

A treats s.306 as the only route; it is a residual power for cases where calling a meeting is impracticable.
B states the wrong threshold.
D states the wrong period and the wrong remedy.
E ignores that written resolutions cannot be used for a s.168 removal, and in any event the members’ s.292 right to require circulation of a written resolution is a separate mechanism.

Q3 — D. Model Article 9: any director may call a board meeting, and notice must be given to each director but need not be in writing. There is no minimum period; the requirement is that notice be reasonable in the circumstances. The quorum under Model Article 11 is two, which was satisfied, and board decisions are taken by simple majority.

A contradicts MA 9(2) expressly.
B imports the general meeting notice period.
C contradicts MA 9(3), which addresses directors absent from the UK.
E confuses quorum with unanimity.

Q4 — B. Re Duomatic Ltd, preserved by s.281(4)(a). The unanimous informal assent of all members entitled to vote, given with full knowledge, is as effective as a formal resolution. All four assented and the company is solvent, so none of the principle’s limits is triggered.

A and E deny the principle altogether.
C imposes a formality Duomatic exists to dispense with.
D applies a special resolution threshold; Duomatic requires unanimity, which is present.

title: 3  Running the business
text:
3.6 Records, filing and disclosure
The specification asks about “documentary, record-keeping, statutory filing and disclosure requirements”. This is dry, and it is examined, because deadlines make clean single-best-answer questions.

3.6.1 What the company must keep








Record
Provision
Retention




Register of members
s.113
Must be kept; the option for a private company to keep it at Companies House was removed on 18 November 2025


Minutes of general meetings
s.355
10 years


Minutes of directors’ meetings
s.248
10 years


Directors’ service contracts
s.228
Duration plus 1 year


Adequate accounting records
s.386
3 years (private), 6 years (public) — s.388


Copies of charging instruments
s.859P
For the life of the charge


Contracts for off-market purchase of own shares
s.702
10 years









Verify before relying on this



From 18 November 2025 the requirement for a company to keep its own register of directors, register of directors’ residential addresses, register of secretaries and PSC register was removed. Those particulars are now filed with and held centrally by the Registrar. The register of members must still be kept by the company. If your sitting’s cut-off falls before 18 November 2025, the pre-reform position — local registers for all of these — is the examinable one.




3.6.2 What must be filed, and when







Event
Deadline




Confirmation statement
Within 14 days of the end of each review period (12 months), confirming the company’s information and its lawful purposes


Annual accounts
9 months after the accounting reference date (private); 6 months (public) — s.442


Appointment, removal or change in particulars of a director
14 days (s.167)


Change of PSC particulars
14 days to obtain and confirm, then 14 days to notify


Creation of a charge
21 days beginning with the day after the date of creation (s.859A)


Allotment of shares — return and statement of capital
1 month (s.555)


Special resolutions and certain ordinary resolutions
15 days (s.30)


Amended articles
15 days (s.26)


Change of registered office
Effective on registration by the Registrar (s.87)



Failure to file is usually an offence by the company and every officer in default, punishable by fine, with civil penalties for late accounts that escalate with delay. Persistent default is a ground for disqualification under s.3 CDDA, and can lead the Registrar to strike the company off. Only in one case does non-compliance destroy a right: failure to register a charge within 21 days makes it void against a liquidator, an administrator and any creditor of the company (s.859H) — see Chapter 5.


3.6.3 Accounts and audit
Directors must prepare accounts for each financial year (s.394), circulate them to members (s.423), and file them (s.441). Directors are also responsible for the directors’ report (s.415), and a company that is not small must include a strategic report (s.414A), which for a large company must contain a statement describing how the directors have had regard to the s.172(1) factors.
Small company exemptions. A company that qualifies as small may file abridged or filleted accounts and, if it also qualifies for the audit exemption, need not have its accounts audited (s.477).






Thresholds — check these against your sitting



For financial years beginning on or after 6 April 2025, a company is small if it meets at least two of: turnover not more than £15 million; balance sheet total not more than £7.5 million; not more than 50 employees. A micro-entity meets two of: turnover not more than £1 million; balance sheet total not more than £500,000; not more than 10 employees. The previous small company limits were £10.2 million / £5.1 million / 50 employees.
The size test generally requires the conditions to be met (or failed) for two consecutive years before the classification changes, except in the company’s first financial year.


Audit exemption is not available, however small the company, to a public company, an authorised insurance company, a banking company, an e-money issuer, a MiFID investment firm, a UCITS management company, or a company carrying on insurance market activity, nor generally to a member of an ineligible group. And under s.476, members holding 10% or more of the nominal value of the issued share capital (or any class of it), or 10% of the members if there is no share capital, may by notice require an audit — a minority protection that survives every exemption.


3.6.4 Persons with significant control
A PSC is an individual who, in relation to the company:

holds, directly or indirectly, more than 25% of the shares; or
holds, directly or indirectly, more than 25% of the voting rights; or
holds the right, directly or indirectly, to appoint or remove a majority of the board; or
otherwise exercises, or has the right to exercise, significant influence or control; or
exercises, or has the right to exercise, significant influence or control over a trust or firm which itself satisfies any of the above.

The company must take reasonable steps to identify its PSCs and may serve notices requiring information; failure to respond can lead to restrictions being placed on the relevant shares. PSC particulars are filed with the Registrar, and since 18 November 2025 individual PSCs must verify their identity.

title: 3  Running the business
text:
3.7 Partnership and LLP decision-making
The specification names “partnership decision-making and authority of partners” separately, and the rules are set out in full in Chapter 2. The comparison worth holding in your head:









Partnership (PA 1890 defaults)
Private company (Model Articles)




Who manages
Every partner (s.24(5))
The board (MA 3)


Ordinary decisions
Majority of partners (s.24(8)) — one partner, one vote
Simple majority of directors at a quorate board meeting


Change in the nature of the business
Unanimity (s.24(8))
Board decision; objects are unrestricted unless the articles restrict them


Admitting a new owner
Unanimity (s.24(7))
Board allotment or transfer, subject to the articles and pre-emption rights


Expelling an owner
Not possible without express agreement (s.25)
Directors removable by ordinary resolution (s.168); shareholders cannot be expelled


Binding the business to outsiders
Every partner is an agent (s.5)
The board, and those it authorises; s.40 protects third parties


Ending it
Any partner may dissolve a partnership at will by notice (s.26)
Special resolution to wind up voluntarily









Exam trap



Partnership voting is per capita, not by capital or profit share, unless the agreement says otherwise. A partner with 60% of the capital has one vote under s.24(8), the same as a partner with 5%. Company voting is by shares. Mixing the two is a reliable way to lose a mark.


For an LLP, the default regulations reproduce the partnership position — every member may take part in management, ordinary matters by majority, change in the nature of the business by unanimity, no new member without unanimity, and no power of expulsion — but with the two differences noted in Chapter 2: a member may resign on reasonable notice, and no member can dissolve the LLP.

title: 3  Running the business
text:
3.8 The solicitor’s position
Who is the client? When a solicitor is instructed by a company, the client is the company, not the director giving the instructions. Where the director’s personal interests diverge from the company’s — a substantial property transaction with himself, a loan, an ex gratia payment — the solicitor must be clear that they act for the company, must not advise the director personally on the same matter without addressing the conflict, and should ensure that the disinterested members of the board understand the position.
Taking instructions from one director. A solicitor may generally act on instructions from a person with authority to give them, but should be alert to a director purporting to commit the company to a transaction that requires a board or members’ resolution. Where the transaction plainly requires approval that has not been obtained, proceeding on one director’s say-so risks facilitating a breach of duty.
Confidentiality and the board. Information given to the solicitor by the company is the company’s, not any individual director’s. A director who resigns cannot demand the company’s confidential material, and a solicitor should not disclose company information to a former director without authority.
When directors and shareholders disagree. A solicitor acting for the company owes duties to the company as an entity. Advising a majority shareholder on how to remove the directors, while also acting for the company, is a conflict; the usual answer is that the solicitor must decline to act for one of them, and may need to cease acting for both.

title: 3  Running the business
text:
3.9 Chapter review
Q1. A private company has three directors and four shareholders. One shareholder holds 55%, and the three directors hold 15% each. The 55% shareholder wishes to (i) remove one of the directors and (ii) change the company’s name. The articles are the unamended Model Articles.
Which of the following correctly identifies the procedure for both?
A. An ordinary resolution by written resolution for (i), and a special resolution by written resolution for (ii).
B. An ordinary resolution at a general meeting on special notice for (i), and a special resolution (which may be a written resolution) for (ii) — although with only 55% of the votes she cannot pass the special resolution.
C. A special resolution for both, at a general meeting.
D. A board resolution for (i) and a special resolution for (ii).
E. An ordinary resolution at a general meeting for both.
Q2. A director of a private company arranges for the company to lend him £30,000, repayable in twelve months, to fund the purchase of a holiday home. The company is not associated with any public company and is not a money-lending company. The director has no other outstanding transaction with the company. No members’ resolution is passed.
Which of the following is correct?
A. No approval is required, because the loan provisions apply only to public companies and companies associated with a public company.
B. No approval is required, because the loan falls within the exception in s.207(1) for minor transactions.
C. Approval by ordinary resolution, supported by a memorandum made available to the members, was required; the loan is voidable at the company’s instance and the director must account for any gain and indemnify the company for any loss.
D. Approval by special resolution was required, because the loan exceeds £15,000.
E. The loan is prohibited outright and cannot be authorised by any resolution.
Q3. The sole director and 100% shareholder of a company, having taken no advice, causes the company to make a payment that turns out to be a breach of the duty of care in s.174. The company later enters insolvent liquidation and the liquidator brings a claim.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The director may rely on his own approval as sole shareholder to ratify the breach under s.239.
B. The director may not rely on ratification, because on a resolution under s.239 his own votes as the director in question are disregarded, and in any event the Duomatic principle does not validate acts that prejudice creditors of an insolvent company.
C. The claim must fail, because a sole director cannot be in breach of duty to a company he wholly owns.
D. The claim must fail, because the company may indemnify the director under s.234.
E. The claim must succeed in full, because s.1157 relief is available only to non-executive directors.
Q4. Which of the following requires filing at Companies House within 21 days?
A. A special resolution amending the articles.
B. The appointment of a new director.
C. The creation of a charge over the company’s property.
D. A return of allotment of shares.
E. The annual accounts of a private company.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. Removal of a director requires an ordinary resolution under s.168, which cannot be passed as a written resolution (s.288(2)) and requires special notice (s.312). The 55% holder has enough votes for an ordinary resolution at a general meeting. Changing the name requires a special resolution (s.77), for which 75% is needed — and 55% is not enough, whether at a meeting or by written resolution.

A overlooks the s.288(2) exclusion and the 75% threshold.
C applies a special resolution to the removal.
D gives the board a removal power it does not have.
E applies an ordinary resolution to the change of name.

Q2 — C. Section 197 applies to all companies, private and public alike: a loan to a director requires approval by ordinary resolution, with a memorandum of the transaction made available to members for at least 15 days before the meeting and at the meeting. The exception in s.207(1) covers loans and quasi-loans whose aggregate value does not exceed £10,000, and £30,000 exceeds it. Section 213 makes the unapproved transaction voidable at the company’s instance and requires the director to account for any gain and indemnify the company for any loss.

A confuses s.197 with ss.198 and 201. It is quasi-loans and credit transactions that are confined to public companies and their associates. Ordinary loans are caught whatever the company.
B applies the £10,000 exception to a £30,000 loan.
D applies the wrong resolution and the wrong threshold — £15,000 is the s.207(2) limit for credit transactions, not loans, and the resolution required is an ordinary one.
E invents an absolute prohibition; the point of s.197 is that members may approve.

Q3 — B. Two independent obstacles. On a s.239 resolution the votes of the director in question are disregarded, so a sole director-shareholder cannot ratify his own breach by voting his own shares. And the Duomatic principle does not extend to validating acts that prejudice creditors where the company is insolvent or approaching insolvency.

A ignores s.239(4).
C contradicts Salomon: the duty is owed to the company, which is a separate person from its sole member.
D misapplies s.234, which permits an indemnity against liability to third parties, not to the company; s.232 makes an indemnity against liability to the company void.
E invents a restriction on s.1157, which is available to any officer who acted honestly and reasonably.

Q4 — C. Section 859A: particulars of a charge, with the instrument, must be delivered within 21 days beginning with the day after the date of creation. This is also the one filing whose omission has a substantive consequence — the charge becomes void against a liquidator, administrator or creditor (s.859H).

A — 15 days (s.30).
B — 14 days (s.167).
D — one month (s.555).
E — 9 months after the accounting reference date (s.442).

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.1 Who the stakeholders are, and what they can actually do
A business has several constituencies, and the law gives each of them a different kind of leverage. The single most useful thing to hold in your head is that the strength of a stakeholder’s position depends on the mechanism available to them, not on the strength of their grievance.
crumbs: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
Stakeholder
Principal leverage




Shareholders
Votes; the s.994 petition; the derivative claim; the winding-up petition


Directors
Control of day-to-day management; their service contracts


Creditors
Contract and security; insolvency procedures; the creditor duty as enforced by an office-holder


Employees
Employment law; a “have regard” factor under s.172; preferential status in an insolvency


Partners / LLP members
The agreement; the PA 1890 or LLP default terms; dissolution or resignation
crumbs: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.2 Shareholders

4.2.1 What a share is
A share is not a slice of the company’s assets. Borland’s Trustee v Steel Brothers & Co Ltd [1901] 1 Ch 279 describes it as “the interest of a shareholder in the company measured by a sum of money, for the purpose of liability in the first place, and of interest in the second, but also consisting of a series of mutual covenants entered into by all the shareholders”. It is an item of personal property (s.541 CA 2006), transferable in accordance with the articles (s.544).
The rights attached to a share come from the articles, subject to the Act. A single ordinary share in a company with unamended Model Articles carries:

the right to vote — one vote on a show of hands (per member), one vote per share on a poll;
the right to a dividend if one is lawfully declared;
the right to a return of capital on a winding up, after creditors have been paid;
the right to transfer the share, subject to any restriction in the articles;
the right to receive notice of general meetings, to attend, and to appoint a proxy;
the right to receive the annual accounts;
the right to inspect the register of members and the minutes of general meetings.

None of these is a right to be involved in management, to be employed by the company, or to be paid a dividend. Those are the three expectations that generate unfair prejudice litigation.


4.2.2 Becoming and ceasing to be a member
Section 112: the subscribers to the memorandum are members on registration; every other person who agrees to become a member and whose name is entered in the register of members is a member. Entry on the register is what makes you a member — not the share certificate, and not the transfer form.
A person ceases to be a member on transfer and registration of the transferee, on forfeiture or surrender, on a valid buyback, or on death or bankruptcy followed by registration of the personal representative or trustee.






Exam trap



A shareholder cannot be expelled. There is no company law equivalent of an expulsion clause in a partnership agreement, unless the articles contain a compulsory transfer provision — which good drafting supplies as “leaver” provisions. If the question tells you the majority “voted to remove her as a shareholder”, the answer is that they cannot: they can remove her from the board under s.168, but her shares are her property.




4.2.3 The percentage thresholds
More marks turn on this table than on any other single page of the subject. Learn it in both directions: what a given percentage lets you do, and what it lets you block.







Holding
What it enables




100%
Unanimous informal assent (Duomatic); introduce entrenchment (s.22)


90% (majority in number holding 90% in nominal value)
Consent to short notice of a general meeting of a private company (95% for a public company)


75%
Pass a special resolution: amend the articles, change the name, disapply pre-emption rights, reduce capital, approve a buyback out of capital, wind up voluntarily, direct the board under MA 4


More than 50%
Pass an ordinary resolution: appoint and remove directors, approve SPTs, loans, payments for loss of office, service contracts; declare a final dividend; grant s.551 authority to allot


More than 25%
Block a special resolution


15% of the issued shares of a class
Apply to court to have a variation of class rights cancelled (s.633)


10%
Demand a poll (s.321); require an audit where the company would otherwise be exempt (s.476)


5%
Require the directors to call a general meeting (s.303); require circulation of a written resolution (s.292) or of a statement (s.314)


Any single share
Petition for unfair prejudice (s.994); apply for permission to bring a derivative claim (s.260); petition for a just and equitable winding up (s.122(1)(g) IA 1986)









Worked example



A company has 100 shares: A holds 74, B holds 26.
A cannot amend the articles, because she needs 75 and B’s 26 blocks her. A can remove B from the board, appoint herself sole director, and approve any transaction requiring an ordinary resolution. B cannot pass anything, but he can: block every special resolution; requisition a general meeting; require an audit; demand a poll; petition under s.994; and seek permission for a derivative claim.
Now give A 75 and B 25. A can do everything by resolution. B’s blocking power has gone — but every one of his individual rights survives, and it is those, not his votes, that the exam is usually about.
crumbs: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.3 Minority protection

4.3.1 The problem, and the starting point
The default rule is majority rule, and the courts do not run companies. Foss v Harbottle (1843) 2 Hare 461 supplies the two principles that everything else is an exception to:

The proper claimant rule — where a wrong is done to the company, the company is the proper claimant.
The internal management rule — the court will not interfere in a matter that the company in general meeting can itself ratify.

Three statutory or equitable routes cut through this: the unfair prejudice petition, the derivative claim, and the just and equitable winding up.


4.3.2 Unfair prejudice: s.994 CA 2006
A member may petition on the ground that the company’s affairs are being, or have been, conducted in a manner that is unfairly prejudicial to the interests of members generally or of some part of the members (including at least himself), or that an actual or proposed act or omission is or would be so prejudicial.
Both limbs are needed, and they are separate. Conduct can be prejudicial without being unfair (the company genuinely needs to retain profits) and unfair without being prejudicial (a technical breach causing no harm).
Re Saul D Harrison & Sons plc [1995] 1 BCLC 14 — Hoffmann LJ: fairness is judged in the context of a commercial relationship whose terms are contained in the articles and any collateral agreements. A member’s expectations are ordinarily those set out in the constitution.
O’Neill v Phillips [1999] 1 WLR 1092, the only House of Lords decision on the section, supplies the test:

Unfairness ordinarily requires either a breach of the terms on which it was agreed the company’s affairs would be conducted, or the use of rules “in a manner which equity would regard as contrary to good faith”.
Equitable considerations of that kind arise most readily in a quasi-partnership: a company formed on the basis of a personal relationship involving mutual confidence, with an understanding that all or some of the members will participate in management, and with restrictions on the transfer of shares.
There is no “no-fault divorce”. A member who simply wants out, because trust has broken down and there is no market for his shares, has no remedy under s.994 absent some unfair conduct.
An offer to buy the petitioner’s shares at a fair value determined by an independent expert, with equality of access to information and provision for costs, will usually make it unfair for the petition to continue.

Conduct commonly held to be unfairly prejudicial:

Exclusion from management in a quasi-partnership, where there was an understanding of participation.
Diversion of the company’s business or opportunities to a competing entity controlled by the majority.
Payment of excessive remuneration to the controllers, coupled with a persistent refusal to pay dividends — the classic way of appropriating profit while starving the minority.
Serious mismanagement causing loss, though mere commercial misjudgment is not enough.
Improper allotment of shares to dilute the minority.
Breaches of the articles or of a shareholders’ agreement, where more than trivial.

Conduct usually held not to be:

A single or trivial breach causing no prejudice.
A genuine commercial decision the minority dislikes.
Non-payment of dividends where there is a proper commercial reason to retain profits.
Loss of trust and confidence without more, in a company that is not a quasi-partnership.

Remedies (s.996). The court may make “such order as it thinks fit”, and s.996(2) gives a non-exhaustive list: regulating the conduct of the company’s affairs in future; requiring the company to do or refrain from doing an act; authorising civil proceedings in the company’s name; restraining alterations to the articles without leave; and — overwhelmingly the usual order — requiring the purchase of the petitioner’s shares by other members or by the company itself, with a corresponding reduction of capital.
Valuation is where these cases are actually fought:

In a quasi-partnership where the petitioner has been unfairly excluded, the shares are normally valued pro rata, without a minority discount (Re Bird Precision Bellows Ltd [1986] Ch 658).
Where the company is not a quasi-partnership, or the petitioner acquired the shares as an investment, a discount for a minority holding may be applied.
The valuation date is at the court’s discretion, and is commonly the date of the order or the date of the unfair conduct, whichever better reflects the injustice.







Exam trap



Two errors recur. First, candidates treat every falling-out as unfair prejudice; O’Neill v Phillips says otherwise, and the discriminating fact is usually whether there was an agreed understanding (express or equitable) that has been broken. Second, candidates forget that a reasonable buy-out offer defeats the petition — if the majority has offered fair value determined by an independent expert, the right answer is usually that the petition should not proceed.




4.3.3 Derivative claims: ss.260–264 CA 2006
A derivative claim is brought by a member, on behalf of the company, in respect of a cause of action vested in the company, seeking relief on the company’s behalf. Any recovery goes to the company, not the claimant.
Scope (s.260(3)). The cause of action must arise from an actual or proposed act or omission involving negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust by a director. It may be brought against the director or another person, or both. It is available:

whether the cause of action arose before or after the claimant became a member (s.260(4)); and
against a former director, a shadow director, and (by s.260(5)) is not confined to breaches from which the director personally benefited — negligence alone suffices, which is a significant widening of the common law.

Permission is required, and there are two stages (s.261):

Stage one, on the papers. The member applies for permission, with evidence. If the application and the evidence do not disclose a prima facie case, the court must dismiss it and may make any consequential order. No notice need be given to the company at this stage; the company takes no part.
Stage two, at a hearing. If a prima facie case is shown, the court directs the company to provide evidence, and decides whether to give permission.

Mandatory refusal (s.263(2)). The court must refuse permission if satisfied that:

a person acting in accordance with s.172 (the duty to promote the success of the company) would not seek to continue the claim; or
the act or omission has been authorised by the company before it occurred; or
the act or omission has been ratified by the company since it occurred.

Discretionary factors (s.263(3)). Otherwise the court must take into account, in particular:

whether the member is acting in good faith;
the importance a person acting under s.172 would attach to continuing the claim;
where the act has not yet occurred, whether it would be likely to be authorised or ratified;
where it has occurred, whether it would be likely to be ratified;
whether the company has decided not to pursue the claim; and
whether the act gives rise to a cause of action the member could pursue in his own right.

Section 263(4): the court must have particular regard to the views of members who have no personal interest, direct or indirect, in the matter.






Exam trap



Choosing between the two remedies is the discrimination the examiner is usually after:









Derivative claim
Unfair prejudice petition




Wrong done to
The company
The member, in their capacity as such


Who recovers
The company
Usually the petitioner, by a buy-out


Permission needed
Yes, two stages
No


Typical facts
Director diverted an opportunity, or was negligent
Exclusion from management; excessive pay; no dividends



If the client wants out at a fair price, the answer is s.994. If the client wants the company to recover what a director took, and to stay in the company, the answer is a derivative claim. And note that a s.994 petition may itself result in an order authorising proceedings in the company’s name under s.996(2)(c) — a route that avoids the s.261 permission filter.




4.3.4 Reflective loss
A shareholder cannot sue in their own name for a loss which is merely the reflection of a loss suffered by the company — a fall in the value of their shares, or in the dividends they would have received — where the company has its own claim.

Prudential Assurance Co Ltd v Newman Industries Ltd (No 2) [1982] Ch 204 established the rule.
Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1 confirmed and explained it.
Sevilleja v Marex Financial Ltd [2020] UKSC 31 narrowed it decisively: the rule is a bright line confined to claims by a shareholder, in that capacity, for loss reflective of the company’s loss. It does not bar claims by creditors, nor claims by a shareholder for a loss that is separate and distinct from the company’s.



4.3.5 Just and equitable winding up
Section 122(1)(g) IA 1986: a company may be wound up by the court if the court is of the opinion that it is just and equitable to do so. A contributory (a member) may petition, but must generally have held the shares for at least six of the last eighteen months (s.124(2)).
Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries Ltd [1973] AC 360 is the leading case, and the source of the quasi-partnership concept. Ebrahimi and Nazar traded as partners, incorporated the business, and later brought in Nazar’s son; the two of them then used their majority to remove Ebrahimi from the board under what is now s.168. The removal was lawful. The House of Lords nevertheless wound the company up: the statutory powers are subject to equitable considerations “which may make it unjust or inequitable to insist on legal rights”. Lord Wilberforce identified the typical elements — an association formed on a personal relationship of mutual confidence, an understanding that all or some members will participate in management, and restrictions on transfer so that a member cannot simply take his stake out and go.
Other established grounds: the substratum of the company has failed (its whole purpose has gone); the company was formed for a fraudulent purpose; there is complete deadlock; or there has been a justifiable loss of confidence in the management arising from a lack of probity.






Exam trap



Winding up is a remedy of last resort and destroys the value it is supposed to protect. Section 125(2) makes this explicit: where the petitioners are entitled to relief either by winding up or by some other remedy, the court must not make a winding-up order if it is of the opinion that some other remedy is available and that they are acting unreasonably in seeking winding up rather than pursuing it. Where the majority has offered to buy the minority out at a fair value, a winding-up petition will normally fail. In an exam, if s.994 would give the client what they want, s.994 is the answer.




4.3.6 Check yourself: minority protection
Q1. Three friends incorporated a company fifteen years ago. Each holds one third of the shares, and each has always been a director drawing an equal salary; there has never been a dividend, and the articles restrict transfers. Following a personal falling-out, the other two use their combined votes to remove the third from the board under s.168 and to stop her salary. She remains a shareholder. The removal complied in every respect with the statutory procedure.
Which of the following is the best advice?
A. She has no remedy, because the removal complied with s.168 and the majority is entitled to exercise its votes as it wishes.
B. She should bring a derivative claim, because the removal was a breach of the directors’ duties owed to the company.
C. She should petition under s.994: this has the hallmarks of a quasi-partnership with an understanding of participation in management, and her exclusion is likely to be unfairly prejudicial; the usual remedy is an order that her shares be bought at a value with no minority discount.
D. She should petition for a just and equitable winding up under s.122(1)(g), which is the primary remedy for exclusion from management.
E. She should sue the other two shareholders personally for the fall in the value of her shares.
Q2. A director of a company diverted a contract worth £900,000 to a business he controls. The board comprises that director and two others who are his appointees and have declined to take any action. A member holding 4% of the shares wishes to see the company recover the profit, and wishes to remain a shareholder.
Which of the following is the most appropriate course?
A. An unfair prejudice petition, because the member has been prejudiced by the loss in value of her shares.
B. A personal claim in the member’s own name for the diminution in the value of her shares.
C. An application for permission to bring a derivative claim under ss.260–264, since the cause of action is vested in the company and arises from a breach of duty by a director.
D. A petition for a just and equitable winding up.
E. Nothing, because a member holding less than 5% has no standing to bring proceedings.
Q3. A member petitions under s.994, complaining of exclusion from management in a quasi-partnership. Before the hearing, the majority shareholders offer in writing to purchase her shares at a price to be determined by an independent accountant as an expert, on a pro rata basis with no minority discount, with both sides having equal access to the company’s information, and offering to pay her costs to date.
What is the likely effect of the offer?
A. None; an offer to purchase cannot affect a petition once presented.
B. The court is likely to hold that it is no longer unfair for the petitioner to be excluded, and to strike out or dismiss the petition, because a fair offer of the remedy she would obtain has been made.
C. The offer is irrelevant unless it is accepted.
D. The offer converts the petition into a derivative claim.
E. The offer will be disregarded because the price is not fixed at the date of the offer.
Q4. A member applies for permission to continue a derivative claim. The company’s independent members, who have no personal interest in the matter, have resolved that pursuing the claim would harm the company’s commercial relationships and that it should not be brought. The alleged breach has not been ratified.
Which of the following best describes the court’s approach?
A. The court must grant permission, because the breach has not been ratified.
B. The court must refuse permission, because the members have decided not to pursue the claim.
C. The court must refuse permission if satisfied that a person acting in accordance with s.172 would not seek to continue the claim; otherwise it will weigh the discretionary factors in s.263(3), giving particular regard under s.263(4) to the views of members with no personal interest.
D. The court will grant permission only if the member holds at least 5% of the shares.
E. The court will grant permission automatically once a prima facie case is shown at the first stage.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. Every hallmark of a quasi-partnership identified in Ebrahimi is present: a company formed on a personal relationship, an understanding that all members participate in management, and restrictions on transfer. Removal that is lawful under s.168 can still be unfairly prejudicial, because equitable considerations may make it unjust to insist on strict legal rights (O’Neill v Phillips). The standard remedy under s.996 is a buy-out order, and in a quasi-partnership exclusion case the shares are normally valued pro rata without a minority discount (Re Bird Precision Bellows).

A states the Foss v Harbottle starting point and ignores the statutory exception.
B misidentifies the wrong: the harm is to her as a member, not to the company, so a derivative claim is the wrong vehicle.
D is available in principle (Ebrahimi itself was a winding-up case) but is a remedy of last resort; s.125(2) IA 1986 means a petitioner who could obtain a buy-out under s.994 and unreasonably insists on winding up will be refused.
E runs into the reflective loss principle: a fall in share value mirroring the company’s loss is not separately recoverable by a member (Prudential, Johnson v Gore Wood, Sevilleja v Marex).

Q2 — C. The cause of action — breach of the s.175 duty to avoid conflicts, and the exploitation of a corporate opportunity — is vested in the company. The client wants the company to recover and wants to stay in. That is the derivative claim, and s.260(3) covers it exactly. There is no minimum shareholding.

A would give her a buy-out, which is not what she wants, and the loss she has suffered is the company’s loss reflected in her shares.
B is barred by the reflective loss principle.
D destroys the company for no gain.
E invents a standing threshold. Any member may apply under s.260.

Q3 — B. O’Neill v Phillips. Where the majority offers to buy the petitioner’s shares at a fair value determined by a competent independent expert, on a pro rata basis in a quasi-partnership, with equality of information and provision for costs, it will usually cease to be unfair to exclude the petitioner from the company, and the petition should not proceed. The offer here has each of those features.

A and C deny the effect of a fair offer, which is the practical core of O’Neill.
D confuses the two remedies.
E misstates the requirement: a fair offer does not need a fixed price, and independent expert determination is precisely what makes it fair.

Q4 — C. Section 263(2)(a) requires mandatory refusal only where the court is satisfied that a person acting under s.172 would not seek to continue the claim. A decision by the company not to pursue is a discretionary factor under s.263(3)(e), and the views of disinterested members attract particular regard under s.263(4) — they are weighty, but not determinative.

A treats the absence of ratification as sufficient. It removes one mandatory bar, not the discretion.
B elevates a discretionary factor to a mandatory bar.
D invents a shareholding requirement.
E ignores the second stage: a prima facie case gets the applicant past s.261(2), no further.
crumbs: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.4 Directors as stakeholders
Directors are stakeholders in their own right, and their interests can conflict with the company’s in ways the Act tries to manage.
Remuneration. Directors have no automatic right to be paid for acting as directors; the entitlement comes from the articles or a service contract. Model Article 19 permits the directors to undertake any services for the company and to be paid such remuneration as the directors determine — which is why a company controlled by its directors can pay them what it likes, and why excessive remuneration combined with a refusal to declare dividends is such a common s.994 complaint.
Service contracts. See Chapter 3: s.188 approval for terms over two years, s.228 inspection rights for members, and the preservation of contractual claims on removal by s.168(5).
The tension with s.172. A director appointed by, and beholden to, a controlling shareholder still owes the duty to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole — including the minority — and must exercise independent judgment under s.173. A nominee who simply votes as instructed is in breach of both. The point recurs in group scenarios: a director of a subsidiary owes duties to the subsidiary, not to the parent, and a decision that benefits the group at the subsidiary’s expense is a breach.
Directors as employees. An executive director is usually also an employee, which gives them the protections of employment law and preferential status in an insolvency for limited amounts — but a non-executive director is not, and a director who is dismissed as an employee is not thereby removed from the board.
crumbs: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.5 Creditors
Creditors have no rights under the constitution and no vote. Their leverage is contractual, and then statutory.
Contract and security. A creditor’s real protection is taken in advance: security over assets (Chapter 5), personal guarantees from the directors, retention of title, and covenants restricting what the borrower may do. A trade creditor with none of these is at the bottom of the priority order.
The creditor duty. As explained in Chapter 3, BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA [2022] UKSC 25 holds that when a company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or an insolvent liquidation or administration is probable, the directors’ s.172 duty is modified so that they must consider the interests of creditors, with increasing weight as insolvency approaches. Three points:

The duty is owed to the company, not to individual creditors. It is enforced by a liquidator or administrator after the event, not by a creditor suing directly.
It is not triggered by a mere “real risk” of insolvency at some future date.
Because it is a modification of s.172, breach is a breach of duty, with the ordinary consequences — and a director’s conduct on this front will also feature in any wrongful trading or disqualification claim.

Statutory protection. The clawback provisions (ss.238, 239, 245, 423 IA 1986), wrongful and fraudulent trading, and the priority rules are the creditors’ real remedies. They are dealt with in Chapter 7.

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.6 Employees
Employees are the stakeholder the Act mentions most and protects least, at least within company law:

Section 172(1)(b) requires directors to have regard to employees’ interests. It creates no right of action for employees.
Section 247 permits a company to make provision for employees on the cessation or transfer of its business — an express reversal of the old rule that such payments were beyond the company’s objects — exercisable by the directors if the articles allow, or by ordinary resolution.
On an insolvency, employees are ordinary preferential creditors for limited amounts: unpaid wages for the four months before the relevant date, capped per employee, accrued holiday pay, and certain pension contributions. Claims above the cap rank as unsecured. See Chapter 7.
crumbs: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.7 Partners and LLP members
The stakeholder analysis for unincorporated and hybrid vehicles is different in kind, because the owners are the managers.
Rights. Under the PA 1890 defaults: to take part in management (s.24(5)); to an equal share of capital and profits (s.24(1)); to be indemnified for proper payments (s.24(2)); to 5% interest on advances beyond agreed capital (s.24(3)); to inspect the books (s.24(9)); to true accounts and full information (s.28); and to have partners account for private profits (s.29) and competing business (s.30).
No expulsion. Section 25 means a majority cannot expel a partner unless the agreement confers the power — the direct analogue of the rule that a shareholder cannot be removed. The same is true of an LLP member under the default regulations.
Exit. A partner in a partnership at will may dissolve it by notice (s.26); an LLP member may resign on reasonable notice but cannot dissolve the LLP.
On dissolution. Section 44 PA 1890 sets the order in which assets are applied: first, losses, including losses of capital, are paid out of profits, then out of capital, and then by the partners individually in the proportion in which they share profits. The assets are then applied: (1) in paying the debts and liabilities to non-partners; (2) in repaying to each partner rateably what is due for advances; (3) in repaying rateably what is due in respect of capital; and (4) the residue is divided in the profit-sharing ratio.
Minority protection. Section 994 CA 2006 is applied to LLPs by regulation, but the members may exclude it by unanimous written agreement — an option not available to company shareholders. For a general partnership there is no s.994 equivalent: the remedies are the agreement, dissolution, and a court order under s.35 PA 1890 (permanent incapacity, conduct prejudicial to the business, wilful or persistent breach, carrying on only at a loss, or just and equitable).






Exam trap



Section 44 is the provision that produces the counter-intuitive result. Where a partnership dissolves with a capital deficiency, the loss of capital is a loss like any other, borne in the profit-sharing ratio — so a partner who contributed nothing to capital may still have to contribute to making good the loss of a partner who did. Candidates assume that a partner who put in no capital cannot lose any.
crumbs: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.8 The solicitor’s position
Acting for the company when instructed by the majority. A solicitor instructed by the company must remember that the company is the client, and that the majority shareholder is not. Advice on how to exclude the minority, or on how to structure a transaction that benefits the majority at the company’s expense, is advice to the majority — and if the solicitor is also acting for the company there is a conflict.
Acting for two shareholders in dispute. Where two clients’ interests conflict, or there is a significant risk that they will, the solicitor must not act for both. The narrow exceptions — substantially common interest, or competing for the same objective — require informed written consent, effective safeguards and a reasonable belief that acting is in both clients’ best interests. A falling-out between shareholders is very rarely a substantially common interest.
Confidentiality across a group. Information obtained while acting for one company in a group is confidential to that company. Passing it to the parent without authority breaches the duty of confidentiality, even where the parent owns 100% of the shares.

title: 4  Stakeholders: rights, powers and protection
text:
4.9 Chapter review
Q1. A shareholder holds 26% of the shares in a private company. The other 74% is held by the managing director.
Which of the following can the minority shareholder do without the majority’s cooperation?
A. Remove the managing director from the board.
B. Amend the articles to introduce a pre-emption right on transfer.
C. Block a special resolution, require the directors to call a general meeting, require an audit, and petition under s.994.
D. Compel the payment of a dividend.
E. Compel the company to buy back her shares.
Q2. In a partnership dissolution, after all outside creditors have been paid, the remaining assets are £120,000. Partner X is owed £30,000 in respect of an advance made to the firm; X’s capital account stands at £150,000 and Y’s at £50,000. X and Y share profits equally.
Applying s.44 PA 1890, which of the following is correct?
A. The £120,000 is divided equally between X and Y.
B. X is repaid the £30,000 advance first; the remaining £90,000 is applied towards capital of £200,000, leaving a capital deficiency of £110,000, which is a loss borne equally, so each partner bears £55,000.
C. The £120,000 is applied first to capital in proportion to the capital accounts, and X’s advance ranks last.
D. X is repaid the £30,000 and the balance of £90,000 is paid to X in part satisfaction of capital, because X’s capital contribution was larger.
E. The £120,000 is retained by the firm until the partners agree its distribution.
Q3. A shareholder in a company that is not a quasi-partnership is dissatisfied with the board’s strategy, which she considers commercially misguided. The company is profitable, dividends are paid, and there is no breach of the articles or of any agreement. She wishes to exit but there is no market for her shares.
Which of the following is the best advice?
A. She may petition under s.994, because the absence of a market for her shares is itself unfairly prejudicial.
B. She may petition for a just and equitable winding up, because there has been an irretrievable breakdown in her relationship with the board.
C. She has no remedy on these facts: there is no “no-fault divorce” under s.994, disagreement with a genuine commercial decision is not unfair prejudice, and winding up is a remedy of last resort.
D. She may bring a derivative claim in respect of the board’s strategic decisions.
E. She may require the company to purchase her shares under s.994 as of right.
Q4. A creditor of a company believes that the directors continued to trade and paid a large dividend at a time when insolvent administration was probable. The company is now in administration.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The creditor may sue the directors directly for breach of the duty owed to creditors under s.172(3).
B. The creditor has no remedy of any kind, because directors’ duties are owed only to the company.
C. The creditor cannot sue on the duty directly, because it is a modification of the duty owed to the company; it is for the administrator to pursue the breach, and the administrator may also consider wrongful trading and the clawback provisions.
D. The creditor may petition under s.994.
E. The creditor may bring a derivative claim under s.260.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. A 26% holding blocks a special resolution (more than 25% is needed), exceeds the 5% threshold for requiring a general meeting under s.303, exceeds the 10% threshold for requiring an audit under s.476, and — like any single share — supports a s.994 petition.

A requires an ordinary resolution, which she cannot pass.
B requires a special resolution, which she cannot pass.
D is not within any shareholder’s power: a final dividend is recommended by the directors and declared by ordinary resolution, and cannot exceed the recommendation.
E is not a right; a buy-out follows only from an order under s.996 or an agreement.

Q2 — B. Section 44(b) sets the order: outside creditors first, then advances, then capital, then the residue in the profit-sharing ratio. X’s £30,000 advance is repaid before any capital. The remaining £90,000 is insufficient to repay £200,000 of capital, leaving a deficiency of £110,000. Under s.44(a) a loss of capital is a loss, borne by the partners in the proportions in which they share profits — equally here, so £55,000 each.

A ignores both the priority of advances and the capital accounts.
C inverts the order of advances and capital.
D invents a preference for the larger contributor.
E describes no rule.

Q3 — C. O’Neill v Phillips: there is no no-fault divorce under s.994, and unfairness ordinarily requires a breach of the agreed terms or use of the rules contrary to good faith. Disagreement with a genuine commercial decision, in a company that is not a quasi-partnership and is complying with its constitution, is neither unfair nor a ground for winding up; and s.125(2) IA 1986 makes winding up a last resort.

A is precisely the argument O’Neill rejected.
B applies quasi-partnership reasoning where the facts exclude it.
D requires a cause of action vested in the company arising from a director’s breach of duty; a strategic decision within the board’s powers is not one.
E treats a s.994 remedy as an entitlement rather than a discretionary order following proof of unfair prejudice.

Q4 — C. BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA. The creditor duty is not owed to creditors individually; it is a modification of the s.172 duty owed to the company, enforced by the office-holder. The administrator may pursue breach of duty, and should also consider wrongful trading under s.214 IA 1986 and the clawback provisions in ss.238, 239 and 423.

A is the recurring structural error.
B over-corrects: the creditor’s interests are protected through the office-holder’s claims and the insolvency regime.
D is not open to a creditor; s.994 is a member’s remedy.
E is not open to a creditor either; s.260 requires the claimant to be a member.

5.1 Debt or equity: the choice that frames the chapter
A company that needs money has two sources, and the difference between them runs through everything below.
