title: 6  Taxation of the business and its stakeholders
text:
6.6 Corporation tax

6.6.1 The charge
Corporation tax is charged on the taxable total profits of a company for an accounting period, which cannot exceed 12 months. Unlike an individual, a company pays a single tax on both its income profits and its capital gains.
    Trading income (adjusted profits, after capital allowances)
  + Property income
  + Non-trading loan relationship profits (interest receivable)
  + Chargeable gains
  = Total profits
  − Reliefs and deductions (including loss relief and qualifying charitable donations)
  = Taxable total profits (TTP)
Adjustments to the accounting profit follow the same logic as for a sole trader — add back depreciation, client entertaining, fines and capital expenditure; deduct capital allowances. Two differences matter: a company can deduct directors’ and employees’ salaries and the employer’s NICs on them (there is no appropriation problem, because the company is a separate person), and a company cannot deduct the dividends it pays.


6.6.2 Chargeable gains in a company
Computed broadly as for CGT, but with three differences:

No annual exempt amount.
Indexation allowance is available for the period of ownership up to December 2017, when it was frozen. It can reduce a gain to nil but cannot create or increase a loss.
The substantial shareholding exemption exempts gains on the disposal of shares where a trading company has held at least 10% of another trading company for a continuous 12-month period within the preceding six years.

The rate is the corporation tax rate — there is no separate capital gains rate for companies.


6.6.3 Rates






Rates — financial year 2026










Augmented profits
Rate




Up to £50,000
19% (small profits rate)


£50,000 to £250,000
25% with marginal relief, giving an effective rate rising from 19% to 25% — and a marginal rate of 26.5% on each extra pound in the band


£250,000 and above
25% (main rate)



The marginal relief fraction is 3/200. Both limits are divided by one plus the number of associated companies, and are reduced proportionately for an accounting period of less than 12 months.


Marginal relief is computed as:
    Standard fraction × (Upper limit − Augmented profits) × (TTP ÷ Augmented profits)
and is deducted from the tax charged at the main rate.






Worked example



A company with no associated companies has taxable total profits of £100,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027, and no franked investment income, so augmented profits are also £100,000.

Tax at the main rate: £100,000 × 25% = £25,000
Marginal relief: 3/200 × (£250,000 − £100,000) × (£100,000 ÷ £100,000) = 3/200 × £150,000 = £2,250
Corporation tax payable: £25,000 − £2,250 = £22,750, an effective rate of 22.75%

Note the practical point that the effective rate is not the marginal rate. If the company earned one more pound of profit, that pound would bear tax at 26.5% — higher than the main rate itself, which is why companies near the £250,000 threshold receive so much advice about timing.




6.6.4 Relieving trading losses







Relief
What it does




s.37 CTA 2010
Set the loss against total profits of the same accounting period, and/or carry it back 12 months against total profits


s.45A CTA 2010
Carry forward against total profits of later periods (for losses arising on or after 1 April 2017), and surrender within a group


s.45 CTA 2010
Losses arising before 1 April 2017 carry forward only against profits of the same trade


Terminal loss relief
On cessation, carry back three years


Group relief
Surrender current-period losses to a 75% group company



Carried-forward losses are subject to a restriction: a company (or group) may use its £5 million deductions allowance in full, but beyond that may relieve only 50% of remaining profits with carried-forward losses.


6.6.5 Payment and collection

Payment: 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period, for a company that is not “large”.
Large companies (augmented profits above £1.5 million) pay by quarterly instalments; very large companies (above £20 million) pay on an accelerated instalment timetable. The £1.5 million and £20 million limits are also divided among associated companies.
Return: form CT600, within 12 months of the end of the accounting period. Note that the filing deadline is later than the payment deadline, which is counter-intuitive and examinable.
A company must notify HMRC that it is chargeable within three months of starting business activity.



6.6.6 Distributions and close companies
Dividends paid by a company are a distribution of taxed profit and are not deductible. Dividends received by a UK company from another company are, in most cases, exempt from corporation tax, which prevents the same profit being taxed repeatedly as it moves up a group.
A close company is one under the control of five or fewer participators, or of participators who are directors. Almost every owner-managed company is close. Two anti-avoidance charges follow, and the first is regularly examined because it catches the director’s loan account:

Section 455 CTA 2010: where a close company makes a loan to a participator, the company must pay a charge on the amount of the loan at the dividend upper rate, due 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period. It is refundable when the loan is repaid, released or written off. The rate is 35.75% for loans made on or after 6 April 2026 and 33.75% for loans made before then — it tracks the dividend upper rate, so it moved when that rate moved. This is a charge on the company, and it sits alongside — not instead of — the s.197 CA 2006 requirement for members’ approval and any benefit-in-kind charge on the director.
Section 464A: a similar charge where a close company confers a benefit on a participator otherwise than by way of a loan.



6.6.7 Anti-avoidance in outline
The specification asks for the scope of anti-avoidance provisions, not their detail:

The General Anti-Abuse Rule (Finance Act 2013) counteracts tax advantages arising from abusive arrangements — those that cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action — applying a “double reasonableness” test, with an independent GAAR Advisory Panel.
Transfer pricing requires transactions between connected parties to be priced on arm’s length terms.
DOTAS requires the disclosure of notifiable tax avoidance schemes, giving each a scheme reference number that users must report.
The corporate interest restriction limits the deductibility of interest for large groups.
Transactions in securities rules counteract arrangements designed to convert what would be income into capital.
The distinction that underlies all of it: tax avoidance is lawful but may be counteracted; tax evasion is criminal, and a solicitor who assists it commits an offence and breaches the SRA Principles.

title: 6  Taxation of the business and its stakeholders
text:
6.7 Value added tax

6.7.1 The scope of the charge
VAT is charged on any supply of goods or services made in the United Kingdom, where it is a taxable supply made by a taxable person in the course or furtherance of any business carried on by them (s.4 VATA 1994). All four elements must be present.
VAT is a tax on consumption, collected in stages. A registered business charges output tax on its supplies, recovers input tax on its purchases, and accounts to HMRC for the difference. The burden falls on the final, unregistered consumer.


6.7.2 Rates and categories








Category
Rate
Input tax recoverable?




Standard-rated
20%
Yes


Reduced-rated — domestic fuel and power, children’s car seats, certain energy-saving materials
5%
Yes


Zero-rated — most food, books and newspapers, children’s clothing, new residential construction, public transport, most drugs and medicines on prescription
0%
Yes


Exempt — insurance, most financial services, education, health and welfare, postal services, most supplies of land
No VAT charged
No


Outside the scope
No VAT
No









Exam trap



Zero-rated is not the same as exempt, and the difference is worth real money. A business making zero-rated supplies charges no output tax but recovers its input tax in full — so it is typically in a repayment position with HMRC. A business making exempt supplies charges no output tax and cannot recover its input tax, which becomes an irrecoverable cost. This is the single most reliable VAT question in the subject.




6.7.3 Registration






Thresholds — 2026/27




Registration threshold: taxable turnover of £90,000
Deregistration threshold: £88,000

Both have been at these levels since 1 April 2024.


Registration is compulsory under either of two tests:

The historic test. Taxable turnover in the preceding 12 months (a rolling period, not a financial year) has exceeded the threshold. The business must notify HMRC within 30 days of the end of the month in which the threshold was exceeded, and is registered from the first day of the second month after that.
The future test. There are reasonable grounds to believe that taxable turnover in the next 30 days alone will exceed the threshold. The business must notify by the end of that 30-day period, and is registered from the beginning of it.

Exception: HMRC may grant an exception from registration under the historic test where the business can satisfy them that turnover in the following 12 months will not exceed the deregistration threshold.
Voluntary registration is available below the threshold, and is worth taking where the business makes zero-rated supplies or sells mainly to other registered businesses, because it unlocks input tax recovery.
Deregistration may be requested where turnover falls below the deregistration threshold, and is compulsory where the business ceases to make taxable supplies.






Exam trap



The two tests use different periods and produce different registration dates. The historic test looks back over 12 months and gives a start date roughly six weeks later; the future test looks forward 30 days only and registers the business from the start of that period, with no grace. A scenario in which a business wins a single large contract that will take it over the threshold within a month is a future test question, and the answer is immediate registration.




6.7.4 Input tax, tax points, invoices and returns
Blocked input tax cannot be recovered even by a fully taxable business: business entertainment, cars (unless used exclusively for business), and anything not used for business purposes. Where a business makes both taxable and exempt supplies it is partially exempt and must apportion.
The tax point determines the return period in which VAT is accounted for:

The basic tax point is the date the goods are removed or made available, or the date the services are completed.
An actual tax point overrides it if a VAT invoice is issued or payment is received before the basic tax point (that earlier date applies), or if a VAT invoice is issued within 14 days after the basic tax point (the invoice date applies).

VAT invoices must be issued to other registered persons within 30 days of the supply, and must contain the prescribed particulars — an identifying number, the supplier’s name, address and VAT registration number, the tax point, the customer’s name and address, a description of the goods or services, the amount excluding VAT, the rate, and the VAT charged.
Returns and records: returns are normally quarterly, filed and paid within one month and seven days of the end of the period. Making Tax Digital requires digital record-keeping and submission through compatible software. Records must be kept for six years. Late filing is dealt with by a points-based penalty regime, and late payment by escalating penalties and interest.

title: 6  Taxation of the business and its stakeholders
text:
6.8 Inheritance tax: business property relief
The specification limits IHT in Business Law and Practice to business property relief. What you need around it is minimal: IHT is charged at 40% on the death estate above the nil rate band (£325,000), and at 20% on lifetime chargeable transfers above it.
Business property relief (IHTA 1984 ss.103–114) reduces the value transferred by a transfer of value attributable to relevant business property. It applies both to lifetime transfers and on death, and it is applied before the nil rate band.

6.8.1 What qualifies, and at what rate







Relevant business property
Rate (historic position)




A business or an interest in a business — a sole trade, or a partnership or LLP share
100%


Unquoted shares in a company
100%


Quoted shares or securities which gave the transferor control of the company
50%


Land, buildings, plant or machinery owned personally and used in a business carried on by a company the transferor controlled, or by a partnership of which they were a partner
50%


Such assets held in a trust in which the transferor had an interest in possession and used in their business
50%





6.8.2 The conditions

Two years’ ownership (s.106). The property must have been owned by the transferor throughout the two years immediately before the transfer. Section 107 allows replacement property to count, and s.108/109 aggregate periods on succession — notably, property inherited from a spouse counts from the spouse’s acquisition, and the two-year test is dispensed with where the transferor inherited it on the spouse’s death.
Not an excluded business (s.105(3)). No relief where the business consists wholly or mainly of dealing in securities, stocks or shares, land or buildings, or making or holding investments. This is the provision that denies relief to a property investment business, while a property development or trading business qualifies. The test is applied “in the round” to the business as a whole.
No excepted assets (s.112). Relief is denied for the value attributable to assets that were neither used wholly or mainly for the business throughout the last two years nor required for its future use — the classic example being a large cash balance far in excess of the business’s needs.
No binding contract for sale (s.113). If the property is subject to a binding contract for sale at the date of transfer, it is not relevant business property. This is why partnership and shareholders’ agreements use cross-option agreements (reciprocal put and call options, exercisable on death) rather than automatic buy-and-sell provisions: an option is not a binding contract for sale, so relief is preserved.







A major change takes effect on 6 April 2026 — verify against your cut-off



From 6 April 2026 the 100% rate is capped. An allowance applies to the combined value of agricultural property qualifying for agricultural property relief and business property qualifying for BPR: value within the allowance attracts 100% relief, and value above it attracts 50%.
The allowance was announced at the Autumn Budget 2024 at £1 million, and was increased to £2.5 million on 23 December 2025. It is transferable between spouses and civil partners.
Separately, shares designated as “not listed” on the markets of a recognised stock exchange — AIM shares being the obvious case — move to a flat 50% relief, and the allowance is not available against them.
This is recent, and the figure moved twice. Check the position at your sitting’s cut-off date before relying on it, and check whether the pre-6 April 2026 position (uncapped 100% relief) is the examinable one for you.








Exam trap



The two BPR traps that appear most often are the investment business exclusion in s.105(3) — a company whose business is letting property gets no relief, however substantial — and the binding contract for sale point in s.113, which is set up by telling you the partnership agreement requires the surviving partners to buy the deceased’s share.

title: 6  Taxation of the business and its stakeholders
section: 6.9 Putting it together: the structuring questions
text:
6.9 Putting it together: the structuring questions

6.9.1 Salary or dividend?
For an owner-manager, the arithmetic is driven by four facts:

Salary is deductible in computing the company’s corporation tax; a dividend is not.
Salary attracts National Insurance — the employee’s Class 1 and, more expensively, the employer’s Class 1 secondary at 15%. A dividend attracts none.
A dividend can be paid only out of distributable profits (s.830 CA 2006 — see Chapter 5). Paying one without them is unlawful, whatever its tax attractions.
Dividend income is taxed at lower rates than earned income, but out of already-taxed profits.

The usual advice is a modest salary — enough to preserve a National Insurance record and to use allowances — with the balance as dividends, subject to there being distributable profits and to the company’s needs. The rise in dividend rates from 6 April 2026 has narrowed the advantage.


6.9.2 Incorporating an existing business
The tax consequences of transferring a sole trade or partnership to a company:

CGT: a disposal of the business assets at market value, with incorporation relief (s.162) available automatically where the whole business goes across as a going concern for shares — or hold-over relief (s.165) as an alternative on a transfer of assets. Business asset disposal relief may be preferable where the client wants to crystallise the gain at the reduced rate.
Capital allowances: balancing charges or allowances arise unless the assets are transferred at tax written-down value under a joint election.
VAT: a transfer of a going concern is outside the scope of VAT provided the conditions are met, including that the transferee is or becomes registered.
Stamp duty land tax on any land transferred, and stamp duty on any subsequent transfer of the shares.
Losses: unrelieved trading losses may be carried forward under s.86 ITA 2007 against income the individual receives from the company.







Exam trap



Incorporation relief is automatic where its conditions are met — the taxpayer does not claim it, they elect out of it under s.162A. That is the opposite of hold-over relief under s.165, which requires a joint claim. Questions test the difference by asking what the client must do.

title: 6  Taxation of the business and its stakeholders
text:
6.10 The solicitor’s position
Tax evasion. A solicitor who knowingly assists a client to evade tax commits a criminal offence and breaches the SRA Principles. The distinction from lawful avoidance is one of legality, not of morality: misrepresenting facts to HMRC, concealing income, or backdating documents is evasion.
Failure to prevent the facilitation of tax evasion. The Criminal Finances Act 2017 creates corporate offences for a body (including a law firm) that fails to prevent an associated person from criminally facilitating tax evasion. The defence is having reasonable prevention procedures.
Competence. A solicitor must only act within their competence. Business tax is a specialist field, and the right answer in many scenarios is that the solicitor should advise the client to obtain specialist tax advice rather than opine on a computation themselves.
Reporting. Suspicion that funds represent the proceeds of crime — and tax evaded is a benefit from criminal conduct — engages the money laundering reporting obligations, and the solicitor must not tip the client off.

title: 6  Taxation of the business and its stakeholders
text:
6.11 Chapter review
Q1. A UK trading company has taxable total profits of £180,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. It has no associated companies and no franked investment income.
Which of the following correctly describes the corporation tax position?
A. The whole profit is taxed at 19%, because it is below £250,000.
B. The whole profit is taxed at 25%, with no relief.
C. The profit is taxed at the main rate of 25% with marginal relief, giving an effective rate between 19% and 25%; each additional pound of profit in this band bears tax at a marginal rate of 26.5%.
D. The first £50,000 is taxed at 19% and the balance at 25%, as separate slices.
E. The company may choose between the small profits rate and the main rate.
Q2. A business supplies children’s clothing, which is zero-rated. It incurs substantial input VAT on its purchases and overheads.
Which of the following is correct?
A. It cannot register for VAT, because it makes no standard-rated supplies.
B. It charges no output VAT and cannot recover its input VAT, which is an irrecoverable cost.
C. It charges output VAT at 0% and may recover its input VAT in full, so it will usually be in a repayment position with HMRC.
D. It charges output VAT at 5% and may recover its input VAT in full.
E. Its supplies are exempt, so registration is not available.
Q3. A client owns 100% of the shares in an unquoted company whose business consists wholly of buying residential property, letting it to tenants and holding it for capital growth. He has owned the shares for fifteen years. He dies, leaving the shares to his son.
What is the position on business property relief?
A. 100% relief, because the shares are unquoted and were owned for more than two years.
B. 50% relief, because the shares gave him control.
C. No relief, because the business consists wholly or mainly of making or holding investments and is excluded by s.105(3) IHTA 1984.
D. 100% relief, but only up to the available allowance, with 50% above it.
E. Relief is available only if the son continues the business for two years.
Q4. A close company lends £60,000 to its sole shareholder-director. The loan is outstanding at the end of the accounting period and remains outstanding nine months and one day afterwards.
Which of the following is correct?
A. There is no tax consequence, because a director’s loan is a balance sheet item.
B. The company must pay a charge under s.455 CTA 2010 on the amount of the loan at the dividend upper rate, due nine months and one day after the end of the accounting period; the charge is repayable when the loan is repaid, released or written off.
C. The shareholder must pay income tax on the loan as if it were a dividend.
D. The company must pay corporation tax on the loan at the main rate of 25%.
E. The loan is void, because a company may not lend to its own shareholder.
Q5. A sole trader’s business is expanding fast. Her taxable turnover for the twelve months to 31 May 2027 was £71,000. On 3 June 2027 she signs a contract to deliver £95,000 of services within the following four weeks.
What must she do?
A. Nothing yet, because her turnover in the preceding 12 months has not exceeded £90,000.
B. Notify HMRC by 30 June 2027, because she has reasonable grounds to believe her taxable turnover in the next 30 days alone will exceed £90,000; she will be registered from the beginning of that 30-day period.
C. Notify HMRC within 30 days of the end of June 2027, and will be registered from 1 August 2027.
D. Register only once her rolling 12-month turnover exceeds £90,000.
E. Apply for an exception from registration, because the increase is a one-off.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. Augmented profits of £180,000 fall between the lower limit of £50,000 and the upper limit of £250,000, so tax is charged at the main rate of 25% and reduced by marginal relief of 3/200 × (£250,000 − £180,000) × (£180,000 ÷ £180,000) = £1,050. The result is an effective rate between 19% and 25%, and the marginal rate within the band is 26.5%.

A applies the small profits rate above its limit.
B ignores marginal relief.
D describes a slice system that corporation tax does not use — this is the most common error, and it is borrowed from income tax.
E invents an election.

Q2 — C. Zero-rated supplies are taxable supplies charged at 0%. The business charges no VAT to its customers but recovers input tax in full, and therefore usually reclaims from HMRC. It counts towards the registration threshold and may register voluntarily below it.

A and E confuse zero-rated with exempt.
B describes the exempt position.
D applies the reduced rate.

Q3 — C. Section 105(3) IHTA 1984 excludes from relevant business property a business consisting wholly or mainly of dealing in securities, stocks or shares, land or buildings, or making or holding investments. A residential property letting business is the paradigm case. No BPR is available, however long the shares have been held and however substantial the business.

A applies the general rule for unquoted shares without checking the exclusion.
B applies the 50% rate for quoted controlling shareholdings.
D applies the post-6 April 2026 allowance, which is irrelevant where the property is not relevant business property at all.
E invents a continuation condition.

Q4 — B. Section 455 CTA 2010. A loan by a close company to a participator triggers a charge on the company at the dividend upper rate — 35.75% for loans made on or after 6 April 2026, and 33.75% for loans made before that date — payable at the same time as the corporation tax for the period, and refundable when the loan is repaid, released or written off. Note that the s.197 CA 2006 requirement for members’ approval applies independently, and there may also be a benefit-in-kind charge on the director if the loan is interest-free.

A ignores the charge entirely.
C describes the treatment if the loan is written off, not while it is outstanding.
D applies the wrong rate and mischaracterises the charge.
E invents a prohibition.

Q5 — B. The future test: where there are reasonable grounds to believe that taxable turnover in the next 30 days alone will exceed the threshold, the business must notify HMRC by the end of that 30-day period and is registered from its beginning. £95,000 in four weeks exceeds £90,000.

A and D apply only the historic test and miss the forward-looking one.
C applies the historic test’s notification and registration dates, which are different.
E misapplies the exception, which is available under the historic test where future turnover will fall below the deregistration threshold — the opposite of these facts.

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
text:
7.2 Terminating a solvent business

7.2.1 Members’ voluntary liquidation
An MVL is the orderly winding up of a solvent company. The mechanism:

The directors — or a majority of them, at a directors’ meeting — make a statutory declaration of solvency under s.89 IA 1986: that they have made a full inquiry into the company’s affairs and have formed the opinion that the company will be able to pay its debts in full, together with interest at the official rate, within a period not exceeding 12 months from the commencement of the winding up. A statement of the company’s assets and liabilities is annexed.
The declaration must be made within the five weeks immediately preceding the resolution to wind up, or on the date of it, and must be delivered to the Registrar within 15 days after the resolution.
The members pass a special resolution to wind up voluntarily (s.84(1)(b)), and appoint a liquidator by ordinary resolution.
The liquidator realises the assets, pays the creditors in full with interest, distributes the surplus to the members, and the company is dissolved three months after the final account is filed.

Two sanctions attach to the declaration. Making it without reasonable grounds is a criminal offence (s.89(4)), and if the debts are not paid within the stated period it is presumed that the director had no reasonable grounds (s.89(5)). If the liquidator later forms the opinion that the company will not be able to pay its debts in full within the stated period, the liquidation converts to a creditors’ voluntary liquidation.


7.2.2 Striking off
For a company with no assets, no liabilities and nothing to distribute, striking off is far cheaper than an MVL. Section 1003 CA 2006: the company applies to the Registrar to be struck off. The application must be made by a majority of the directors.
The application cannot be made if, at any time in the previous three months, the company has:

traded or otherwise carried on business;
changed its name;
disposed of property or rights for value that, immediately before ceasing to trade, it held for disposal or gain in the normal course of trading; or
engaged in any other activity, except one necessary or expedient for making the application, concluding the company’s affairs, or complying with a statutory requirement.

Nor can it be made while the company is subject to insolvency proceedings or a s.895 compromise (s.1005).
The directors must send a copy of the application to every member, creditor, employee, director who did not sign it, and pension trustee within seven days (s.1006). The Registrar advertises in the Gazette and, if no objection is received, strikes the company off after not less than two months.






Exam trap



On dissolution, all the company’s remaining property vests in the Crown as bona vacantia (s.1012). A client who strikes off a company with a bank balance or an undistributed asset loses it. The right advice is to distribute everything first — or to use an MVL, which also has a tax advantage, because distributions in a winding up are capital receipts potentially attracting business asset disposal relief rather than income distributions.
Restoration is possible: administrative restoration by application to the Registrar within six years where the company was struck off under s.1000–1001 while carrying on business (s.1024), or by court order under s.1029, generally within six years.




7.2.3 Dissolving a partnership
The PA 1890 grounds (see Chapter 2 for the detail):







Section
Ground




s.32
Expiry of a fixed term; completion of the single adventure; notice by any partner in a partnership at will


s.33
Death or bankruptcy of any partner (subject to contrary agreement); at the option of the other partners, where a partner’s share is charged for their separate debt


s.34
Illegality — mandatory, and cannot be excluded by agreement


s.35
Court order: permanent incapacity; conduct prejudicial to the business; wilful or persistent breach of the agreement; carrying on the business only at a loss; just and equitable



On dissolution, s.38 preserves each partner’s authority so far as necessary to wind up and complete unfinished transactions, and s.44 governs the distribution of assets — the order and the rule that a loss of capital is a loss like any other, borne in the profit-sharing ratio (Chapter 4).

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
section: 7.3 Is the company insolvent? The statutory tests
text:
7.3 Is the company insolvent? The statutory tests
Section 123 IA 1986 provides the tests, and they are alternatives — satisfying any one is enough.

s.123(1)(a) — the statutory demand. A creditor owed a sum exceeding £750, then due, serves a written demand in the prescribed form at the company’s registered office, and the company for three weeks neglects to pay, secure or compound for it.
s.123(1)(b) — execution or other process on a judgment is returned unsatisfied.
s.123(1)(e) — the cash flow test. The company is unable to pay its debts as they fall due.
s.123(2) — the balance sheet test. The value of the company’s assets is less than the amount of its liabilities, taking into account its contingent and prospective liabilities.

BNY Corporate Trustee Services Ltd v Eurosail-UK 2007-3BL plc [2013] UKSC 28 held that the balance sheet test is not a mechanical exercise. The court asks whether the company has reached the “point of no return” — whether, on the balance of probabilities, it will be unable to meet its liabilities. A temporary excess of liabilities over assets in a company with a long-dated liability profile does not make it insolvent.






Exam trap



Insolvency is not a synonym for “in financial difficulty” or “in a loss-making year”. It is the satisfaction of one of the s.123 tests. Note also that the statutory demand route is a deemed inability to pay, so a company that could pay but simply has not may be wound up on it — while a company that disputes the debt on substantial grounds cannot, because the petition would be an abuse of process.

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
text:
7.4 The corporate procedures
The discriminator between them is what each is for, not their mechanics. Learn the purposes.







Procedure
What it is for




Part A1 moratorium
Breathing space: a payment holiday while a rescue is put together


Administration
Rescue, or a better outcome for creditors than winding up; comes with a strong moratorium


Company voluntary arrangement
A compromise with the unsecured creditors so that the company can continue trading


Restructuring plan
A court-sanctioned compromise that can bind dissenting classes, including secured creditors


Creditors’ voluntary liquidation
Ending an insolvent company, on the members’ initiative


Compulsory liquidation
Ending a company, usually on a creditor’s petition


Fixed charge receivership
Realising a specific charged asset for the benefit of the appointing chargee




7.4.1 The Part A1 moratorium
Introduced by the Corporate Insolvency and Governance Act 2020. A free-standing moratorium, obtained by the directors filing the relevant documents at court, which does not displace the directors: they remain in office and the company remains under their control, supervised by a monitor (a licensed insolvency practitioner) who must state that, in their view, it is likely that a moratorium would result in the rescue of the company as a going concern.
It lasts an initial 20 business days, extendable by the directors for a further 20 without creditor consent, and beyond that with creditor consent or by the court. During it the company has a payment holiday for pre-moratorium debts — but must continue to pay moratorium debts and certain excluded pre-moratorium debts, including rent for the moratorium period, wages and salary, goods and services supplied during the moratorium, and debts under financial contracts. Creditors cannot enforce security or commence proceedings without the court’s permission.


7.4.2 Administration
Administration is the principal rescue procedure, and its structure is examined closely.
The purpose (paragraph 3, Schedule B1), which is a hierarchy, not a menu:

rescuing the company as a going concern; or
achieving a better result for the company’s creditors as a whole than would be likely if the company were wound up without first being in administration; or
realising property in order to make a distribution to one or more secured or preferential creditors.

The administrator must perform their functions with the objective of (a) unless they think either that it is not reasonably practicable, or that (b) would achieve a better result for the creditors as a whole. They may pursue (c) only if they think it is not reasonably practicable to achieve (a) or (b), and they do not unnecessarily harm the interests of the creditors as a whole.
Appointment — three routes, and the differences matter:








Route
Who
Requirements




Court order (para 12)
The company, the directors, or one or more creditors
The company is or is likely to become unable to pay its debts, and the order is reasonably likely to achieve the purpose


Out of court (para 14)
A qualifying floating charge holder
A qualifying floating charge over the whole or substantially the whole of the company’s property, which is enforceable; two business days’ notice to any prior QFCH


Out of court (para 22)
The company or its directors
Five business days’ notice to any QFCH; not available if a winding-up petition is pending or an administrative receiver is in office, or if the company has been in administration on its own or its directors’ appointment in the previous 12 months



The moratorium (paragraphs 42–44) is the practical value of administration. Once an administrator is appointed — and, on an interim basis, from the filing of a notice of intention — no resolution or order may be made for winding up, no step may be taken to enforce security or to repossess goods under a hire-purchase agreement, no forfeiture by peaceable re-entry, and no legal process may be commenced or continued, without the administrator’s consent or the permission of the court.
Status and duties. The administrator is an officer of the court, acts as agent of the company, and must perform their functions in the interests of the company’s creditors as a whole. They may remove and appoint directors, and the directors may not exercise a management power without consent.
Duration: one year from appointment, extendable by consent of the creditors for up to one further year (once), or by the court for a specified period.
Distributions: the administrator may distribute to secured and preferential creditors, but needs the permission of the court to distribute to unsecured creditors (other than the prescribed part).
Exit: automatic termination after a year; conversion to a creditors’ voluntary liquidation (para 83) where there will be a distribution to unsecured creditors; dissolution (para 84) where there will not; or a court order.
Pre-pack administrations — a sale of the business negotiated before appointment and executed immediately afterwards — preserve value but are open to the objection that creditors have no say. Where the buyer is connected to the company, the administrator must either obtain the approval of the creditors or an independent written opinion from a qualified evaluator before completing the disposal in the first eight weeks.


7.4.3 Receivership
Administrative receivership is largely abolished. Section 72A of the Insolvency Act 1986, inserted by the Enterprise Act 2002, prevents the holder of a qualifying floating charge created on or after 15 September 2003 from appointing an administrative receiver, subject to narrow exceptions (capital market arrangements, public-private partnerships, utility, project finance, financial market, registered social landlord and protected railway companies). Its replacement is the QFCH’s power to appoint an administrator out of court.
Fixed charge receivership survives, and the specification names it. A fixed asset receiver (often an LPA receiver, appointed under the charge or under s.101 Law of Property Act 1925) takes control of the specific charged asset, realises it, and accounts to the appointing chargee. The receiver’s primary duty is to the appointor, not to the general body of creditors — which is precisely the difference from an administrator.


7.4.4 Company voluntary arrangement
A CVA is a composition in satisfaction of debts or a scheme of arrangement with the company’s creditors, under Part I IA 1986. It is a contractual compromise, supervised by an insolvency practitioner, that leaves the directors in control of the business.

The directors (or an administrator or liquidator) prepare the proposal with a nominee, who reports on whether it has a reasonable prospect of being approved and implemented.
The proposal goes to the creditors by a decision procedure, and to the members at a meeting.
Approval by creditors requires 75% or more in value of those responding or voting. It is invalid if more than half of the total value of creditors who are not connected with the company vote against it.
The members decide by simple majority; if the two decisions differ, the creditors’ decision prevails, subject to a member’s right to apply to court within 28 days.
Once approved, it binds every unsecured creditor entitled to vote who had notice, including those who voted against and those who did not vote at all.
It cannot affect the rights of a secured creditor to enforce their security, or the priority of a preferential debt, without that creditor’s consent.
A creditor or member may challenge it within 28 days on the ground of unfair prejudice or a material irregularity (s.6).







Exam trap



A CVA has no moratorium of its own. If the company needs protection from enforcement while the proposal is prepared, it must obtain a Part A1 moratorium or go into administration and propose the CVA from there. And a CVA cannot bind a secured creditor without consent — which is the gap that the Part 26A restructuring plan was created to fill.




7.4.5 Restructuring plan
Part 26A of the Companies Act 2006, introduced by CIGA 2020. Available where the company has encountered or is likely to encounter financial difficulties affecting its ability to carry on business as a going concern, and the plan’s purpose is to eliminate, reduce, prevent or mitigate the effect of those difficulties.
Creditors and members are divided into classes. A class approves by 75% in value of those voting (there is no majority-in-number requirement, unlike a Part 26 scheme). The court then sanctions the plan — and the distinctive feature is the cross-class cram down: the court may sanction the plan notwithstanding that a class has voted against it, if satisfied that:

members of the dissenting class would be no worse off than they would be in the relevant alternative (what would happen if the plan were not sanctioned); and
the plan has been approved by at least one class who would receive a payment, or have a genuine economic interest, in that relevant alternative.

The Court of Appeal in Re AGPS BondCo plc [2024] EWCA Civ 24 (the Adler appeal) emphasised that the cram-down power is a discretion, that the “no worse off” test is a threshold rather than the whole inquiry, and that the court will scrutinise whether the plan fairly allocates the benefits of the restructuring between classes.
Compare the Part 26 scheme of arrangement, which requires a majority in number representing 75% in value of each class and has no cram-down.


7.4.6 Liquidation
Creditors’ voluntary liquidation. Used where the company is insolvent and the members initiate the process:

The directors resolve to convene a general meeting; the members pass a special resolution to wind up voluntarily (s.84(1)(b)) and nominate a liquidator.
Within 14 days, the creditors decide on a liquidator by a decision procedure — deemed consent or a virtual meeting. The creditors’ nominee prevails over the members’.
The directors prepare a statement of affairs.
A liquidation committee may be appointed.

Compulsory liquidation. A petition to the court under s.124, presented by the company, the directors, a creditor, a contributory (a member, who must generally have held the shares for at least six of the last eighteen months), the Secretary of State, or the official receiver. The grounds are in s.122(1), and two matter:

s.122(1)(f) — the company is unable to pay its debts within s.123;
s.122(1)(g) — it is just and equitable to wind the company up (Chapter 4).

Three consequences of the order are examinable:

The winding up is deemed to commence at the presentation of the petition (s.129), not at the order.
Section 127: any disposition of the company’s property made after the presentation of the petition is void unless the court orders otherwise. This is why a company facing a petition applies for a validation order to keep trading and to keep its bank account operating.
Section 130(2): no action or proceeding may be commenced or continued against the company without the permission of the court.

The official receiver becomes liquidator on the making of the order, unless and until another is appointed.
A liquidator’s functions in any liquidation: to take control of and realise the assets, to investigate the company’s affairs and the directors’ conduct, to report to the Secretary of State on whether the directors are unfit, to pursue clawback and misfeasance claims, and to distribute in the statutory order.


7.4.7 Check yourself: procedures
Q1. A company is trading at a loss and cannot pay its trade creditors as they fall due, but the directors believe that with a few months’ protection they could sell the business as a going concern for substantially more than a break-up would realise. A creditor has threatened to present a winding-up petition.
Which procedure is most appropriate?
A. A members’ voluntary liquidation, because the directors believe the business has value.
B. A company voluntary arrangement, which will impose an immediate moratorium preventing the creditor from petitioning.
C. Administration, whose statutory purpose includes achieving a better result for creditors as a whole than winding up, and which imposes a moratorium preventing the presentation of a winding-up petition and the enforcement of security without consent or permission.
D. A creditors’ voluntary liquidation, which will preserve the business.
E. An application to strike the company off under s.1003 CA 2006.
Q2. A company proposes a CVA under which unsecured creditors will be paid 40 pence in the pound over three years. At the creditors’ decision procedure, creditors representing 78% in value of those voting support it. Of the creditors who are not connected with the company, 55% in value vote against it. A secured creditor with a fixed charge over the company’s premises did not vote and does not consent.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The CVA is approved, because 78% in value exceeds the 75% threshold, and it binds the secured creditor.
B. The CVA is not approved, because more than half of the total value of unconnected creditors voted against it.
C. The CVA is approved and binds all unsecured creditors, but not the secured creditor.
D. The CVA is approved, but only in respect of creditors who voted in favour.
E. The CVA requires the approval of 75% in number as well as in value.
Q3. A winding-up petition is presented against a company on 4 May. On 20 May, before any order is made, the company pays a supplier £30,000 for goods delivered that week and continues to draw on its bank account. A winding-up order is made on 30 June.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The payments are valid, because the winding up commenced on 30 June.
B. The payments are void under s.127 IA 1986 unless the court orders otherwise, because the winding up is deemed to have commenced on 4 May, when the petition was presented; the company should have applied for a validation order.
C. The payments are voidable as preferences under s.239.
D. The payments are valid, because they were made in the ordinary course of business.
E. The payments are void, and the court has no power to validate them.
Q4. A bank holds a qualifying floating charge over the whole of a company’s undertaking, created in 2021. The charge has become enforceable.
Which of the following may the bank do?
A. Appoint an administrative receiver, because it holds a floating charge over the whole of the undertaking.
B. Appoint an administrator out of court, having given two business days’ notice to any prior qualifying floating charge holder.
C. Present a winding-up petition without proving that the company is unable to pay its debts.
D. Appoint a fixed charge receiver over the whole of the company’s undertaking.
E. Nothing without a court order, because out-of-court appointments were abolished by the Enterprise Act 2002.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. Administration is the rescue procedure, its statutory purposes include achieving a better result for the creditors as a whole than winding up (paragraph 3(1)(b), Schedule B1), and the moratorium in paragraphs 42–44 prevents a winding-up order or resolution, the enforcement of security and the commencement of legal process without consent or the court’s permission. It is designed for exactly these facts.

A requires solvency and a declaration under s.89 that the company can pay its debts in full within 12 months, which the directors cannot make.
B is the strongest distractor: a CVA is a good tool for compromising unsecured debt, but it has no moratorium of its own. The company would need a Part A1 moratorium or an administration.
D and E both bring the company to an end without any attempt to preserve the business, and striking off is unavailable to a company that has traded in the last three months or is subject to insolvency proceedings.

Q2 — B. Approval of a CVA requires 75% or more in value of the creditors voting, and it is invalid if more than half of the total value of creditors who are not connected with the company vote against it. The 78% is satisfied but the second condition is not: 55% of unconnected creditors by value voted against.

A fails both on the second condition and on the proposition that a CVA binds a secured creditor, which it cannot without consent.
C gets the secured creditor point right but overlooks the unconnected creditor test.
D misdescribes the effect of a CVA, which binds all unsecured creditors entitled to vote who had notice.
E imports the majority-in-number requirement from a Part 26 scheme of arrangement.

Q3 — B. Section 129: in a compulsory winding up the winding up is deemed to commence at the time of the presentation of the petition. Section 127: any disposition of the company’s property after that time is void unless the court otherwise orders. Payments out of the company’s bank account are dispositions. The remedy is a validation order, applied for as soon as the petition is presented.

A takes the date of the order.
C applies the preference regime, which requires a desire to prefer a creditor and has its own time limits; s.127 operates automatically and needs no such element.
D invents an ordinary course exception, though the ordinary course of business is a factor the court weighs in deciding whether to validate.
E denies the court’s express power to order otherwise.

Q4 — B. Paragraph 14 of Schedule B1: the holder of a qualifying floating charge over the whole or substantially the whole of the company’s property may appoint an administrator out of court once the charge is enforceable, giving two business days’ notice to the holder of any prior qualifying floating charge.

A is barred by s.72A IA 1986 for floating charges created on or after 15 September 2003, subject to exceptions that do not apply to an ordinary trading company.
C requires a ground under s.122(1), which must be established.
D confuses a fixed charge receivership, which attaches to specific charged assets, with a general appointment over the undertaking.
E is the opposite of the position: out-of-court appointment of an administrator is precisely what the Enterprise Act introduced.

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
section: 7.5 Clawing assets back for the creditors
text:
7.5 Clawing assets back for the creditors
Five provisions, and the discrimination between them is the examinable skill. Two definitions first:

“Onset of insolvency” — in administration, the date on which the application or the notice of intention to appoint was filed, or the appointment took effect; in liquidation, the date of the commencement of the winding up.
“Connected person” — a director or shadow director, an associate of one, or an associate of the company. This includes relatives, spouses and civil partners, business partners, and companies under common control. The insolvency definition of “associate” is wider than the CA 2006 definition of a connected person, and includes siblings.


7.5.1 The table

7.5.2 Transactions at an undervalue (s.238)
The company made a gift, or entered into a transaction for a consideration significantly less in value than the consideration provided by the company. Compare the value in money or money’s worth on each side, from the company’s perspective.
Defence (s.238(5)): no order will be made if the company entered into the transaction in good faith and for the purpose of carrying on its business, and at the time there were reasonable grounds for believing that it would benefit the company.


7.5.3 Preferences (s.239)
The company did something which puts a creditor, a surety or a guarantor of the company’s debts into a position which, on the company’s insolvent liquidation, would be better than it would otherwise have been in — and in deciding to do it the company was influenced by a desire to produce that effect.
Re MC Bacon Ltd [1990] BCLC 324 is the case, and it is examined for two propositions:

Desire, not intention. The company must positively want to improve the creditor’s position; it is not enough that it knew that would be the consequence.
Granting security to a bank in order to secure the bank’s continued support, under commercial pressure, is not a preference: the company desired to keep trading, not to prefer the bank.

The desire is presumed where the beneficiary is a connected person — other than a person connected by reason only of being an employee — and the burden shifts to them to rebut it.






Exam trap



The two most productive fact patterns:
A director repays their own loan account shortly before liquidation. The director is a creditor, they are connected, so the look-back is two years and the desire to prefer is presumed. This is the classic preference.
A company grants a floating charge to its bank to secure an existing overdraft. That is not a transaction at an undervalue (the company gave security, not value), and it may fail the MC Bacon desire test — but s.245 catches it precisely: a floating charge given for past value is invalid, because the provision protects only value given at the same time as or after the creation of the charge.




7.5.4 Extortionate credit transactions (s.244)
A transaction providing credit to the company, entered into in the three years before the company entered administration or went into liquidation, whose terms require grossly exorbitant payments or otherwise grossly contravene ordinary principles of fair dealing. The transaction is presumed extortionate unless the contrary is proved.


7.5.5 Avoidance of floating charges (s.245)
A floating charge created within the relevant time is invalid, except to the extent of the aggregate of:

the value of money paid, or goods or services supplied, to the company;
the value of any debt of the company discharged or reduced;

in each case at the same time as, or after, the creation of the charge; plus interest on those amounts.
The relevant time is 12 months before the onset of insolvency, or two years if the charge was created in favour of a connected person. For an unconnected person, the company must in addition have been unable to pay its debts at the time of the charge or have become so in consequence of it; for a connected person, that condition does not apply.
Note what s.245 does not do: it does not avoid the debt, only the security. The lender becomes an unsecured creditor for the amount not covered.






Worked example



A company grants a floating charge to its bank on 1 March to secure its overdraft, which then stands at £400,000. Over the following months the bank advances a further £150,000. The company enters administration on 1 December of the same year. The bank is not connected with the company, and the company was unable to pay its debts on 1 March.
The charge was created within 12 months of the onset of insolvency, and the insolvency condition is satisfied. It is therefore invalid except to the extent of value given at the same time as or after its creation — the £150,000 advanced afterwards, plus interest. The security for the pre-existing £400,000 is invalid, and the bank ranks as an unsecured creditor for that sum.
Change one fact: the charge was granted to a director rather than the bank. The look-back becomes two years, and the requirement to show that the company was unable to pay its debts falls away entirely.




7.5.6 Transactions defrauding creditors (s.423)
The most flexible provision, and the one with no time limit. It requires:

a transaction at an undervalue (defined as in s.238); and
that it was entered into for the purpose of putting assets beyond the reach of a person who is making, or may at some time make, a claim against the debtor, or of otherwise prejudicing that person’s interests.

There is no insolvency requirement, no look-back period, and it applies to individuals as well as companies. The application may be made by an office-holder or by a victim of the transaction (with the court’s permission where the debtor is in liquidation or administration). The purpose need not be the sole or dominant purpose, but it must be a real, substantial purpose.
BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA [2022] UKSC 25 confirmed that a dividend, though lawfully paid, can be a transaction at an undervalue within s.423.


7.5.7 Personal liability of directors









Provision

What must be shown
Consequence

Misapplication or retention of money or property, or breach of fiduciary or other duty

s.214 wrongful trading

The company has gone into insolvent liquidation (or insolvent administration, s.246ZB), and at some point before the commencement the director knew or ought to have concluded that there was no reasonable prospect that the company would avoid it
