ss.216–217 prohibited names
Directors and shadow directors in the 12 months before insolvent liquidation
Being a director of, or concerned in the management of, a company with the same or a similar name within five years
Criminal offence and personal liability for the debts of the new company



Wrongful trading is the one that repays attention:

The standard in s.214(4) is the same dual objective/subjective standard as s.174 CA 2006: the general knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of a person carrying out those functions, and the general knowledge, skill and experience the director actually has.
The defence in s.214(3) is exacting: the director must show they took every step with a view to minimising the potential loss to the company’s creditors. Resigning is generally the wrong step; continuing to trade in the hope of a turnaround is the wrong step. Insisting on proper information, taking insolvency advice, and pressing for the company to cease trading are the right ones.
Re Produce Marketing Consortium Ltd (No 2) (1989) 5 BCC 569 — the first successful claim, and the source of the measure of contribution: the increase in the company’s net deficiency between the date the directors ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect and the date of liquidation.
Re Continental Assurance Co of London plc [2007] 2 BCLC 287 — the liquidator must show that the continued trading actually caused loss; a claim fails if the deficiency would have been the same anyway.
Re Patrick and Lyon Ltd [1933] Ch 786 sets the contrast for fraudulent trading: “actual dishonesty involving … real moral blame”. Its criminal counterpart is s.993 CA 2006, which applies whether or not the company is being wound up.







Exam trap



Fraudulent trading requires dishonesty; wrongful trading does not. Because dishonesty is hard to prove, s.214 is the practical claim, and a question describing directors who were merely over-optimistic is a wrongful trading question. Conversely, a question describing directors who took deposits for goods they knew could never be delivered is describing fraudulent trading — and note that s.213 catches any person knowingly party to it, including a solicitor or accountant.

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
text:
7.6 The order of priority
This ranking is examined directly and repays memorising. In a liquidation, the assets are applied:

Fixed charge holders, out of the proceeds of the assets subject to their charge. (Strictly, those assets are outside the estate; any surplus falls into it, and any shortfall makes the chargee an unsecured creditor for the balance.)
Expenses of the winding up, including the liquidator’s remuneration.
Preferential debts, and within them:

Ordinary preferential debts — employees’ unpaid wages for the four months before the relevant date, capped at £800 per employee; accrued holiday pay (uncapped); certain occupational pension scheme contributions; and money advanced to pay those wages.
Secondary preferential debts — HMRC in respect of VAT, PAYE, employee NICs, construction industry scheme deductions and student loan deductions, for debts arising from 1 December 2020.

The prescribed part — a fund carved out of the floating charge realisations for the unsecured creditors: 50% of the first £10,000, plus 20% of the remainder, subject to a cap of £800,000 where the floating charge was created on or after 6 April 2020 (£600,000 for earlier charges). It need not be set aside if the net property is less than £10,000 and the office-holder thinks the cost of distributing it would be disproportionate.
Floating charge holders.
Unsecured (non-preferential) creditors, pari passu.
Interest on the unsecured debts since the commencement of the winding up.
Shareholders, in accordance with the rights attaching to their shares — preference capital first if the articles so provide, then the ordinary shareholders.







Exam trap



Three points generate most of the wrong answers.
HMRC is only partly preferential. VAT, PAYE and employee NICs are secondary preferential debts, because the company collected that money from others. Corporation tax and employer’s NICs are not — they rank as ordinary unsecured debts.
Crystallisation does not promote a floating charge. A floating charge that has crystallised is still a floating charge for the purposes of this ranking. It remains behind the expenses, the preferential creditors and the prescribed part.
The prescribed part comes out of the floating charge holder’s money, not out of the fixed charge realisations, and it is for the unsecured creditors only. A floating charge holder who is left with a shortfall cannot claim a share of the prescribed part for that shortfall.

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
text:
7.7 Personal bankruptcy

7.7.1 Getting there
A creditor’s petition requires a debt (or aggregate debts) of at least £5,000, which is unsecured, for a liquidated sum, payable immediately or at a future date, and which the debtor appears unable to pay or to have no reasonable prospect of paying. Inability is usually established by serving a statutory demand which the debtor fails to comply with, or to apply to set aside, within three weeks.
A debtor no longer petitions. Since 2016 they make an online application to an adjudicator, who makes the bankruptcy order if the criteria are met.
The supervisor of, or a person bound by, an IVA may also petition.


7.7.2 The consequences
On the making of the order, the official receiver becomes trustee unless and until an insolvency practitioner is appointed. The bankrupt’s estate vests automatically in the trustee — no conveyance is needed.
The estate is all property belonging to or vested in the bankrupt at the commencement of the bankruptcy. Excluded:

tools, books, vehicles and other items of equipment necessary to the bankrupt for use personally in their employment, business or vocation;
clothing, bedding, furniture, household equipment and provisions necessary for satisfying the basic domestic needs of the bankrupt and their family;
property held by the bankrupt on trust for another;
most pension rights, and certain tenancies.

Income is not part of the estate, but the trustee may obtain an income payments order — or agree an income payments agreement — requiring the bankrupt to pay over surplus income for up to three years, leaving enough to meet the reasonable domestic needs of the bankrupt and their family.
After-acquired property may be claimed by the trustee by notice, generally within 42 days of becoming aware of it.
The family home attracts two special rules:

Section 283A: the bankrupt’s interest in a dwelling house which is the sole or principal residence of the bankrupt, their spouse or civil partner, or a former spouse or civil partner, revests in the bankrupt if the trustee takes no relevant step within three years — the “use it or lose it” rule.
Section 335A: on an application for an order for sale, the court weighs the creditors’ interests against the needs of the family; but after one year from vesting, it must assume, unless the circumstances are exceptional, that the interests of the creditors outweigh all other considerations. Exceptional circumstances are construed narrowly, and the ordinary hardship of losing a home is not enough.

Restrictions during bankruptcy: the bankrupt may not obtain credit of £500 or more without disclosing their status, may not act as a company director or be concerned in the management of a company without the court’s leave, and may not trade under a different name without disclosure.


7.7.3 Getting out
Discharge is automatic after one year (s.279), and may be earlier on the official receiver’s certificate. Discharge releases the bankrupt from most bankruptcy debts, but not from:

fines and other penalties;
obligations under a family maintenance or property order;
student loans;
damages for personal injury (unless the court orders otherwise);
debts incurred by fraud or fraudulent breach of trust.

Where the bankrupt’s conduct was culpable, the court may make a bankruptcy restrictions order, or the bankrupt may give an undertaking, for between two and fifteen years, continuing the restrictions after discharge.
Clawback in bankruptcy mirrors the corporate provisions: s.339 transactions at an undervalue (5 years), s.340 preferences (6 months, or 2 years if in favour of an associate), with the insolvency requirement presumed for associates, and s.423 transactions defrauding creditors.


7.7.4 The alternatives
Individual voluntary arrangement (Part VIII IA 1986). A composition or scheme with creditors, proposed by the debtor with a nominee and, if approved, implemented by a supervisor. The debtor may apply for an interim order giving protection from enforcement while the proposal is considered. Approval requires 75% or more in value of the creditors responding to the decision procedure, and is invalid if more than half in value of the creditors who are not associates vote against. It binds every unsecured creditor entitled to vote who had notice, and does not affect secured creditors’ rights without consent. A creditor may challenge within 28 days for unfair prejudice or material irregularity.
An IVA avoids the stigma, the restrictions and the automatic vesting of bankruptcy, and usually produces a better return for creditors — which is why it is the answer where the debtor has a continuing income or a business worth preserving.
Debt relief order. For debtors with very little: qualifying debts of £50,000 or less, assets of £2,000 or less (disregarding a single motor vehicle worth up to £4,000), and surplus monthly income of £75 or less. Applied for through an approved intermediary to the official receiver, with no fee. It imposes a 12-month moratorium, after which the qualifying debts are discharged.


7.7.5 Check yourself: insolvency and bankruptcy
Q1. Eight months before the company entered insolvent liquidation, a director procured the company to repay in full a £70,000 loan he had made to it, at a time when the company was unable to pay its debts. Other creditors received nothing.
Which of the following is correct?
A. There is no remedy, because the director was entitled to be repaid a debt genuinely owed.
B. The liquidator may apply to set the repayment aside as a preference under s.239: the director is a creditor who was put in a better position, the look-back period for a connected person is two years, and the desire to prefer is presumed.
C. The liquidator may apply under s.238, because the company received no consideration for the payment.
D. The repayment may be attacked only under s.423, because there is no time limit.
E. There is no remedy, because the payment was made more than six months before the liquidation.
Q2. A company granted a floating charge to its bank on 1 September to secure its existing overdraft of £250,000. The bank advanced no new money afterwards. The company, which was unable to pay its debts on 1 September, entered administration on 1 June the following year. The bank is unconnected with the company.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The charge is valid in full, because it was properly registered within 21 days.
B. The charge is invalid in full under s.245 IA 1986, because no money was paid, no goods or services were supplied and no debt was discharged at the same time as or after its creation; the bank ranks as an unsecured creditor for the £250,000.
C. The charge is valid, because the look-back period for an unconnected person is six months.
D. The charge is invalid, and the underlying debt of £250,000 is also extinguished.
E. The charge is valid, because the company received consideration in the form of the bank’s forbearance.
Q3. A company goes into liquidation. After paying the fixed charge holder out of the charged property and meeting the expenses of the liquidation, the liquidator has £900,000 of floating charge realisations. Employees are owed £30,000 in wages for the last four months (five employees, £6,000 each), HMRC is owed £120,000 of VAT and PAYE and £80,000 of corporation tax, and the floating charge holder is owed £2 million. Unsecured trade creditors are owed £700,000. The floating charge was created in 2023.
Which of the following correctly states the order in which the £900,000 is applied?
A. Floating charge holder in full, then anything left to the preferential creditors and then the unsecured creditors.
B. Preferential debts (employees up to £800 each, then HMRC’s VAT and PAYE), then the prescribed part for the unsecured creditors, then the floating charge holder, then the remaining unsecured creditors including HMRC’s corporation tax claim.
C. All of HMRC’s claims as preferential debts, then the employees, then the floating charge holder.
D. The unsecured creditors pari passu with the floating charge holder.
E. Employees in full, then the floating charge holder, then HMRC.
Q4. A bankrupt’s only substantial asset is a half share in the family home, in which his spouse and two young children live. Fourteen months after the bankruptcy order, the trustee applies for an order for sale. The spouse resists on the ground that the children would have to change schools.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The court will refuse an order for sale, because the interests of the children are paramount.
B. The trustee cannot apply, because the interest in the home has revested in the bankrupt.
C. Under s.335A IA 1986, more than one year having elapsed since the interest vested in the trustee, the court must assume that the interests of the creditors outweigh all other considerations unless the circumstances are exceptional; the need to change schools is unlikely to be exceptional.
D. The court will postpone sale until the youngest child reaches 18.
E. The bankrupt’s interest in a family home never forms part of the estate.
Q5. A director realises that his company has no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation. He continues trading for a further eight months, hoping for a large contract that never comes, and takes no advice. The company’s net deficiency increases by £400,000 over that period.
Which of the following is correct?
A. He is liable for fraudulent trading under s.213, because he knew the company could not pay.
B. He has a defence under s.214(3), because he honestly believed the contract would materialise.
C. He may be ordered to contribute to the company’s assets for wrongful trading under s.214: he ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation, and he did not take every step to minimise the potential loss to creditors; the measure is the increase in the net deficiency.
D. He has no liability, because a director owes duties only to the company and not to creditors.
E. He may resign to avoid liability, because s.214 applies only to directors in office at the date of liquidation.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. Section 239: the repayment put a creditor (the director) in a better position on the company’s insolvent liquidation than he would otherwise have been in. He is a connected person, so the relevant time under s.240 is two years rather than six months, and the requisite desire to prefer is presumed unless he rebuts it. The company was insolvent at the time, satisfying s.240(2).

A confuses entitlement to the debt with the propriety of paying it ahead of everyone else.
C misidentifies the provision: the company discharged a genuine liability, so it received consideration and this is not a transaction at an undervalue.
D is available in principle only if the transaction were at an undervalue, which it is not.
E applies the unconnected look-back period.

Q2 — B. Section 245. The charge was created within 12 months of the onset of insolvency and the company was unable to pay its debts at the time, so the charge is invalid except to the extent of value given at the same time as or after its creation. Nothing was given: the charge secured a past debt. The charge is therefore invalid in its entirety and the bank is unsecured for £250,000.

A confuses registration with validity. A properly registered charge can still be avoided by s.245.
C states the wrong period.
D overstates the effect: s.245 invalidates the security, not the debt.
E is the tempting commercial answer, but forbearance is not “money paid, or goods or services supplied” within s.245(2).

Q3 — B. The statutory order. Preferential debts come before the floating charge holder: the employees’ wages, but capped at £800 each (£4,000 in total, with the remaining £26,000 ranking as unsecured), and HMRC’s VAT and PAYE as secondary preferential debts. Corporation tax is not preferential and ranks as an ordinary unsecured debt. The prescribed part is then carved out of the floating charge realisations for the unsecured creditors — 50% of the first £10,000 plus 20% of the remainder, capped at £800,000. Only then does the floating charge holder take.

A inverts the whole ranking.
C treats all of HMRC’s claims as preferential and puts them ahead of the employees; ordinary preferential debts rank ahead of secondary preferential debts.
D ignores the security altogether.
E pays the employees in full, ignoring the £800 cap, and omits the prescribed part.

Q4 — C. Section 335A(3): where the application is made more than one year after the first vesting of the estate in the trustee, the court must assume, unless the circumstances of the case are exceptional, that the interests of the bankrupt’s creditors outweigh all other considerations. The ordinary consequences of a family losing its home — including disruption to children’s schooling — are not exceptional.

A applies a paramountcy principle that does not exist here.
B misapplies s.283A: revesting occurs after three years, and only if the trustee has taken no relevant step. Fourteen months is well within the period, and the application is itself a relevant step.
D describes an order the court would make only in genuinely exceptional circumstances.
E is simply wrong: the bankrupt’s beneficial interest in the home forms part of the estate.

Q5 — C. Section 214 IA 1986. The company went into insolvent liquidation; before the commencement the director knew, or ought to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding it; and he cannot show under s.214(3) that he took every step with a view to minimising the potential loss to creditors — trading on in hope, without advice, is the opposite. The contribution is measured by the increase in the net deficiency caused (Re Produce Marketing Consortium (No 2)), here £400,000, subject to the causation requirement in Re Continental Assurance.

A requires dishonesty and “real moral blame” (Re Patrick and Lyon). Misplaced optimism is not fraud.
B misstates the defence: honest belief is not the test; taking every step to minimise loss is.
D is the Sequana structural error, and in any event s.214 is a statutory liability independent of the general duties.
E is wrong: s.214 applies to a person who was a director at the relevant time, and resigning is generally not a step that minimises loss to creditors.

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
text:
7.8 The solicitor’s position
Discovering that a client company is trading while insolvent. This is the scenario the specification invites, and the answer has several strands:

Advise the directors of their duties: that the s.172 duty is now modified so that creditors’ interests must be considered (Sequana), and of the risk of personal liability under s.214, of disqualification, and of the clawback provisions.
Advise them to take specialist insolvency advice immediately, from a licensed insolvency practitioner, and to keep a written record of the board’s deliberations. The record is often the best evidence of whether they took every step to minimise loss.
Do not advise or assist a course of action that would be a fraud on creditors — disposing of assets at an undervalue, preferring a connected creditor, or continuing to take deposits for goods that cannot be supplied. Assisting knowingly makes the solicitor a party to fraudulent trading under s.213 and, in the criminal sphere, s.993 CA 2006.
Remember who the client is. The company is the client, not the directors. Where their interests diverge — as they do once personal liability is in prospect — the directors need separate advice.
Confidentiality is owed to the company and survives; it is not displaced merely because the solicitor disapproves of the directors’ conduct. The limited exceptions are narrow.
Money laundering. If the solicitor knows or suspects that property represents the proceeds of criminal conduct, the reporting obligations under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 are engaged, and tipping off is an offence.
Fees. A solicitor who takes payment from a company they know to be insolvent, in preference to other creditors, may find the payment attacked as a preference — and should consider taking money on account from a third party instead.

title: 7  Termination, insolvency and bankruptcy
text:
7.9 Chapter review
Q1. A company has ceased trading, has no assets and no liabilities, and its two directors want the cheapest way to bring it to an end. It last traded five months ago and has done nothing since except close its bank account.
Which of the following is correct?
A. It must go into members’ voluntary liquidation, because only a liquidator can dissolve a company.
B. The directors may apply to the Registrar to strike the company off under s.1003 CA 2006, having not traded for more than three months; they must send a copy of the application to every member, creditor, employee and pension trustee within seven days.
C. It must go into creditors’ voluntary liquidation, because it has ceased trading.
D. The directors may simply stop filing, and the company will be struck off automatically without further obligation.
E. Striking off is unavailable because the company has traded within the last twelve months.
Q2. Which of the following statements about the Sequana creditor duty is correct?
A. It is a free-standing duty owed directly to creditors, who may sue the directors.
B. It is engaged whenever a company has any contingent liability that might one day exceed its assets.
C. It is a modification of the s.172 duty owed to the company, engaged when the company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or when an insolvent liquidation or administration is probable, with creditors’ interests weighing more heavily as insolvency approaches.
D. It replaces the s.172 duty entirely from the moment the company makes a loss.
E. It applies only after a liquidator has been appointed.
Q3. An individual owes £46,000 to a range of creditors, has no assets beyond a car worth £3,200 and household goods, and has £60 a month of surplus income after meeting reasonable domestic needs.
Which procedure is most likely to be appropriate?
A. Bankruptcy on a creditor’s petition, since the debts exceed £5,000.
B. An individual voluntary arrangement, since 75% in value of the creditors will approve it.
C. A debt relief order: the qualifying debts are under £50,000, the assets are under £2,000 disregarding a motor vehicle worth up to £4,000, and the surplus monthly income is under £75.
D. A Part A1 moratorium.
E. A company voluntary arrangement.
Q4. A creditor is owed £4,000 by a company which has ignored every request for payment. The creditor wishes to present a winding-up petition and serves a statutory demand.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The demand is ineffective, because a company statutory demand requires a debt of at least £5,000.
B. The demand may found a petition: s.123(1)(a) requires only a debt exceeding £750, and the creditor may petition once three weeks have elapsed — though the company may restrain the petition if it disputes the debt on substantial grounds.
C. The demand is effective, but the creditor must in addition prove that the company is balance sheet insolvent under s.123(2).
D. The creditor must first obtain judgment against the company before serving a statutory demand.
E. The demand is effective only if it is served personally on a director of the company.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. Section 1003 CA 2006 permits a company to apply to be struck off provided it has not, in the previous three months, traded, changed its name, disposed of property for value held for disposal in the normal course of trading, or engaged in any other activity except one necessary for the application or for concluding its affairs. Five months since trading satisfies that. Section 1006 requires the copy application to go to members, creditors, employees, non-signing directors and pension trustees within seven days.

A and C impose a liquidation that is unnecessary where there are no assets and no liabilities.
D describes what may happen in practice but ignores the application procedure and the directors’ obligations, and exposes them to filing offences and disqualification under s.3 CDDA.
E applies the wrong period; the bar is three months, not twelve.

Q2 — C. BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA [2022] UKSC 25.

A is the recurring structural error; the duty is owed to the company.
B applies the “real risk” trigger the Supreme Court rejected.
D and E state the wrong trigger points; the duty modifies s.172 rather than replacing it, and it operates before any office-holder is appointed.

Q3 — C. The DRO criteria are met on every limb: qualifying debts of £50,000 or less, assets of £2,000 or less disregarding a single motor vehicle worth up to £4,000, and surplus monthly income of £75 or less. A DRO costs nothing and produces discharge after a 12-month moratorium.

A is available to a creditor but is disproportionate and would recover almost nothing.
B presupposes an outcome and, with £60 a month, offers creditors very little.
D and E are corporate procedures and are not available to an individual.

Q4 — B. Section 123(1)(a) requires a debt exceeding £750, and £4,000 does. The £5,000 threshold belongs to a bankruptcy petition against an individual, and that contrast is what the question is testing. The qualification in option B is real: a company that disputes the debt on substantial grounds can restrain the petition as an abuse of process, so a statutory demand is the wrong tool for a genuinely disputed debt.

A imports the bankruptcy threshold.
C treats the s.123 tests as cumulative. They are alternatives: satisfying s.123(1)(a) is enough, and the balance sheet test need not also be proved.
D invents a judgment requirement; the statutory demand exists precisely so that judgment is not needed.
E invents a service requirement. Section 123(1)(a) requires the demand to be served by leaving it at the company’s registered office.

text:

Candidates are required to apply relevant core legal principles and rules appropriately and effectively, at the level of a competent newly qualified solicitor in practice, to realistic client-based and ethical problems and situations in the following areas:
Candidates must demonstrate their ability to act honestly and with integrity and in accordance with the Statement of Solicitor Competence, the SRA Principles and the Code of Conduct.

title: 8  Dispute Resolution: what is examined
section: 8.2 The examinable content, in the SRA’s own words
text:
8.2 The examinable content, in the SRA’s own words
Different options for dispute resolution — the characteristics of arbitration, mediation and litigation which make them an appropriate mechanism to resolve a dispute.
Resolving a dispute through a civil claim — preliminary considerations: limitation, pre-action protocols; parties and causes of action; calculating limitation periods for claims in contract and tort; Practice Direction – Pre-action Conduct; principles and purpose of pre-action protocols governing particular claims and consequences for failure to follow their terms; applicable law — mechanisms to determine which country’s laws apply to a contractual or tortious claim issued in the courts of England and Wales; jurisdiction — mechanisms to determine jurisdiction over an international contractual or tortious claim.
Where to start proceedings — allocation of business between the High Court and the County Court; jurisdiction of the specialist courts.
Issuing and serving proceedings — issuing a claim form; adding, removing or substituting parties; service of a claim form within the jurisdiction; procedure for service outside the jurisdiction (with or without the court’s permission) and mechanisms for effecting valid service in another jurisdiction; deemed dates of service and time limits for serving proceedings; service by an alternative method.
Responding to a claim — admitting the claim; acknowledging service and filing a defence and/or counterclaim; disputing the court’s jurisdiction; entering and setting aside judgment in default; discontinuance and settlement; time limits for responding to a claim.
Statements of case — purpose, structure and content of a claim form, particulars of claim, or defence relating to a claim in contract or tort; purpose, structure and content of a reply, Part 20 claim, or defence to Part 20 claim; requests for further information; amendments.
Interim applications — procedure for making an application; purpose, procedure and evidence required for summary judgment, interim payments and interim injunctions.
Case management — the overriding objective; track allocation; case management directions for cases proceeding on the fast or multi-tracks; non-compliance with orders, sanctions and relief; costs and case management conferences.
Evidence — relevance, hearsay and admissibility; the burden and standard of proof; expert evidence (opinion evidence, duties of experts, single joint experts, discussion between experts); witness evidence (witness statements, affidavits).
Disclosure and inspection — standard disclosure; orders for disclosure; specific disclosure; pre-action and non-party disclosure; electronic disclosure; privilege and without prejudice communications; waiver of privilege.
Trial — summoning witnesses; preparations for trial (purpose of pre-trial checklists and hearings; purpose of trial bundles); trial procedure; the nature and effect of judgment.
Costs — costs management and budgeting; inter-partes costs orders (interim and final); non-party costs; qualified one-way costs shifting; Part 36 and other offers; security for costs; fixed and assessed costs.
Appeals — permission; destination of appeals; grounds for appeals.
Enforcement of money judgments — oral examination; methods of enforcement; procedure and mechanisms for effecting valid enforcement in another jurisdiction.






Exam trap



Notice what the specification does not say. There is no mention of the small claims track procedure in detail, of family or criminal procedure, or of judicial review. And notice what it does say that candidates routinely skip: applicable law and jurisdiction, non-party costs, enforcement abroad, and destination of appeals. Those four are small topics with a high question-per-page ratio, precisely because they are neglected.

section: 8.4 The shape of a civil claim
text:
8.4 The shape of a civil claim
Almost every Dispute Resolution question sits at one point on this timeline. Locating the question on it is usually half the work.







Stage
What happens




Analysis
Cause of action, parties, limitation, evidence, merits, funding, the defendant’s ability to pay


Pre-action
Letter of claim, response, disclosure, ADR — under the relevant protocol or the Practice Direction


Issue
Claim form issued; limitation stops


Service
Claim form served within 4 months (6 outside the jurisdiction); particulars of claim


Response
Acknowledgment of service within 14 days; defence within 14 or 28 days; counterclaim; or default judgment


Allocation
Directions questionnaire; allocation to the small claims, fast, intermediate or multi-track


Case management
Directions; costs budgets on the multi-track; CMC or CCMC; interim applications


Disclosure
Lists of documents; inspection; privilege


Evidence
Exchange of witness statements; expert reports; experts’ discussions


Pre-trial
Pre-trial checklists; pre-trial review; trial bundle


Trial
Openings, evidence, submissions, judgment, costs


After
Appeal (21 days); enforcement

title: 8  Dispute Resolution: what is examined
section: 8.5 Six ideas that decide most questions
text:
8.5 Six ideas that decide most questions
Limitation stops on issue, not service. The claim is brought when the claim form is received by the court, not when it is sealed and not when it reaches the defendant.
The court’s permission is the hinge. Service out, adding a party after limitation, amending after limitation, relief from sanctions, expert evidence, an appeal, distributing to unsecured creditors — each turns on whether permission is needed and on what test.
Every deadline has a consequence. Miss the deadline for filing a defence and the claimant may enter default judgment. Miss the deadline for a costs budget and you are treated as having filed one comprising only the court fees. Miss the deadline for service of the claim form and, in most cases, the claim is over.
Track allocation drives everything downstream. It decides the directions, the extent of expert evidence, the trial length, whether costs are budgeted, and whether costs are fixed or assessed.
Costs are a weapon, not an afterthought. Part 36, budgets, indemnity costs and QOCS are examined as tactical instruments, because that is how they are used.
Conduct is embedded. The duty not to mislead the court, the limits on what a solicitor may do with a client’s untruthful instructions, and the rules on undertakings surface constantly in litigation scenarios.
crumbs: 8  Dispute Resolution: what is examined

title: 8  Dispute Resolution: what is examined
text:
8.6 Check yourself
Q1. Which of the following is not part of the examinable content for Dispute Resolution?
A. The mechanisms for determining which country’s law applies to a tortious claim issued in the courts of England and Wales.
B. The grounds on which permission to appeal may be granted.
C. The procedure for applying for judicial review of a decision of a public body.
D. Qualified one-way costs shifting.
E. Pre-action and non-party disclosure.
Q2. A solicitor is asked at what point in the life of a claim the limitation clock is stopped.
Which of the following is correct?
A. When the letter of claim is sent under the relevant pre-action protocol.
B. When the claim form is received by the court.
C. When the claim form is sealed and issued by the court.
D. When the claim form is served on the defendant.
E. When the particulars of claim are served.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. Judicial review is not within the Dispute Resolution content list. Constitutional and administrative law appears elsewhere in FLK1, but the procedural machinery of judicial review is not examined here. Each of the other four is named expressly in the specification.
Q2 — B. For limitation purposes a claim is brought when the claim form is received by the court office, not when it is issued. Practice Direction 7A makes this explicit, and it matters because a claim form delivered on the last day of the limitation period but not sealed until several days later is still in time.

A confuses the protocol stage with the commencement of proceedings; a letter of claim does not stop time.
C is the near-miss and the answer most candidates give. Issue is when proceedings start for the purposes of CPR 7.2; receipt is what stops the limitation clock.
D and E are later still — service can lawfully occur four months after issue.

title: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum
text:
9.1 Analysing the merits
Before a solicitor advises anyone to sue, six questions have to be answered. A question that asks “what should the solicitor advise?” is usually testing whether you worked through them in order.
crumbs: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum

title: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum
text:
9.1.1 1. Is there a cause of action?
Identify the legal wrong and its elements, then check that the facts supply each one.







Cause of action
Elements to establish




Breach of contract
A contract existed (offer, acceptance, consideration, intention, certainty); its terms; breach of a term; causation; loss not too remote


Negligence
Duty of care; breach; causation (factual and legal); loss of a recognised kind, not too remote


Other torts
The elements of the specific tort — nuisance, Rylands v Fletcher, occupiers’ liability, product liability


Debt
A liquidated sum due under a contract; no need to prove loss, and no duty to mitigate









Exam trap



A claim for a debt is not a claim for damages. The claimant need not prove loss, need not mitigate, and remoteness is irrelevant. That difference decides whether a defendant’s “you could have sold the goods elsewhere” argument goes anywhere, and it decides whether the claim is for a specified or an unspecified sum on the claim form.




9.1.2 2. Who are the correct parties?
Getting this wrong is expensive, because correcting it after limitation has expired requires the court’s permission on a restrictive test (Chapter 11).







Defendant
Named as




Individual
Full name


Sole trader
“Name trading as Business Name”


Partnership
The firm name, where the partners carried on business in that name when the cause of action accrued


Company
Its full registered name, with “Limited” or “plc”


LLP
Its full registered name


Deceased person’s estate
The personal representatives


Child or protected party
Through a litigation friend



Also consider: is there more than one potential defendant? Are they jointly and severally liable, so that the claimant may sue any of them for the whole? Is there a claim for a contribution under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978 — for which the limitation period is two years from the judgment or settlement fixing the contributor’s liability?


9.1.3 3. Is the claim in time?
Limitation is dealt with fully in Chapter 10. It comes second in the analysis only because you cannot date the accrual of a cause of action until you have identified it.


9.1.4 4. Can it be proved?
The burden is on the party who asserts, and the standard is the balance of probabilities. Ask what documents exist, who the witnesses are, whether expert evidence will be needed and whether the court will permit it, and what the other side is likely to disclose.


9.1.5 5. Is the defendant worth suing?
A judgment is worthless against a defendant with no assets. Before proceedings, check whether the defendant is a company still on the register and filing accounts, whether it is subject to insolvency proceedings, whether it owns land, and whether there is insurance or a guarantor. Advising a client to litigate against a shell company without raising this is a competence failure, not a tactical one.


9.1.6 6. What will it cost, and who pays?

The costs risk. The general rule is that the unsuccessful party pays the successful party’s costs (CPR 44.2(2)(a)), and a claimant who loses will face a bill for the other side’s costs as well as its own.
Funding options: private retainer; conditional fee agreement (CFA), with a success fee that is not recoverable from the losing party; damages-based agreement (DBA); before- or after-the-event insurance; third party litigation funding; legal expenses insurance; trade union funding.
Recovery is never complete. On the standard basis a successful party typically recovers around 60–70% of what it has actually spent, and on the fast and intermediate tracks recovery is fixed by the regime in CPR Part 45 regardless of what was spent.







Third party funding after PACCAR



In R (PACCAR Inc) v Competition Appeal Tribunal [2023] UKSC 28 the Supreme Court held that a litigation funding agreement under which the funder’s return was calculated as a share of the damages was a damages-based agreement — and therefore unenforceable unless it complied with the DBA Regulations. The funding market responded by restructuring agreements to calculate the return by reference to a multiple of the funding provided rather than a share of the recovery. Legislation to reverse the decision has been under consideration; check the position at your sitting’s cut-off before treating any reform as in force.
crumbs: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum

title: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum
text:
9.2 Choosing the forum
The specification asks for “the characteristics of arbitration, mediation and litigation which make them an appropriate mechanism to resolve a dispute”. That is a comparison question, and it is best learned as a table plus a set of discriminating facts.

9.2.1 The comparison










Litigation
Arbitration
Mediation




Nature
Adjudicative, by the state
Adjudicative, by a private tribunal
Facilitative — the mediator does not decide anything


Consent
None needed; a claimant may sue
Requires an arbitration agreement
Requires agreement to mediate (but the court may now order the parties to engage)


Outcome
Judgment, binding and enforceable
Award, binding and enforceable
No outcome unless the parties settle; a settlement binds as a contract


Who decides
A judge assigned by the court
An arbitrator chosen by the parties, often with technical expertise
Nobody


Privacy
Public — hearings and judgments are public
Private and confidential
Private and without prejudice


Procedure
The CPR
Whatever the parties agree, subject to the Arbitration Act 1996
Entirely flexible


Speed
Slow; often 18 months to trial or more
Variable; can be slow in complex cases
Days, and often a single session


Cost
High, but the court itself is subsidised
High — the parties pay the arbitrators and the venue
Low


Appeal
Available with permission
Very limited — ss.67–69 Arbitration Act 1996
Not applicable


Third parties
Can be joined
Cannot be joined without consent
Can attend by agreement


Relationship
Adversarial; usually destroys it
Adversarial, but less publicly
Preserves it


Enforcement abroad
Depends on treaties; patchy
Excellent — the New York Convention, with over 170 states
Only as a contract





9.2.2 The discriminating facts
Exam questions signal the answer through the facts. Learn the signals.
Points to mediation: the parties have an ongoing commercial relationship they want to preserve; the dispute involves emotion or reputation as much as money; the sums are modest relative to the costs; the parties want a creative outcome a court could not order (an apology, a new supply contract, a payment plan); speed matters; confidentiality matters.
Points to arbitration: the contract already contains an arbitration clause; the dispute is technical and the parties want a decision-maker who understands the subject; the parties are in different countries and enforcement will be needed abroad; confidentiality is essential; finality is wanted, with no long appeal process.
Points to litigation: there is no agreement to arbitrate or mediate and the other side will not engage; the claimant needs a precedent or a public vindication; the claim needs a remedy only a court can give — an injunction against a third party, a freezing order, or default judgment; a third party must be joined; the claim is a straightforward debt where summary judgment is likely; the limitation period is about to expire.






Exam trap



Two errors recur. First, candidates describe mediation as producing a “binding decision”. It does not: the mediator has no power to decide. What binds is the settlement agreement the parties sign, and until they sign, either can walk away. Second, candidates treat an arbitration clause as optional. It is not: if the contract contains one, the court will normally stay court proceedings brought in breach of it under s.9 of the Arbitration Act 1996, unless the arbitration agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed.




9.2.3 Arbitration in a little more detail
Arbitration in England and Wales is governed by the Arbitration Act 1996.

Founded on agreement. Section 6: an arbitration agreement is an agreement to submit present or future disputes to arbitration. It is separable from the contract containing it (s.7), so a challenge to the validity of the main contract does not of itself destroy the arbitration agreement.
Party autonomy. Section 1 sets out the principles: the object is the fair resolution of disputes by an impartial tribunal without unnecessary delay or expense; the parties are free to agree how their disputes are resolved, subject to safeguards in the public interest; and the court should not intervene except as provided by the Act.
The stay. Section 9: a party to an arbitration agreement against whom court proceedings are brought may apply for a stay, and the court must grant it unless satisfied that the agreement is null and void, inoperative, or incapable of being performed.
The tribunal. The parties choose the number of arbitrators and the method of appointment (ss.15–16); the tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction (s.30 — competence-competence).
The award is final and binding (s.58) and enforceable with the court’s permission as if it were a judgment (s.66).
Challenges are narrow: s.67 (substantive jurisdiction), s.68 (serious irregularity causing substantial injustice), and s.69 (appeal on a point of law, which the parties may exclude by agreement and which in any event requires permission).







The Arbitration Act 2025 — verify against your cut-off



The Arbitration Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 24 February 2025 and its substantive amendments to the 1996 Act came into force on 1 August 2025, applying to arbitrations and related court proceedings commenced on or after that date. The main changes:

Governing law of the arbitration agreement: where the parties have not expressly chosen it, the law of the seat applies — reversing the previous common law default.
Summary disposal: a new s.39A empowers a tribunal, on a party’s application, to make an award on a summary basis where a party has no real prospect of succeeding on a claim, defence or issue.
Arbitrator’s duty of disclosure: a statutory duty to disclose circumstances that might reasonably give rise to justifiable doubts as to impartiality.
Section 44 orders may be made against third parties.
Emergency arbitrators are expressly recognised where the parties have adopted rules providing for them.
Section 67 challenges to jurisdiction are restricted, so that a party that participated in the arbitration cannot generally run new evidence or new grounds on a full rehearing.

Check whether this is within your examinable law cut-off. If it is, note that the 1996 Act remains the governing statute — the 2025 Act amends it rather than replacing it.




9.2.4 Mediation, and the court’s power to compel it
Mediation is a facilitated negotiation. A neutral third party helps the parties reach their own settlement; the mediator has no power to impose one. Sessions are conducted without prejudice and under a confidentiality agreement, so what is said cannot later be put before the court.
The law here moved decisively, and it is the most likely ADR question on the paper.

Halsey v Milton Keynes General NHS Trust [2004] EWCA Civ 576 held — or was long read as holding — that to oblige unwilling parties to mediate would obstruct their right of access to the court under Article 6 ECHR. It also established that a successful party who unreasonably refuses ADR may be penalised in costs, and set out the factors: the nature of the dispute, the merits, the extent of other settlement attempts, whether the costs of ADR would be disproportionately high, delay, and whether ADR had a reasonable prospect of success.
Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council [2023] EWCA Civ 1416 held that the passage in Halsey was not binding, and that the court can lawfully stay proceedings and order the parties to engage in a non-court-based dispute resolution process — provided the order does not impair the claimant’s right to a judicial hearing, and is proportionate to the legitimate aim of settling the dispute fairly, quickly and at reasonable cost.
The CPR were amended on 1 October 2024 to reflect this. The overriding objective now expressly includes “promoting or using alternative dispute resolution” (CPR 1.1(2)(f)), and active case management includes “ordering or encouraging the parties to use, and facilitating the use of, alternative dispute resolution” (CPR 1.4(2)(e)). Corresponding changes were made to the court’s powers on allocation and directions.
Separately, since 22 May 2024, mediation through the free Small Claims Mediation Service has been compulsory for most Part 7 money claims allocated to the small claims track with a value up to £10,000.







Exam trap



An option that says “the court cannot compel the parties to mediate, because that would breach Article 6” states the pre-Churchill position and is wrong. But do not overcorrect: the court still cannot compel the parties to settle, and the refusal-to-mediate costs sanction in Halsey survives — what Churchill changed is the court’s power to order engagement with a process.
crumbs: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum

title: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum
section: 9.3 The solicitor’s duty to advise on ADR
text:
9.3 The solicitor’s duty to advise on ADR
A solicitor must advise the client on the options for resolving the dispute, and must do so at the outset and keep it under review. This is not merely good practice:

The Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols requires the parties to consider whether negotiation or some other form of ADR may enable settlement, and warns that the court may require evidence that the parties considered it.
Costs consequences follow from an unreasonable refusal (Halsey), and the court may now order engagement (Churchill).
Under the Code of Conduct, a solicitor must provide a competent service and must give the client information in a way they can understand, so that the client can make informed decisions — including about the costs and risks of litigating rather than settling.







Exam trap



The client decides whether to mediate; the solicitor advises. But a solicitor who fails to raise ADR at all, or who advises that a refusal carries no risk, has given negligent advice. The right answer in a scenario where the client says “I want my day in court” is usually that the solicitor should advise on the costs risk of refusing, record the advice, and — if the client persists — act on instructions, not that the solicitor must refuse to act or must mediate anyway.
crumbs: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum

title: 9  Analysing the dispute and choosing the forum
text:
9.4 Check yourself
Q1. Two companies have traded together for fifteen years. A dispute has arisen over the quality of goods supplied under the most recent order, worth £60,000. Both wish to continue trading together. The supply contract contains no dispute resolution clause. The buyer’s solicitor is asked to advise on the most appropriate mechanism.
Which of the following is the best advice?
A. Arbitration, because the dispute is technical and an arbitrator can be chosen for their expertise.
B. Litigation, because only a court can order the supplier to pay.
C. Mediation, because it is quick and inexpensive, is confidential, allows a commercially creative outcome, and is the mechanism most likely to preserve the trading relationship — and the parties remain free to litigate if it fails.
D. Arbitration, because the parties can be compelled to arbitrate under s.9 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
E. Litigation, because there is no arbitration agreement and the court will not permit mediation without one.
Q2. A contract between an English company and a German company contains a clause providing that all disputes shall be referred to arbitration in London. The German company nevertheless issues proceedings in the High Court in London. The English company wishes to hold it to the arbitration clause.
What should the English company do, and what is the likely outcome?
A. File a defence and ask the court to transfer the claim to arbitration.
B. Apply under s.9 of the Arbitration Act 1996 for a stay of the court proceedings; the court must grant the stay unless satisfied that the arbitration agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed.
C. Apply for summary judgment, because the claim is bound to fail.
D. Do nothing, because the arbitration clause automatically deprives the court of jurisdiction.
E. Apply to strike the claim out under CPR 3.4 as an abuse of process.
Q3. A defendant in a multi-track claim refuses the claimant’s repeated invitations to mediate, giving no reason. The defendant wins at trial.
Which of the following best describes the court’s approach to costs?
A. The defendant will recover its costs in full, because the successful party is always entitled to its costs.
B. The court has no power to take a refusal to mediate into account.
C. The court may reduce or disallow part of the successful defendant’s costs if the refusal was unreasonable, applying the factors in Halsey; and since 1 October 2024 the overriding objective expressly includes promoting or using alternative dispute resolution.
D. The defendant will be ordered to pay the claimant’s costs, because it refused to mediate.
E. The refusal is irrelevant, because mediation is voluntary and cannot be ordered.
Q4. A client asks whether a mediator will decide who is right.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The mediator will make a binding determination, which may be appealed only on a point of law.
B. The mediator will make a recommendation which becomes binding after 21 days unless rejected.
C. The mediator has no power to decide the dispute; the process is facilitative, and any outcome takes effect as a settlement contract between the parties.
D. The mediator will make a binding determination unless the parties agree otherwise in advance.
E. The mediator will decide the dispute, but the decision is enforceable only if the court approves it.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — C. Every fact in the question points to mediation: a long-standing relationship both sides want to preserve, a modest sum relative to litigation costs, and no dispute resolution clause forcing another route. Mediation is confidential, cheap, fast, and can produce outcomes a court cannot order — a credit note, a revised specification, a continuing supply arrangement. Crucially, it costs the client nothing in rights: if it fails, litigation remains available.

A is a plausible distractor, but arbitration requires an agreement, and there is none. The parties could agree to arbitrate now, but that is slower, more expensive and no better at preserving the relationship.
B and E overstate the case for litigation. A mediated settlement is enforceable as a contract, and can be converted into a consent order.
D inverts s.9, which allows a party to stay court proceedings brought in breach of an arbitration agreement. It cannot create an obligation to arbitrate where none was agreed.

Q2 — B. Section 9 Arbitration Act 1996. A party to an arbitration agreement against whom proceedings are brought in respect of a matter within that agreement may apply for a stay, and the court must grant it unless satisfied that the agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed. The stay is mandatory, not discretionary.

A is doubly wrong: there is no mechanism to “transfer” a claim to arbitration, and filing a defence risks being treated as a step in the proceedings, which bars a s.9 application.
C and E attack the merits or the propriety of the claim; the objection is to the forum.
D overstates the effect: an arbitration clause does not deprive the court of jurisdiction automatically. The defendant must apply, and must do so before taking a step in the proceedings.

Q3 — C. Halsey v Milton Keynes General NHS Trust established that a successful party who unreasonably refuses ADR may be deprived of some or all of its costs, and set out the factors for assessing reasonableness. The 1 October 2024 amendments strengthened the position by writing “promoting or using alternative dispute resolution” into CPR 1.1(2)(f) and the case management duty into CPR 1.4(2)(e).

A overstates CPR 44.2(2)(a): costs follow the event, but “the court may make a different order”, and conduct is an express factor under 44.2(4)(a).
B and E deny a power the court plainly has — and E additionally states the pre-Churchill position.
D goes too far the other way. The usual sanction is a reduction in or disallowance of the successful party’s costs, not a reversal of the costs order.

Q4 — C. Mediation is facilitative. The mediator helps the parties negotiate but has no adjudicative power. If the parties reach terms, those terms bind as a contract, and are commonly recorded in a settlement agreement or a consent or Tomlin order. Until then either party may walk away.

A and D describe arbitration.
B describes something closer to early neutral evaluation or expert determination with a contractual acceptance mechanism, and in any event misstates it.
E invents a court approval requirement.
