title: 10  Before proceedings
text:
10.1 Limitation
Limitation is the first thing a litigator checks and the last thing they can fix. It is examined by calculation, so learn the period, the trigger date, and the exceptions.

title: 10  Before proceedings
text:
10.1.1 The periods









Claim
Period
Runs from
Provision




Simple contract
6 years
The date of breach
s.5 Limitation Act 1980


Contract under deed (specialty)
12 years
The date of breach
s.8


Tort generally
6 years
The date the cause of action accrued — for negligence, when damage is suffered
s.2


Negligence causing latent damage (not personal injury)
6 years from accrual or 3 years from the starting date, whichever expires later — subject to a 15-year longstop
Knowledge of the material facts about the damage
ss.14A, 14B


Personal injury
3 years
The later of the date of accrual and the claimant’s date of knowledge
ss.11, 14


Fatal accidents
3 years
The later of the date of death and the dependant’s date of knowledge
s.12


Defective products (Consumer Protection Act 1987)
3 years, with a 10-year longstop from when the product was put into circulation
Damage or knowledge
s.11A


Contribution between wrongdoers
2 years
The judgment or settlement fixing the liability to be contributed to
s.10


Recovery of land
12 years
Accrual
s.15









Exam trap



For a contract claim, time runs from the breach — not from when the claimant discovered it, and not from when the loss was suffered. For a tort claim in negligence, time runs from when damage occurs, which may be much later than the negligent act. A question that gives you a negligently drafted document, a breach years later, and damage later still is testing exactly this: the contract claim may be statute-barred while the tortious claim is alive.




10.1.2 Knowledge, and the extensions
Date of knowledge (s.14) for a personal injury claim: the date on which the claimant first knew that the injury was significant, that it was attributable in whole or in part to the act or omission alleged to constitute negligence, and the identity of the defendant. Knowledge includes what the claimant might reasonably have been expected to acquire, including from expert advice it was reasonable to seek. Knowledge that, as a matter of law, the act amounted to negligence is irrelevant.
Section 14A applies the same idea to other negligence claims: the claimant gets the longer of six years from accrual, or three years from the date they had both the knowledge required to bring the action and the right to bring it — subject to the absolute 15-year longstop in s.14B, which runs from the negligent act or omission and applies even if the claimant never had knowledge.
Section 28 — disability. If the claimant was a child or lacked capacity when the cause of action accrued, time does not begin to run until the disability ends: a child’s period therefore runs from their 18th birthday, so a child injured at seven has until their 21st birthday to bring a personal injury claim. Supervening disability does not stop the clock.
Section 32 — fraud, concealment and mistake. Where the action is based on the defendant’s fraud, where a fact relevant to the claimant’s right of action has been deliberately concealed by the defendant, or where the action is for relief from the consequences of a mistake, time does not begin to run until the claimant has discovered the fraud, concealment or mistake, or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it.
Sections 29–31 — acknowledgment and part payment. In a claim for a debt or other liquidated sum, a written, signed acknowledgment of the debt, or a part payment, restarts the six-year clock — but cannot revive a claim already statute-barred.
Section 33 — the discretion. In personal injury and fatal accident claims only, the court has an equitable discretion to disapply the primary limitation period where it is equitable to do so, having regard to the prejudice to each party and to the s.33(3) factors: the length of and reasons for the delay, the effect of the delay on the cogency of the evidence, the defendant’s conduct after the cause of action arose, the duration of any disability, how promptly the claimant acted once they knew, and the steps the claimant took to obtain advice.






Exam trap



Section 33 is confined to personal injury and fatal accident claims. There is no general judicial discretion to extend limitation in a contract or property claim, however sympathetic the facts. An option offering the court a discretion to disapply the six-year contract period is always wrong.




10.1.3 How limitation operates

It is a procedural defence. It bars the remedy, not the right, and it must be pleaded in the defence — the court will not take the point of its own motion. (Conversion under s.3 and land under s.17 are the exceptions, where title is extinguished.)
The claim is brought when the claim form is received by the court office, not when it is sealed. Practice Direction 7A says so, and a claim form delivered on the last day is in time even if it is issued days later.
If the period is about to expire and the pre-action protocol has not been complied with, the claimant should issue to protect the position and then invite the court to stay the proceedings so that the protocol steps can be completed.
Parties may agree a standstill agreement to suspend time while they negotiate. Draft it carefully: an agreement that merely says the parties “will not take a limitation point” is a contractual promise, not an extension.

title: 10  Before proceedings
section: 10.2 Practice Direction – Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols
text:
10.2 Practice Direction – Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols
Where no approved protocol covers the dispute, the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols applies. Its aims (para 3) are that the parties should:

understand each other’s position;
make decisions about how to proceed;
try to settle the issues without proceedings;
consider a form of ADR;
support the efficient management of proceedings; and
reduce the costs of resolving the dispute.


10.2.1 The steps
Paragraph 6 sets out what the parties should do where no protocol applies:

The claimant writes to the defendant with concise details of the claim — the basis on which it is made, a summary of the facts, what the claimant wants from the defendant, and, if money, how the amount is calculated.
The defendant responds within a reasonable time — 14 days in a straightforward case, and no more than three months in a very complex one — saying whether the claim is accepted and, if not, the reasons, together with an explanation of which facts and parts of the claim are disputed and whether the defendant is making a counterclaim.
The parties disclose key documents relevant to the issues in dispute.
The parties consider ADR.

Paragraph 4 imposes proportionality: the steps taken must be proportionate, and the Practice Direction must not be used as a tactical device to generate costs or to gain an unfair advantage.


10.2.2 ADR and the last resort principle
Litigation is a last resort (para 8). The parties should consider whether negotiation or another form of ADR might enable them to settle, and the court may require evidence that the parties considered it. Silence in response to an invitation to participate may itself be unreasonable and may lead to a costs sanction.


10.2.3 Non-compliance and its consequences
The court will look at whether the parties have complied in substance; minor or technical failures are not penalised. Where there has been a significant failure, the court may:

stay the proceedings while the missed steps are taken;
order the party at fault to pay costs, in whole or in part;
order those costs on the indemnity basis;
if the party at fault is a claimant who has been awarded a sum of money, deprive it of interest or award interest at a lower rate;
if the party at fault is a defendant ordered to pay a sum of money, award interest at a rate up to 10% above base rate.







Exam trap



Failure to comply with a protocol does not invalidate the claim, and it is not a ground for striking out. The sanctions are about costs and interest, and occasionally a stay. An option saying the claim will be struck out because the claimant did not send a letter before claim is wrong.




10.2.4 The approved protocols
Where an approved protocol applies, it displaces the Practice Direction’s generic steps. Those most likely to appear:







Protocol
Distinctive features




Personal Injury
Letter of claim in two copies (one for insurers); defendant has 21 days to acknowledge and 3 months thereafter to investigate and state whether liability is admitted; agreed expert procedure with the claimant nominating names


Debt Claims
Applies where a business claims from an individual. Letter of claim with an information sheet, reply form and financial statement; the debtor has 30 days to respond; a further 30 days if documents are requested; the creditor must give 14 days’ notice before issuing


Professional Negligence
Preliminary notice; letter of claim; the professional has 21 days to acknowledge and 3 months to investigate and provide a letter of response and/or settlement


Construction and Engineering
Letter of claim, response, and a pre-action meeting


Clinical Disputes
Request for records; letter of claim; 4 months to respond



Each shares a common shape — letter of claim, acknowledgment, substantive response, disclosure of key documents, consideration of ADR — and each attaches its own timetable. The structure is examinable; the individual timetables less so, except for the debt claims protocol, which is distinctive because it protects consumers.

title: 10  Before proceedings
text:
10.3 Applicable law
Which country’s law governs the dispute is decided by assimilated versions of the Rome I and Rome II Regulations, which continue to apply in England and Wales after Brexit.

10.3.1 Contract: Rome I
Article 3 — party choice. The contract is governed by the law chosen by the parties. The choice must be express or clearly demonstrated by the terms or the circumstances. Parties may choose the law for the whole or part of the contract, and may change it.
Article 4 — no choice. A cascade:

Specific rules by contract type:







Contract
Governing law




Sale of goods
The seller’s habitual residence


Provision of services
The service provider’s habitual residence


A right in rem in, or a tenancy of, immovable property
Where the property is situated


Franchise
The franchisee’s habitual residence


Distribution
The distributor’s habitual residence


Sale of goods by auction
Where the auction takes place



Otherwise, or where the contract falls into more than one category: the law of the country where the party required to effect the characteristic performance has their habitual residence.
Escape clause (Art 4(3)): if it is clear from all the circumstances that the contract is manifestly more closely connected with another country, that country’s law applies.
Failing all of that (Art 4(4)): the law of the country with which it is most closely connected.

Protective rules. Article 6 (consumer contracts) and Article 8 (individual employment contracts) provide that a choice of law cannot deprive the consumer of the protection of the mandatory rules of their habitual residence, or the employee of the mandatory rules of the country where they habitually work. Article 9 preserves the overriding mandatory provisions of the forum, and Article 21 allows the court to refuse to apply a foreign rule that is manifestly incompatible with public policy.
For a company, “habitual residence” means its place of central administration; for a person acting in the course of business, their principal place of business.


10.3.2 Tort: Rome II
Article 4(1) — the general rule. The applicable law is that of the country in which the damage occurs, irrespective of the country in which the event giving rise to the damage occurred, and irrespective of the countries in which the indirect consequences of that event occur.
Article 4(2). If, at the time the damage occurs, both the person claimed to be liable and the person sustaining damage have their habitual residence in the same country, the law of that country applies instead.
Article 4(3) — escape clause. If the tort is manifestly more closely connected with another country, that country’s law applies. A pre-existing relationship between the parties, such as a contract, is expressly identified as capable of establishing that connection.
Article 14 — choice. The parties may choose the applicable law: after the event giving rise to the damage, or before it if all the parties are pursuing a commercial activity and the agreement is freely negotiated.
Special regimes: product liability (Art 5, a cascade), unfair competition (Art 6), environmental damage (Art 7, where the claimant may elect for the law of the country in which the event occurred), and intellectual property (Art 8, the law of the country for which protection is claimed, with no freedom to choose).






Exam trap



Article 4(1) is counter-intuitive and reliably tested. The law is that of the place where the damage occurs, not where the wrongful act was committed. A defective component made negligently in France and fitted to a machine that injures a worker in England produces English law under Art 4(1) — unless Art 4(2) or Art 4(3) displaces it. Note also that Rome II excludes defamation and privacy, for which the common law rules apply.

title: 10  Before proceedings
text:
10.4 Jurisdiction
Since the end of the transition period the Brussels Recast Regulation no longer applies to proceedings commenced in England and Wales. Three regimes now matter.

10.4.1 Hague 2005 — exclusive choice of court agreements
Where a contract contains an exclusive jurisdiction clause in favour of the courts of a contracting state, the 2005 Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements requires the chosen court to hear the case and other contracting states to decline. The contracting parties include the EU, the UK, Mexico, Singapore and Montenegro. The Convention does not cover asymmetric (one-sided) clauses on the prevailing view, and does not cover non-exclusive clauses.


10.4.2 Hague 2019 — recognition and enforcement
The 2019 Hague Judgments Convention entered into force for the United Kingdom on 1 July 2025, applying to judgments arising out of proceedings issued on or after that date. It provides a treaty basis for the recognition and enforcement of judgments between contracting states — the EU, Ukraine, Uruguay, Albania and Montenegro among them — and is significantly wider than Hague 2005 because it is not confined to exclusive jurisdiction clauses.


10.4.3 The common law rules
Where neither Convention applies, the English court’s jurisdiction depends on service.
Defendant within the jurisdiction. Service of the claim form on a defendant present in England and Wales founds jurisdiction as of right. The defendant’s remedy is to apply for a stay on the ground of forum non conveniens.
Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460 supplies the test: the court will stay proceedings if the defendant shows that there is another available forum which is clearly or distinctly more appropriate — the “natural forum”, with which the action has the most real and substantial connection. The burden then shifts to the claimant to show that justice nevertheless requires the trial to take place in England.
Defendant outside the jurisdiction. The claimant needs the court’s permission to serve out (CPR 6.36), unless one of the exceptions in CPR 6.32–6.33 applies — most importantly where the contract contains a term to the effect that the English court shall have jurisdiction, or where jurisdiction arises under Hague 2005.
To obtain permission, the claimant must establish three things:

A good arguable case that the claim falls within one of the gateways in Practice Direction 6B, paragraph 3.1;
A serious issue to be tried on the merits — a real prospect of success; and
That England is the proper place in which to bring the claim (forum conveniens).

The gateways most often examined:







Category
Gateway




General
The defendant is domiciled within the jurisdiction; a claim for an injunction ordering the defendant to do or refrain from doing an act within the jurisdiction; the defendant is a necessary or proper party to a claim against another defendant


Contract
The contract was made within the jurisdiction; made by or through an agent within the jurisdiction; is governed by English law; contains a term conferring English jurisdiction; or the breach was committed within the jurisdiction


Tort
Damage was or will be sustained within the jurisdiction; or the damage results from an act committed, or likely to be committed, within the jurisdiction



FS Cairo (Nile Plaza) LLC v Brownlie [2021] UKSC 45 confirmed that “damage” in the tort gateway bears its ordinary meaning and covers any significant damage sustained in England — including continuing pain and financial loss suffered here after an accident abroad. The gateway is broad; the real filter is the third requirement, forum conveniens.






Exam trap



Keep the three limbs separate. Satisfying a gateway is not enough: the claimant must also show a serious issue to be tried and that England is the proper place. And keep jurisdiction separate from applicable law — an English court can and often does apply foreign law, so the fact that French law governs a contract does not deprive the English court of jurisdiction.

title: 10  Before proceedings
text:
10.5 Where to start proceedings

10.5.1 High Court or County Court
Practice Direction 7A allocates business between them:







Claim
Where it may be started




Money claim (not personal injury) of £100,000 or less
County Court only


Money claim of more than £100,000
County Court or High Court


Personal injury claim worth less than £50,000
County Court only


Personal injury claim worth £50,000 or more
County Court or High Court



A claimant issuing in the High Court must state in the claim form that it expects to recover more than £100,000 (or, for personal injury, £50,000 or more), or that an enactment requires the claim to be started in the High Court, or that the claim is to proceed in a specialist High Court list.
Beyond value, the factors pointing to the High Court are the financial value and amount in dispute, the complexity of the facts, legal issues, remedies or procedures, and the importance of the outcome to the public in general.
A case started in the wrong court is not a nullity: the court may transfer it (ss.40–42 County Courts Act 1984), and may penalise the claimant in costs for starting in the High Court unnecessarily.


10.5.2 The divisions and the specialist courts
The High Court has three divisions: the King’s Bench Division (contract and tort, including most commercial disputes and personal injury), the Chancery Division (business, property, trusts, land, intellectual property, companies and insolvency), and the Family Division.
The Business and Property Courts are an umbrella for the specialist lists:







Court or list
Business




Commercial Court (KBD)
National and international commercial disputes — sale of goods, insurance, banking, shipping


Circuit Commercial Courts
Commercial claims of lower value, outside London


Technology and Construction Court (KBD)
Building and engineering disputes, professional negligence against construction professionals, IT disputes


Admiralty Court (KBD)
Shipping, collisions, salvage


Financial List
Financial markets claims of £50 million or more, or requiring market expertise


Intellectual Property Enterprise Court (Chancery)
Lower-value IP claims, with a £500,000 damages cap and recoverable costs capped at £60,000 on liability and £30,000 on quantum


Companies, Insolvency, Competition, Property, Trusts, Revenue lists
As their names suggest

title: 10  Before proceedings
text:
10.6 The solicitor’s position
Advising on limitation. A missed limitation period is the archetypal negligence claim against a litigation solicitor. The date must be calculated and diarised at the outset, and where it is close the right course is to issue protectively rather than to complete the protocol.
Not taking unfair advantage. A solicitor must not take unfair advantage of a third party, which constrains the tone and content of a letter before claim to a litigant in person: threatening consequences that cannot follow, or asserting a claim known to be bad, breaches the Code of Conduct. The SRA warning notice on SLAPPs — strategic lawsuits against public participation — is expressly flagged in the assessment specification, and identifies aggressive pre-action correspondence designed to silence rather than to resolve as a conduct risk.
Confidentiality in pre-action correspondence. A letter marked “without prejudice” is protected only if it is a genuine attempt to settle a dispute; the label alone does not create the privilege, and labelling an open assertion of claim “without prejudice” does not make it so.
Undertakings. Any undertaking given in pre-action correspondence — to preserve documents, to hold funds, not to issue before a date — is personally binding on the solicitor and enforceable by the court. Give none that is not within your control.

title: 10  Before proceedings
text:
10.7 Check yourself
Q1. A surveyor negligently valued a property on 1 March 2018. The claimant relied on the valuation and bought the property on 1 June 2018, suffering an immediate loss. The claimant did not discover the negligence until 1 September 2024, when a second survey revealed it. The claimant consults a solicitor on 1 October 2026. There is no contract under deed.
Which of the following is correct?
A. Both the contract and the tort claims are statute-barred, and no extension is available.
B. The contract claim is statute-barred, but the tortious claim may be brought under s.14A of the Limitation Act 1980, which gives the claimant three years from the date of knowledge, expiring on 1 September 2027, subject to the 15-year longstop in s.14B.
C. Both claims remain in time, because time did not begin to run until the negligence was discovered.
D. The court may exercise its discretion under s.33 to disapply the limitation period.
E. The tortious claim is statute-barred, but the contract claim remains in time because a contract claim runs from the date of discovery.
Q2. An English company sells machinery to a Spanish company. The contract contains no choice of law clause and no jurisdiction clause. A dispute arises about whether the machinery conformed to the contract.
Which law governs the contract?
A. Spanish law, because the buyer is Spanish and the goods were delivered there.
B. English law, because the seller has its habitual residence in England and the contract is one for the sale of goods.
C. The law of the country with which the contract is most closely connected, which will always be that of the place of delivery.
D. English law, because proceedings would be issued in England.
E. There is no applicable law until the parties agree one.
Q3. A claimant is injured in a road accident in Portugal caused by the negligent driving of another English resident, who was also on holiday there. Both are habitually resident in England. The claimant issues proceedings in England.
Which law applies to the tort?
A. Portuguese law, under Article 4(1) of Rome II, because that is where the damage occurred.
B. English law, under Article 4(2) of Rome II, because both parties were habitually resident in the same country when the damage occurred.
C. English law, because the claim was issued in England and the forum applies its own law.
D. Portuguese law, because the event giving rise to the damage occurred there and Article 4(1) looks to the place of the event.
E. The claimant may choose which law applies.
Q4. A claimant issues a claim for £85,000 for breach of a commercial supply contract, with no personal injury element, in the High Court.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The claim is properly issued, because a claim for more than £50,000 may be issued in the High Court.
B. The claim should have been started in the County Court, because a money claim of £100,000 or less may only be started there; the court may transfer it and may penalise the claimant in costs.
C. The claim is a nullity and must be reissued.
D. The claim is properly issued, because commercial claims may always be issued in the High Court.
E. The claim should have been issued in the Commercial Court.
Q5. A defendant fails to respond at all to a letter of claim sent under the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols, and ignores an invitation to mediate. Proceedings are issued and the defendant ultimately succeeds at trial.
Which of the following is the most likely consequence of the defendant’s pre-action conduct?
A. The claim will be struck out for failure to comply with the Practice Direction.
B. There is no consequence, because the defendant won.
C. The court may take the non-compliance into account in exercising its discretion as to costs, and may reduce or disallow part of the successful defendant’s costs or order costs on a different basis.
D. The defendant will be ordered to pay interest at up to 10% above base rate.
E. The court must order a stay of the proceedings.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. The contract claim accrued on breach — the negligent valuation on 1 March 2018 — so the six-year period under s.5 expired on 1 March 2024. The tortious claim accrued when damage was suffered on 1 June 2018, so the primary six-year period under s.2 expired on 1 June 2024. But s.14A gives the claimant the longer of six years from accrual and three years from the date of knowledge. Knowledge came on 1 September 2024, so the claim may be brought until 1 September 2027 — comfortably covering a consultation in October 2026. The s.14B 15-year longstop runs from the negligent act (1 March 2018) and does not expire until 2033.

A overlooks s.14A entirely.
C applies a discoverability rule to the contract claim, where none exists.
D applies s.33, which is confined to personal injury and fatal accident claims.
E reverses the position: it is the tort claim that benefits from the knowledge extension, not the contract claim.

Q2 — B. Rome I, Article 4(1)(a): in the absence of choice, a contract for the sale of goods is governed by the law of the country where the seller has their habitual residence. The seller is English, so English law applies. (For a company, habitual residence means its place of central administration.)

A applies the buyer’s law, which is the opposite of the rule.
C skips the specific rules in Art 4(1) and goes straight to a closest-connection test, and then states it inflexibly. Article 4(3) is an escape clause requiring a manifestly closer connection.
D confuses jurisdiction with applicable law. An English court frequently applies foreign law.
E is simply wrong: Rome I supplies the answer where the parties have not.

Q3 — B. Rome II, Article 4(2): where both the person claimed to be liable and the person sustaining damage are habitually resident in the same country when the damage occurs, the law of that country applies instead of the Art 4(1) rule. Both are habitually resident in England, so English law governs — including on quantification of damages.

A and D apply Art 4(1) without checking Art 4(2), and D additionally misstates Art 4(1), which looks to where the damage occurs, not the event.
C assumes the forum applies its own law, which is what the Rome Regulations exist to prevent.
E offers a unilateral choice that exists only under Art 7 (environmental damage). Article 14 requires agreement.

Q4 — B. Practice Direction 7A: proceedings may only be started in the High Court if the value of the claim exceeds £100,000 (or, for personal injury, is £50,000 or more). £85,000 is below the threshold, so the claim belongs in the County Court.

A applies the personal injury threshold to a non-personal injury claim.
C overstates the consequence: starting in the wrong court is an irregularity, not a nullity. The court may transfer under s.40 County Courts Act 1984.
D invents a rule; the Commercial Court has its own criteria and the value here is far below what it would ordinarily take.
E compounds the error.

Q5 — C. Non-compliance with the Practice Direction is taken into account in the exercise of the court’s costs discretion (CPR 44.2(4)(a) — conduct, including conduct before proceedings). The court may reduce or disallow part of the successful party’s costs, or award costs on the indemnity basis against the party at fault. Ignoring an invitation to mediate compounds the point: silence in response to such an invitation may itself be unreasonable.

A overstates the sanction; failure to comply with a protocol does not invalidate or defeat a claim.
B ignores the court’s power to deprive even a successful party of costs for its conduct.
D applies a sanction available against a defendant ordered to pay a sum of money — this defendant won and pays nothing.
E describes a discretionary remedy, and one directed at incomplete protocol steps before trial, not at a defendant who has already succeeded.

title: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding
text:
11.1 Issuing the claim form
Proceedings are started when the court issues a claim form at the claimant’s request (CPR 7.2) — but for limitation purposes the claim is brought when the claim form is received by the court office. Both propositions matter, and they answer different questions.
The Part 7 procedure is the standard route for a disputed claim. Part 8 is for claims where there is unlikely to be a substantial dispute of fact, and where the rules require or permit it.
crumbs: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding

title: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding
text:
11.1.1 The claim form (N1)
CPR 16.2 requires the claim form to:

name the parties correctly;
contain a concise statement of the nature of the claim;
specify the remedy sought — though the court may grant a remedy the claimant has not asked for;
where money is claimed, contain a statement of value (CPR 16.3): the amount claimed, or a statement that the claimant expects to recover not more than £10,000, more than £10,000 but not more than £25,000, more than £25,000 but not more than £100,000, or more than £100,000 — and, if issued in the High Court, why the claimant is entitled to issue there;
be verified by a statement of truth.

The court fee is calculated on the value claimed, so pleading the claim too high is expensive and pleading it too low caps recovery.


11.1.2 Naming the parties







Defendant
Named as




Individual
Full name, with title


Sole trader
“Name trading as Business Name”


Partnership
The firm name, where the partners carried on business under it when the cause of action accrued


Company
The full registered name, including “Limited” or “plc”


LLP
The full registered name


Child or protected party
By or through a litigation friend


Estate
The personal representatives, or if none, an order appointing a person to represent the estate





11.1.3 Adding, removing and substituting parties
CPR 19.2: the court may remove, add or substitute a party where it is desirable so that the court can resolve all matters in dispute, or where there is an issue between an existing party and the new party which it is desirable to resolve.
CPR 19.4: the court’s permission is required to add or substitute a party after the claim form has been served. Before service, the claimant may amend as of right.
CPR 19.6 — after limitation has expired. This is the restrictive rule, and it is examined. The court may add or substitute a party only if:

the relevant limitation period was current when the proceedings were started; and
the addition or substitution is necessary.

It is “necessary” only if the court is satisfied that:

the new party is to be substituted for a party who was named in the claim form by mistake for the new party;
the claim cannot properly be carried on by or against the original party unless the new party is added or substituted; or
the original party has died or had a bankruptcy order made against them and their interest or liability has passed to the new party.







Exam trap



The mistake limb in CPR 19.6(3)(a) covers a mistake as to name, not a change of mind about who to sue. Naming “ABC Trading Ltd” when the contracting party was “ABC Trading (Northern) Ltd” is a mistake. Deciding, after limitation has expired, that you should have sued the director personally as well as the company is not — that is a new claim against a new party, and CPR 19.6 will not permit it.
crumbs: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding

title: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding
text:
11.2 Serving the claim form

11.2.1 The time limit
CPR 7.5: the claimant must complete the step required by 12.00 midnight on the calendar day four months after the date of issue of the claim form. Where the claim form is to be served out of the jurisdiction, the period is six months (CPR 7.5(2)).
The “step required” depends on the method:







Method
Step required




First class post, DX or other next business day delivery
Posting, leaving with, delivering to or collection by the relevant service provider


Delivery to or leaving at a permitted address
Delivering to or leaving the document at the relevant place


Personal service under CPR 6.5
Leaving it with the individual


Electronic method
Sending the email or other transmission









Exam trap



Under CPR 7.5 the claimant must complete the step, not achieve service, within four months. Posting the claim form by first class post on the last day is compliant even though deemed service falls afterwards. This is the single most frequently misunderstood rule in the service topic.




11.2.2 Extending time for service
CPR 7.6. An application to extend must generally be made within the period for service. If made after it has expired, the court may only extend if:

the court has failed to serve the claim form; or
the claimant has taken all reasonable steps to comply with CPR 7.5 but has been unable to do so; and
in either case, the claimant has acted promptly in making the application.

This is deliberately severe, because an extension after limitation has expired deprives the defendant of an accrued limitation defence.


11.2.3 The methods and the address
CPR 6.3 — permitted methods: personal service; first class post, DX or other next business day delivery service; leaving it at a specified place; fax or other means of electronic communication; or any method authorised by the court.






Exam trap



Service by email is valid only where the party to be served, or their solicitor, has indicated in writing that they are willing to accept service by that means and given an address for it. In Barton v Wright Hassall LLP [2018] UKSC 12 a litigant in person emailed the claim form to the defendant’s solicitors on the last day, without having established their willingness to accept email service. The Supreme Court refused to validate it retrospectively under CPR 6.15(2), and the claim was lost.


Who to serve (CPR 6.7): if the defendant has given in writing the business address of a solicitor authorised to accept service, the claim form must be served on that solicitor. Otherwise CPR 6.9 supplies the place:







Defendant
Place of service




Individual
Usual or last known residence


Individual being sued in the name of a business
Usual or last known residence, or the principal or last known place of business


Partnership sued in the firm name
Usual or last known residence of a partner, or the principal or last known place of business of the partnership


Company registered in England and Wales
The principal office, or any place of business having a real connection with the claim



A company may alternatively be served at its registered office under s.1139 Companies Act 2006.


11.2.4 Deemed service
CPR 6.14 — the claim form. A claim form served within the United Kingdom is deemed to be served on the second business day after completion of the relevant step under CPR 7.5(1). There is a single rule and no method-by-method table, whatever the actual date of delivery.
CPR 6.26 — every other document. Here there is a table:







Method
Deemed date of service




First class post, DX or other next business day delivery
The second day after posting, if that is a business day; otherwise the next business day after that day


Delivering to or leaving at a permitted address
If before 4.30 p.m. on a business day, that day; otherwise the next business day


Personal service
Same rule as above


Fax
Same rule as above


Other electronic method
Same rule as above









Worked example



A claim form is issued on Monday 4 May. The claimant posts it by first class post on Friday 28 August.
Is service in time? The four-month period expires at midnight on 4 September. The step required for postal service is posting, which happened on 28 August. Service is in time.
When is it deemed served? CPR 6.14: the second business day after completion of the step. Posting was Friday; the first business day after is Monday 31 August, the second is Tuesday 1 September. Deemed service is Tuesday 1 September, whatever day it actually arrived.
When is the defence due? Fourteen days from service of the particulars of claim. If the particulars were served with the claim form, an acknowledgment of service or defence is due by 15 September; filing an acknowledgment extends the defence to 29 September.




11.2.5 Service by an alternative method
CPR 6.15. Where there is a good reason, the court may authorise service by a method or at a place not otherwise permitted. Under CPR 6.15(2) it may also, on the same test, order that steps already taken to bring the claim form to the defendant’s attention are to be treated as good service. The order must specify the method, the deemed date of service, and the period for responding.


11.2.6 Service out of the jurisdiction
Two routes, and the distinction decides the question:
Without permission (CPR 6.32–6.33). Available where the English court has power to determine the claim under the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982, where the contract contains a term to the effect that the English court shall have jurisdiction, or under the Hague 2005 Convention.
With permission (CPR 6.36). The claimant must satisfy the three requirements set out in Chapter 10: a good arguable case within a PD 6B gateway, a serious issue to be tried, and that England is the proper place. The application is made without notice, supported by evidence, and the claimant owes a duty of full and frank disclosure.
Mechanics abroad. Service may be effected through the foreign government or judicial authority or the British consular authority (CPR 6.42), through a Hague Service Convention channel where the destination state is a party, or by any method permitted by the law of the country in which service is to be effected (CPR 6.40(3)) — but never by a method that is contrary to that country’s law. The period for responding is extended by PD 6B according to the destination.

title: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding
text:
11.3 Statements of case

11.3.1 Particulars of claim
CPR 16.4: a concise statement of the facts on which the claimant relies; a claim for interest if any, with the basis and, for a specified sum, the percentage rate, the dates from and to which it is claimed and the daily rate; any claim for aggravated or exemplary damages or provisional damages; and a statement of truth.
The particulars must be served with the claim form or within 14 days after service of the claim form (CPR 7.4), and in any event within the four-month period for serving the claim form.
The content follows the cause of action:







Contract claim
Tort (negligence) claim




The status of the parties
The status of the parties


The contract: date, parties, whether written or oral, consideration
The facts giving rise to a duty of care


The terms relied on, express or implied
The duty owed


Performance by the claimant
The acts or omissions constituting breach


The breach, with particulars
Causation


Causation and loss, with a schedule of loss
The damage, with a schedule of loss


Interest
Interest





11.3.2 Defence
CPR 16.5 requires the defendant to state, in relation to each allegation, whether it is:

denied — and if so, the defendant must state the reasons for the denial and, if putting forward a different version of events, state that version;
admitted; or
neither admitted nor denied, because the defendant is unable to admit or deny it and requires the claimant to prove it.

Failure to deal with an allegation is a deemed admission — except that a defendant who fails to deal with an allegation but has set out the nature of their case in relation to the issue is taken to require it to be proved, and a defendant who fails to deal with an allegation about the amount of money claimed is taken to require it to be proved. The defence must dispute the claimant’s statement of value if the defendant disputes it, and must give its own.
The defence must also plead any positive case and any limitation defence, and must be verified by a statement of truth.


11.3.3 Reply, Part 20 claims and further information
Reply (CPR 16.7). Optional. A claimant who does not file one is not taken to admit the matters raised in the defence. A reply is needed to answer a positive case in the defence that the particulars of claim do not already address.
Additional claims under Part 20:







Claim
Permission needed?




Counterclaim against the claimant
No, if filed with the defence; otherwise yes (CPR 20.4)


Counterclaim against a person other than the claimant
Yes (CPR 20.5)


Claim for contribution or indemnity against a co-defendant
No, if filed with the defence, or within 28 days of a party being added (CPR 20.6)


Any other additional claim — for example against a third party
No, if issued before or at the same time as the defence is filed; otherwise yes (CPR 20.7)



An additional claim is treated as a claim in its own right, and Part 20 applies the ordinary rules to it with modifications.
Further information (CPR 18). A party may serve a written request for clarification of any matter in dispute or additional information about it, giving a date for response. If the other party does not comply, an application may be made. The request must be concise and strictly confined to what is reasonably necessary and proportionate.


11.3.4 Amendments
CPR 17.1: a party may amend a statement of case at any time before it has been served on any other party. After service, amendment requires the written consent of all the other parties or the permission of the court.
CPR 17.4 — amendment after limitation has expired. Where the relevant limitation period was current when the proceedings started, the court may allow an amendment only:

to add or substitute a new claim arising out of the same facts or substantially the same facts as a claim already made; or
to correct a mistake as to the name of a party, where the mistake was genuine and not one which would cause reasonable doubt as to the identity of the party; or
to alter the capacity in which a party claims.

The court will also consider whether the amendment is in accordance with the overriding objective — lateness, the effect on the trial date and the costs consequences all bear on the discretion.


11.3.5 The statement of truth
Every statement of case must be verified by a statement of truth. Since April 2020 the prescribed wording is:

I believe that the facts stated in this [document] are true. I understand that proceedings for contempt of court may be brought against anyone who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth.

It may be signed by the party, by a person with authority (for a company, a person holding a senior position, who must state which), or by the party’s legal representative — who signs on the party’s behalf and must have the party’s authority and have explained the consequences.






Exam trap



A solicitor may sign a statement of truth on the client’s behalf, but may never verify a statement the solicitor knows or believes to be false. Where the client insists on advancing an account the solicitor knows to be untrue, the solicitor must not draft or sign it, and will usually have to cease to act — without disclosing the reason, because the reason is confidential.
crumbs: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding

title: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding
text:
11.4 Responding to a claim

11.4.1 The time limits







Step
Time limit




Acknowledgment of service
14 days after service of the particulars of claim (CPR 10.3)


Defence, where no acknowledgment filed
14 days after service of the particulars of claim (CPR 15.4)


Defence, where an acknowledgment has been filed
28 days after service of the particulars of claim


Agreed extension of the defence
Up to a further 28 days, by agreement, notifying the court in writing (CPR 15.5) — so a maximum of 56 days without a court order


Application disputing jurisdiction
14 days after filing the acknowledgment of service (CPR 11)





11.4.2 The options
Admit (Part 14). The defendant may admit the whole or part of the claim. For a specified sum, the claimant may then obtain judgment; the defendant may ask for time to pay, and the rate of payment is determined by the court or by agreement.
Defend. File an acknowledgment of service and/or a defence, and consider a counterclaim.
Dispute the court’s jurisdiction (Part 11). The defendant must first file an acknowledgment of service — filing one is not a submission to the jurisdiction — and then apply within 14 days. If the defendant files a defence without applying, they are treated as having accepted that the court has jurisdiction.
Do nothing — and face default judgment.






Exam trap



To challenge jurisdiction, the defendant must acknowledge service and then apply within 14 days. Doing nothing loses the point (default judgment follows) and filing a defence loses it too (submission). The acknowledgment of service form has a tick box for “I intend to contest jurisdiction” precisely for this purpose.




11.4.3 Default judgment
Part 12. The claimant may obtain judgment in default where the defendant has failed to file an acknowledgment of service or a defence, and the time for doing so has expired. It is entered administratively on request for a specified sum, and on application otherwise.
Default judgment is not available where:

the claim is under Part 8;
the defendant has applied for summary judgment or to have the claim struck out, and the application has not been disposed of;
the defendant has satisfied the claim; or
the defendant has admitted the claim and applied for time to pay.

Setting aside (Part 13):

CPR 13.2 — mandatory. The court must set the judgment aside if it was wrongly entered — because the time for responding had not in fact expired, or the claim had been satisfied, or the defendant had filed an acknowledgment or defence in time.
CPR 13.3 — discretionary. The court may set it aside if the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending the claim, or if it appears to the court that there is some other good reason why the judgment should be set aside or the defendant should be allowed to defend. On any such application the court must have regard to whether the application was made promptly.







Worked example



Particulars of claim are deemed served on 1 October. The defendant, who has been abroad, files nothing. On 20 October the claimant enters default judgment. The defendant returns on 5 November, and applies to set the judgment aside on 20 December, saying the goods were defective.
Was the judgment properly entered? The defence was due by 15 October and nothing was filed, so yes. CPR 13.2 does not apply.
Will it be set aside? Only under CPR 13.3, and the defendant must show a real prospect of successfully defending — a defective goods defence may well qualify. But the court must have regard to promptness, and a six-week delay after returning is a serious obstacle. On these facts the application may fail on delay alone, and if it succeeds the defendant will almost certainly bear the costs thrown away.




11.4.4 Discontinuance and settlement
Discontinuance (Part 38). The claimant may discontinue at any time by filing and serving a notice of discontinuance. Permission is required where the court has granted an interim injunction or where any party has given an undertaking to the court, or where the claimant has received an interim payment. Where there is more than one claimant, the consent of the others or the court’s permission is needed. Unless the court orders otherwise, the claimant is liable for the defendant’s costs to the date of discontinuance (CPR 38.6).
Settlement may be recorded by:

a consent order, where the terms are to be enforceable as an order of the court and there is nothing confidential;
a Tomlin order — an order staying the proceedings on agreed terms set out in a schedule, with permission to apply for the purpose of carrying those terms into effect. The schedule is not part of the order and need not be a matter of public record, which is why it is used where the terms are confidential or go beyond what the court could order;
acceptance of a Part 36 offer, which stays the claim automatically; or
a simple settlement agreement, with the claim then discontinued.

title: 11  Issuing, serving, pleading and responding
text:
11.5 Check yourself
Q1. A claim form is issued on 3 March. On 30 June the claimant’s solicitor posts it to the defendant’s solicitors, who are authorised in writing to accept service, by first class post. It arrives on 2 July.
Which of the following is correct?
A. Service is out of time, because the claim form was not received by the defendant’s solicitors within four months of issue.
B. Service is in time: the step required for postal service is posting, which was completed on 30 June, within four months of issue; the claim form is deemed served on the second business day after posting.
C. Service is in time, and the claim form is deemed served on the day it arrived, 2 July.
D. Service is out of time, because service on solicitors is not permitted.
E. Service is in time, and the claim form is deemed served on the day it was posted, 30 June.
Q2. Particulars of claim are deemed served on a defendant on Tuesday 6 October. The defendant files an acknowledgment of service on 15 October, indicating an intention to defend.
By when must the defence be filed, assuming no agreement or order extending time?
A. 20 October, being 14 days after the acknowledgment of service.
B. 20 October, being 14 days after service of the particulars of claim.
C. 3 November, being 28 days after service of the particulars of claim.
D. 12 November, being 28 days after the acknowledgment of service.
E. 1 December, being 56 days after service of the particulars of claim.
Q3. A claimant sued “Northgate Logistics Limited”. The contracting party was in fact “Northgate Logistics (UK) Limited”, a different company in the same group with a similar name. The limitation period expired two months after the claim form was issued. The claimant now applies to substitute the correct company.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The application must be refused, because the limitation period has expired.
B. The application may be granted under CPR 19.6 if the limitation period was current when the proceedings were started and the substitution is necessary — which it is where the new party is being substituted for a party named in the claim form by mistake for the new party.
C. The application may be granted as of right, because the claim form has not yet been amended.
D. The application must be refused, because the claimant chose to sue a different legal person and that is not a mistake as to name.
E. The claimant must issue fresh proceedings and rely on s.33 of the Limitation Act 1980.
Q4. A defendant based in Germany is served with an English claim form. The defendant believes the English court has no jurisdiction because the contract contains an exclusive German jurisdiction clause.
What must the defendant do to preserve the point?
A. File a defence setting out the jurisdiction objection.
B. Write to the court explaining that it does not accept jurisdiction, and take no further step.
C. File an acknowledgment of service indicating an intention to contest jurisdiction, and apply under Part 11 within 14 days after filing it.
D. Apply for summary judgment under Part 24.
E. Ignore the proceedings, because a foreign defendant cannot be bound by an English judgment.
Q5. A defendant, having filed a defence, wishes to bring a claim for an indemnity against a sub-contractor who is not a party to the proceedings. The defence was filed three weeks ago.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The defendant may issue the additional claim without permission at any time.
B. The defendant requires the court’s permission, because the additional claim was not issued before or at the same time as the defence was filed.
C. The defendant may only bring the claim in separate proceedings.
D. The defendant requires the consent of the claimant.
E. The defendant may issue the additional claim without permission because it is a claim for an indemnity.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. CPR 7.5(1): the claimant must complete the step required within four months of issue, and for first class post that step is posting. Posting on 30 June, from a claim form issued on 3 March, is within four months. Deemed service under CPR 6.14 is the second business day after completion of the step, regardless of actual delivery.

A and D apply the wrong test: what matters is the step, not receipt, and CPR 6.7 requires service on a solicitor authorised in writing to accept it.
C applies the actual date of delivery. CPR 6.14 is a deeming provision and the real date is irrelevant.
E deems service on the day of the step, which is what CPR 6.14 expressly does not do.

Q2 — C. CPR 15.4(1)(b): where the defendant files an acknowledgment of service, the defence must be filed 28 days after service of the particulars of claim — not 28 days after the acknowledgment. Twenty-eight days from 6 October is 3 November.

A and D run time from the acknowledgment, which is the classic error.
B applies the 14-day period that operates only where no acknowledgment is filed.
E applies the maximum available with an agreed extension under CPR 15.5, which the facts exclude.

Q3 — B. CPR 19.6. The limitation period was current when the proceedings were started, and substitution is “necessary” under CPR 19.6(3)(a) where the new party is to be substituted for a party named in the claim form by mistake for the new party. Suing the wrong company in a group because of a similar name is a classic mistake as to identity of this kind, provided the mistake was genuine and would not cause reasonable doubt as to who was intended.

A treats the expiry of limitation as an absolute bar, which CPR 19.6 exists to qualify.
C ignores the need for permission after service and the special rule after limitation.
D is the strongest distractor, and would be right if the claimant had deliberately sued one legal person and later changed its mind. Here the intention was always to sue the contracting party.
E applies s.33, which is available only in personal injury and fatal accident claims.

Q4 — C. CPR Part 11. The defendant must file an acknowledgment of service — which is not a submission to the jurisdiction — and then apply for an order declaring that the court has no jurisdiction, or should not exercise it, within 14 days after filing the acknowledgment.

A is fatal: filing a defence without making the application means the defendant is treated as having accepted that the court has jurisdiction.
B and E invite default judgment.
D attacks the merits, not the forum, and engaging with the merits risks submission.

Q5 — B. CPR 20.7(3): an additional claim other than a counterclaim against the claimant or a claim for contribution or indemnity against an existing co-defendant may be made without permission only if it is issued before or at the same time as the defendant files their defence. The defence was filed three weeks ago, so permission is required.

A and E overlook the timing condition. Note the distinction being tested: CPR 20.6 allows a contribution or indemnity claim against an existing co-defendant without permission if filed with the defence; this sub-contractor is not yet a party, so CPR 20.7 applies.
C is wrong: Part 20 exists so that related claims can be tried together.
D requires a consent the rules do not call for.
