title: 12  Running the claim
text:
12.1 The overriding objective
CPR 1.1(1): the Rules are a new procedural code with the overriding objective of enabling the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost.
CPR 1.1(2): dealing with a case justly and at proportionate cost includes, so far as is practicable:
CPR 1.2 requires the court to give effect to the overriding objective when it exercises any power or interprets any rule. CPR 1.3 imposes a duty on the parties to help the court further it. CPR 1.4 requires the court to further the objective by actively managing cases, which includes encouraging co-operation, identifying the issues at an early stage, deciding promptly which issues need full investigation, fixing timetables, and — under CPR 1.4(2)(e) — “ordering or encouraging the parties to use, and facilitating the use of, alternative dispute resolution”.

title: 12  Running the claim
12  Running the claim
text:
12.2 Allocation to a track

12.2.1 The directions questionnaire
Once a defence is filed, the court provisionally allocates the claim and sends the parties a directions questionnaire (form N180 for the small claims track, N181 for the others). It must be filed by the date specified. The questionnaire asks about settlement and ADR, the track the party considers appropriate, disclosure, witnesses, experts, trial length and availability.
The court may order a stay of up to one month to allow for settlement (CPR 26.5), and in most small claims a referral to the Small Claims Mediation Service now follows automatically (CPR 26.6).


12.2.2 The four tracks
CPR 26.9 sets the scope of each track.








Track
Value
Key features




Small claims
Not more than £10,000 — but personal injury only where general damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity are not more than £1,000, and RTA whiplash claims where those damages are not more than £5,000
Informal hearing; strictly limited costs (CPR 27.14); compulsory mediation for most money claims


Fast track
More than £10,000 but not more than £25,000
Trial of one day or less; oral expert evidence limited to one expert per party per field, in no more than two fields; complexity bands 1–4; fixed recoverable costs


Intermediate track
More than £25,000 but not more than £100,000
Trial of not more than three days; oral expert evidence likely limited to two experts per party; ordinarily no more than three parties; complexity bands 1–4; fixed recoverable costs


Multi-track
More than £100,000, or otherwise unsuitable for a lower track
Case management conference; costs budgeting; assessed rather than fixed costs



The intermediate track was introduced on 1 October 2023 alongside the extension of fixed recoverable costs. Both the fast and intermediate tracks are further assigned to a complexity band (1 to 4), which determines the level of fixed costs — band 1 being the least complex.


12.2.3 The factors
CPR 26.13(1) lists the matters the court considers when allocating:

the financial value of the claim;
the nature of the remedy sought;
the likely complexity of the facts, law or evidence;
the number of parties;
the value of any counterclaim and its complexity;
the amount of oral evidence likely to be required;
the importance of the claim to persons who are not parties;
the views expressed by the parties; and
the circumstances of the parties.







Exam trap



Value is the starting point, not the answer. A £15,000 claim raising a novel point of law, involving five parties and requiring three days of evidence will be allocated to the multi-track despite its value. Conversely the parties’ agreement does not bind the court: CPR 26.13 lists their views as one factor among nine.
Note also how personal injury value is measured on the small claims track. It is the general damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity that must not exceed £1,000 (or £5,000 for RTA whiplash) — not the total claim. A claim worth £8,000 in total but £2,000 in general damages is not a small claim.

title: 12  Running the claim
text:
12.3 Directions and case management conferences

12.3.1 Fast and intermediate tracks
The court gives standard directions without a hearing wherever possible. A typical fast track timetable, running from allocation, is:



Step
Typical timing




Disclosure by list
4 weeks


Inspection
5 weeks


Exchange of witness statements
10 weeks


Exchange of expert reports
14 weeks


Sending of pre-trial checklists
20 weeks


Filing of pre-trial checklists
22 weeks


Trial
30 weeks



The intermediate track has its own standard directions with a similar shape, extended to reflect a trial of up to three days.


12.3.2 Multi-track
The court will either give directions and fix a timetable, or fix a case management conference (CMC) or, where costs budgets are to be considered, a costs and case management conference (CCMC). At a CMC the court will review the statements of case, identify the issues, consider whether the claim can be resolved without trial, decide on disclosure, witness and expert evidence, and fix a trial window.


12.3.3 Costs budgets
CPR 3.12 applies costs management to all Part 7 multi-track claims, with exceptions — notably where the claim is valued at £10 million or more and certain claims involving children.
CPR 3.13: every party except a litigant in person must file and exchange a budget in Precedent H:

where the stated value of the claim is less than £50,000, with the directions questionnaire;
in any other case, not later than 21 days before the first case management conference.

Budget discussion reports must be filed not later than 7 days before the CCMC.
CPR 3.14 — the sanction. A party that fails to file a budget when required will be treated as having filed a budget comprising only the applicable court fees.
The court then makes a costs management order recording the extent to which budgets are agreed or, where not agreed, the figures it approves. Once made, the court will not depart from an approved or agreed budget on assessment unless satisfied that there is good reason to do so — which is what makes budgeting so consequential.






Exam trap



CPR 3.14 is draconian and is examined for that reason. The defaulting party is not merely criticised; it is limited to court fees, and recovering anything more requires relief from sanctions under CPR 3.9 on the Denton test. The rule applies to a failure to file a budget at all, or to file it in time; a budget that is filed late but before the CCMC still engages it, and relief must be sought.

title: 12  Running the claim
text:
12.4 Sanctions and relief from sanctions
CPR 3.8: where a party has failed to comply with a rule, practice direction or court order, any sanction imposed for that failure has effect unless the party in default applies for and obtains relief.
Sanctions may be built into the rules (as with CPR 3.14), or imposed by order — most commonly an unless order, which provides that unless a step is taken by a stated date, a specified consequence follows automatically.
CPR 3.9(1): on an application for relief, the court will consider all the circumstances of the case, so as to enable it to deal justly with the application, including the need:

for litigation to be conducted efficiently and at proportionate cost; and
to enforce compliance with rules, practice directions and orders.


12.4.1 The Denton test
Denton v TH White Ltd [2014] EWCA Civ 906 supplies a three-stage approach, and it should be recited in that order:

Identify and assess the seriousness and significance of the breach. If the breach is neither serious nor significant, relief will usually be granted and the court need not spend much time on stages two and three.
Consider why the default occurred. Is there a good reason for it? Overlooking a deadline, pressure of work, and a solicitor’s oversight are not good reasons; a sudden illness or a debilitating event may be.
Evaluate all the circumstances of the case, so as to deal justly with the application, giving particular weight to the two factors in CPR 3.9(1)(a) and (b).

Denton corrected the over-strict application that followed Mitchell v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2013] EWCA Civ 1537, and the Court of Appeal took the opportunity to warn that opportunistic opposition to reasonable relief applications would itself be penalised in costs.






Exam trap



The two factors in CPR 3.9(1) are given particular weight at stage three, but they are not paramount and they are not a trump. An answer that says relief must be refused because the need to enforce compliance is decisive misstates Denton. Equally, an answer that treats stage three as a free-ranging discretion in which all factors weigh equally misstates it in the other direction.

title: 12  Running the claim
text:
12.5 Striking out
CPR 3.4(2) — the court may strike out a statement of case if it appears:

that the statement of case discloses no reasonable grounds for bringing or defending the claim;
that it is an abuse of the court’s process or is otherwise likely to obstruct the just disposal of the proceedings;
that there has been a failure to comply with a rule, practice direction or court order; or
that the claim is a SLAPP claim and the claimant has failed to show that it is more likely than not that the claim would succeed at trial.







The SLAPP strike-out — verify against your cut-off



Ground (d) implements ss.194–195 of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, which came into force on 18 June 2025, together with a corresponding amendment to the court’s costs discretion in CPR 44.2. A claim is a SLAPP for these purposes where it restrains, or is intended to restrain, freedom of speech; the speech concerns information relating to economic crime; the publication is for a purpose connected with the public interest in combating economic crime; and the claimant’s conduct is intended to cause harassment, alarm, distress, expense or other harm beyond that ordinarily encountered in properly conducted litigation.
The SRA’s warning notice on SLAPPs is named expressly in the assessment specification, so the conduct dimension — a solicitor must not pursue litigation whose purpose is to silence rather than to vindicate a legal right — is as likely to be examined as the rule itself.


Striking out is a draconian remedy and the court will consider whether a lesser sanction, or an opportunity to amend, would meet the case.

title: 12  Running the claim
text:
12.6 Interim applications

12.6.1 The procedure: Part 23

The application is made on form N244, stating what order is sought and why (CPR 23.6), and is supported by evidence — normally a witness statement, though the application notice itself may be verified by a statement of truth and stand as evidence.
It must be served as soon as practicable after issue and, unless a rule provides otherwise, at least three clear days before the hearing (CPR 23.7).
Without notice applications are permitted where there is exceptional urgency, where the overriding objective is best furthered by doing so, by consent, with the court’s permission, where a rule permits it, or where giving notice would defeat the purpose of the application — the freezing injunction being the obvious case. An applicant proceeding without notice owes a duty of full and frank disclosure of everything material, including matters adverse to their case; the respondent may apply to set aside within seven days of service of the order.
The court may deal with an application without a hearing if the parties agree, or if the court does not consider a hearing appropriate.
Costs of an interim application are normally summarily assessed at the end of the hearing.



12.6.2 Summary judgment: Part 24
The test (CPR 24.3). The court may give summary judgment against a claimant or a defendant on the whole of a claim or on a particular issue if:

the party has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim, defence or issue; and
there is no other compelling reason why the case or issue should be disposed of at a trial.

Both limbs are required. A “compelling reason” might be that the claim raises a point of general importance, that further evidence is expected to become available, or that a related claim is to be tried at the same time.
Swain v Hillman [2001] 1 All ER 91: “real” means realistic as opposed to fanciful. The court must not conduct a mini-trial on the documents. Easyair Ltd v Opal Telecom Ltd [2009] EWHC 339 (Ch) collects the principles: the court considers the evidence that can reasonably be expected to be available at trial, and should hesitate to decide a short point of law only where the facts are uncertain or the area of law is developing.
Procedure. A claimant may not apply until the defendant has filed an acknowledgment of service or a defence, unless the court gives permission (CPR 24.4). The respondent must have at least 14 days’ notice of the hearing and of the issues to be decided; the respondent’s evidence must be filed and served at least 7 days before the hearing; and any evidence in reply at least 3 days before.
The possible orders: judgment on the claim; striking out or dismissal of the claim; dismissal of the application; or a conditional order — permitting a party to continue only if it pays money into court or takes a specified step, appropriate where the case is improbable but not fanciful.






Exam trap



Distinguish the three ways of disposing of a case early:







Application
Question asked




Strike out (CPR 3.4(2)(a))
Taking the pleaded facts at their highest and assuming they are true, do they disclose a legally recognisable claim?


Summary judgment (CPR 24.3)
Looking at the evidence, does the party have a real prospect of success?


Default judgment (Part 12)
Has the defendant simply failed to respond in time?



A defective pleading points to strike out; a hopeless case on the evidence points to summary judgment; silence points to default judgment. Applications are commonly made in the alternative.




12.6.3 Interim payments
CPR 25.23 sets out the conditions. The court may order an interim payment only where:

the defendant has admitted liability to pay damages or some other sum of money to the claimant;
the claimant has obtained judgment against the defendant for damages to be assessed or for a sum of money to be assessed;
the court is satisfied that, if the claim went to trial, the claimant would obtain judgment for a substantial amount of money against the defendant from whom the payment is sought;
in a possession claim, the defendant would be held liable to pay a sum for the defendant’s occupation and use of the land; or
there are two or more defendants and the court is satisfied that, if the claim went to trial, the claimant would obtain judgment for a substantial amount of money against at least one of them — subject to conditions about insurance and public funding.

The restriction (CPR 25.20). The court must not order an interim payment of more than a reasonable proportion of the likely amount of the final judgment, and must take into account contributory negligence and any relevant set-off or counterclaim.
The application may not be made before the end of the period for filing an acknowledgment of service, and the fact that an interim payment has been made is not to be disclosed to the trial judge until all questions of liability and quantum have been decided.


12.6.4 Interim injunctions
An interim injunction is a discretionary equitable remedy granted to hold the position until trial. The governing framework is American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396:

Is there a serious question to be tried? This is a low threshold — the claim must not be frivolous or vexatious. The court does not weigh the relative strength of the cases at this stage.
Would damages be an adequate remedy for the claimant if the injunction were refused and the claimant succeeded at trial? If so, no injunction.
If not, would the cross-undertaking in damages adequately compensate the defendant if the injunction were granted and the claimant lost? If so, an injunction is more likely.
If damages would not adequately compensate either side, where does the balance of convenience lie?
If the balance is even, take the course that preserves the status quo.

The applicant must almost always give a cross-undertaking in damages — an undertaking to the court to compensate the respondent for loss caused by the injunction if it turns out to have been wrongly granted. The court will want evidence of the applicant’s ability to honour it.
Modifications to American Cyanamid arise where:

the injunction would in practice dispose of the whole action (for example a restrictive covenant with a short remaining term), where the court will look at the merits more closely;
the application is for a mandatory injunction, requiring a higher degree of assurance that the claimant will succeed; or
the application affects freedom of expression, where s.12(3) Human Rights Act 1998 requires the claimant to establish that it is likely to succeed at trial.

Freezing injunctions (CPR 25.12–25.14) are a distinct species. The applicant must show a good arguable case on the merits, that the respondent has assets, and a real risk of dissipation of those assets — not merely that the respondent may become unable to pay. They are almost always sought without notice, engaging the duty of full and frank disclosure, and the order includes an exception for ordinary living and legal expenses. A freezing order does not give the applicant any security or priority over the frozen assets.
Search orders (CPR 25.15–25.19) permit entry to premises to search for and preserve evidence. They require an extremely strong prima facie case, very serious potential or actual damage, clear evidence that the respondent has incriminating material, and a real possibility that it will be destroyed. A supervising solicitor, independent of the applicant’s firm, must be appointed to serve and oversee execution of the order.

title: 12  Running the claim
text:
12.7 Check yourself
Q1. A claimant brings a claim for £22,000 for breach of a building contract. Liability is disputed on straightforward facts, the trial is expected to take one day, and each party wants to call one expert surveyor. There are two parties.
To which track will the claim be allocated?
A. The small claims track, because the dispute is straightforward.
B. The fast track, because the value is more than £10,000 but not more than £25,000, the trial will last one day, and expert evidence is within the permitted limits.
C. The intermediate track, because expert evidence is required.
D. The multi-track, because the claim involves expert evidence.
E. The fast track, but only if both parties agree.
Q2. A defendant in a multi-track claim worth £600,000 fails to file a costs budget before the CCMC. Its solicitor had diarised the wrong date.
What is the consequence, and what should the defendant do?
A. There is no consequence; the court will simply require the budget to be filed late.
B. The claim will be struck out under CPR 3.4(2)(c).
C. The defendant is treated as having filed a budget comprising only the applicable court fees (CPR 3.14), and must apply for relief from sanctions under CPR 3.9, on which the court will apply the three-stage test in Denton v TH White Ltd.
D. The court will disallow the defendant’s costs entirely and no relief is available.
E. The consequence applies only if the defendant loses at trial.
Q3. A defendant applies for summary judgment. The claimant’s case depends on an oral agreement which the defendant denies was ever made. The claimant has produced a witness statement from a person who says he was present when the agreement was made; the defendant has produced three statements to the contrary and contemporaneous documents that are inconsistent with the claimant’s account.
Which of the following is the most likely outcome?
A. Summary judgment will be granted, because the weight of the evidence favours the defendant.
B. Summary judgment will be refused, because there is a conflict of factual evidence which can only be resolved by hearing the witnesses; the court must not conduct a mini-trial, and the claimant’s case is realistic rather than fanciful.
C. Summary judgment will be granted, because an oral agreement can never be proved.
D. The court will strike out the claim under CPR 3.4(2)(a).
E. The court will enter default judgment for the defendant.
Q4. A claimant seeks an interim injunction to restrain a former employee from working for a competitor, in breach of a restrictive covenant with eleven months left to run. Trial is unlikely to take place within that period.
Which of the following best describes the court’s approach?
A. The court will apply American Cyanamid without modification, and will not consider the merits.
B. The court will grant the injunction automatically, because a covenant is a contractual right.
C. Because the injunction would in practice dispose of the whole action — trial will come too late to matter — the court will look more closely at the merits than the American Cyanamid threshold would normally require; the claimant will also be required to give a cross-undertaking in damages.
D. Interim injunctions are not available in employment cases.
E. The court will refuse the injunction because damages are always an adequate remedy for breach of a restrictive covenant.
Q5. A party misses a deadline for exchanging witness statements by two days because its solicitor was hospitalised unexpectedly. The other party has suffered no prejudice, and the trial date is not affected. The other party opposes the application for relief on the ground that the need to enforce compliance is paramount.
Which of the following is correct?
A. Relief must be refused, because CPR 3.9(1)(b) requires the court to enforce compliance.
B. Relief will be granted: applying Denton, the breach is neither serious nor significant, there is a good reason for it, and all the circumstances favour relief. The opposing party risks a costs sanction for taking an opportunistic point.
C. Relief may be granted only if the party pays the other side’s costs of the entire action.
D. Relief is unavailable because CPR 3.8 provides that sanctions have effect.
E. The court has no discretion where a rule imposes an automatic sanction.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. CPR 26.9: the fast track covers claims of more than £10,000 but not more than £25,000, where the trial is likely to last no longer than one day and oral expert evidence is limited to one expert per party in each of no more than two fields. Every element is satisfied.

A applies the small claims limit of £10,000.
C and D treat expert evidence as pushing the claim up a track. It does not; the fast track expressly contemplates one expert per party.
E makes allocation depend on the parties’ agreement. Under CPR 26.13 their views are one of nine factors, and the decision is the court’s.

Q2 — C. CPR 3.14 provides that a party that fails to file a budget when required will be treated as having filed a budget comprising only the applicable court fees. The remedy is an application for relief from sanctions under CPR 3.9, decided on the three-stage Denton test. A diary error is unlikely to be a good reason at stage two, so the defendant’s prospects turn on stages one and three.

A ignores the automatic sanction.
B applies the wrong rule; strike out is not the sanction for a budget failure.
D overstates the position: relief is available, however difficult.
E invents a condition; the sanction bites on assessment whatever the outcome.

Q3 — B. Swain v Hillman: “real” prospect means realistic, not fanciful, and the court must not conduct a mini-trial. A genuine conflict of oral evidence, supported on the claimant’s side by a witness who says he was present, is quintessentially a matter for trial, however unpromising the documents look.

A invites the court to weigh evidence, which is precisely what Part 24 does not permit.
C is legally wrong: oral contracts are enforceable and provable.
D applies the wrong test. Strike out under CPR 3.4(2)(a) asks whether the pleaded case discloses reasonable grounds, assuming the facts to be true — and here it does.
E misuses default judgment, which is about failure to respond in time.

Q4 — C. Where the practical effect of granting or refusing interim relief is to determine the action — because the covenant will have expired before trial — the court departs from the strict American Cyanamid approach and takes a view on the merits, since the “serious question to be tried” threshold would otherwise decide the case without any assessment of it. A cross-undertaking in damages will be required as a matter of course.

A applies American Cyanamid mechanically and ignores the recognised exception.
B and D state rules that do not exist.
E is too absolute. Damages are frequently an inadequate remedy for breach of a restrictive covenant, because the loss of confidential information or client connection is hard to quantify.

Q5 — B. Denton v TH White Ltd. Stage one: a two-day delay causing no prejudice and not imperilling the trial date is neither serious nor significant, and where that is so relief will usually be granted without much need for stages two and three. Stage two: a solicitor’s sudden hospitalisation is capable of being a good reason. Stage three: all the circumstances plainly favour relief. The Court of Appeal in Denton expressly warned that parties who unreasonably oppose relief applications of this kind should expect to be penalised in costs.

A treats CPR 3.9(1)(b) as paramount. It is given particular weight at stage three, not decisive effect.
C invents a condition out of all proportion to the breach.
D misreads CPR 3.8, which provides that a sanction has effect unless relief is obtained — the rule that makes relief applications necessary, not one that makes them impossible.
E denies the existence of CPR 3.9.

title: 13  Proving the case
text: 13.1 The framework of civil evidence

title: 13  Proving the case
text:
13.1.1 Relevance and admissibility
Evidence is admissible if it is relevant to a fact in issue — that is, if it makes the existence of that fact more or less probable — and is not excluded by a rule. Civil evidence is far more permissive than criminal evidence: hearsay is admissible, and the court’s principal tools are weight and case management rather than exclusion.
CPR 32.1 gives the court a broad power to control evidence: it may give directions as to the issues on which it requires evidence, the nature of the evidence it requires, and the way in which it is to be placed before the court; it may exclude evidence that would otherwise be admissible; and it may limit cross-examination.


13.1.2 Burden and standard of proof

The legal burden rests on the party who asserts — normally the claimant on the elements of the claim, and the defendant on any positive defence (contributory negligence, limitation, frustration, illegality).
The standard is the balance of probabilities: more likely than not. There is no sliding scale for serious allegations, though the inherent improbability of an allegation is a matter the court may take into account in deciding whether it has been proved.
The evidential burden may shift during a trial, and some rules assist a claimant — res ipsa loquitur in negligence, and the presumption in s.11 Civil Evidence Act 1968 that a person convicted of an offence committed it.



13.1.3 Hearsay
Hearsay is a statement made otherwise than by a person giving oral evidence in the proceedings, which is tendered as evidence of the matters stated.
Section 1 Civil Evidence Act 1995: hearsay is not to be excluded in civil proceedings on the ground that it is hearsay. The question is one of weight, not admissibility.
Three consequences follow:

Notice (s.2 CEA 1995 and CPR 33.2). A party who intends to rely on hearsay must give notice. Where the hearsay is contained in a witness statement of a person not being called, the party must inform the other parties when serving the statement and give the reason the witness will not be called. Failure to give notice does not make the evidence inadmissible, but the court may take it into account in weighing the evidence and in costs.
Calling the maker (s.3 CEA 1995 and CPR 33.4). Where the maker of the hearsay statement is not called, another party may apply for permission to call that person for cross-examination on the statement.
Weight (s.4 CEA 1995). The court considers whether it would have been reasonable and practicable to call the maker; whether the statement was made contemporaneously; whether it involves multiple hearsay; whether any person had a motive to conceal or misrepresent; whether the original statement was edited or made in collaboration for a particular purpose; and whether the circumstances suggest an attempt to prevent proper evaluation of its weight.







Exam trap



The instinct carried over from criminal law — that hearsay is inadmissible unless an exception applies — is exactly wrong in civil proceedings. An option stating that a witness statement from an absent witness is “inadmissible because it is hearsay” is wrong. The correct analysis is that it is admissible, that notice should be given, that the other party may apply to call the maker for cross-examination, and that the court will attach less weight to it because it has not been tested.

title: 13  Proving the case
text:
13.2 Witness evidence

13.2.1 Witness statements
A witness statement is a signed statement containing the evidence which that person would be allowed to give orally (CPR 32.4). At trial it stands as the witness’s evidence in chief unless the court orders otherwise (CPR 32.5), and the witness is then tendered for cross-examination.
Requirements under Practice Direction 32:

It must be in the witness’s own words and, so far as practicable, in their own language, expressed in the first person.
It must state the source of any matters of information or belief.
It must not contain argument, opinion (unless the witness is an expert or the opinion is one a lay witness may give, such as speed or identity), or extensive commentary on documents.
It must be verified by a statement of truth, with the contempt of court warning.

Consequences of failure to serve. Under CPR 32.10, if a witness statement is not served within the time specified by the court, the witness may not be called to give oral evidence unless the court gives permission — which requires relief from sanctions.






PD 57AC — trial witness statements in the Business and Property Courts



For trials in the Business and Property Courts, Practice Direction 57AC imposes additional requirements: the statement must set out only matters of fact of which the witness has personal knowledge that are relevant to the issues; it must identify by list the documents the witness has referred to or been referred to for the purpose of providing the evidence; the witness must sign a confirmation of compliance; and the party’s legal representative must endorse a certificate of compliance. Breach can lead to the statement being struck out, withdrawn or redrafted, and to adverse costs orders.




13.2.2 Affidavits
An affidavit is a sworn statement, made on oath or affirmation before a person authorised to administer it. Affidavits are more formal and more expensive than witness statements, and are required only where a rule, practice direction or court order says so — most importantly for applications for freezing injunctions and search orders, and in contempt proceedings. A party may choose to use an affidavit instead of a witness statement, but will not recover the extra cost unless the court orders otherwise.


13.2.3 Compelling attendance
A witness summons (CPR 34) requires a witness to attend court to give evidence or to produce documents. It is issued by the court, and is binding if served at least seven days before the date on which the witness is required to attend — the court may permit shorter service. The party serving it must offer or pay a sum reasonably sufficient to cover the witness’s travel expenses and compensation for loss of time. Failure to comply is a contempt of court.

title: 13  Proving the case
text:
13.3 Expert evidence

13.3.1 The controls
Opinion evidence is generally inadmissible; s.3 Civil Evidence Act 1972 makes an expert’s opinion on a relevant matter admissible where the expert is qualified to give it.
Part 35 exists to restrain the cost and partisanship of expert evidence, and three rules do the work:

CPR 35.1: expert evidence shall be restricted to that which is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings.
CPR 35.4: no party may call an expert or put in an expert’s report without the court’s permission. When applying, the party must identify the field, the issues the evidence will address, where practicable the expert’s name, and an estimate of the costs.
CPR 35.3 — the overriding duty: it is the duty of an expert to help the court on matters within their expertise, and that duty overrides any obligation to the person from whom the expert has received instructions or by whom they are paid.







Exam trap



Permission under CPR 35.4 is the single most examined point in this topic. A party who instructs an expert without first obtaining permission has spent money it may never recover, and cannot rely on the report. An option saying “the party may adduce the report because it obtained it before proceedings” is wrong. Note the further distinction: a shadow or advisory expert, instructed to advise the party rather than to give evidence, needs no permission and is protected by litigation privilege — but cannot be relied on at trial.




13.3.2 The report
Practice Direction 35 prescribes the contents: the expert’s qualifications; the literature and material relied on; a statement of who carried out any test or experiment; the substance of all material instructions, written and oral, on the basis of which the report was written; a summary of the range of opinion where there is one, and reasons for the expert’s own opinion; a summary of conclusions; and a statement that the expert understands and has complied with their duty to the court. It must be verified by a statement of truth in the prescribed form.






Exam trap



The substance of the instructions stated in the report is not privileged, and CPR 35.10(4) provides that the court will not order disclosure of any specific document or permit cross-examination about the instructions unless it is satisfied there are reasonable grounds to consider the statement of instructions to be inaccurate or incomplete. So instructions are partially exposed, but the threshold for going behind the summary is high.




13.3.3 Written questions and discussions
CPR 35.6 — written questions. A party may put written questions to the other side’s expert (or to a single joint expert). Unless the court orders or the other party agrees otherwise, the questions may be put once only, must be put within 28 days of service of the report, and must be for the purpose of clarification of the report. The answers form part of the report. If the expert does not answer, the court may direct that the instructing party may not rely on the evidence, or may not recover the expert’s fees.
CPR 35.12 — discussions between experts. The court may direct a discussion between experts to identify and discuss the issues, and where possible to reach agreement. The court may specify the issues. The experts must prepare a statement for the court showing the issues on which they agree and those on which they disagree, with a summary of the reasons.
Two rules about that discussion are reliably tested:

The content of the discussion is not to be referred to at trial unless the parties agree.
Where the experts reach agreement, that agreement does not bind the parties unless they expressly agree to be bound by it.



13.3.4 Single joint experts
CPR 35.7: where two or more parties wish to submit expert evidence on a particular issue, the court may direct that it be given by a single joint expert. If the parties cannot agree who, the court may select from a list prepared by the parties, or direct the manner of selection.
CPR 35.8: each instructing party may give instructions to the expert, copying them to the other parties. Each instructing party is jointly and severally liable for the expert’s fees.
Single joint experts are the norm on the fast track and on quantum issues, and are less common where a central issue in a high-value dispute turns on contested expert opinion.
Concurrent evidence (“hot-tubbing”) is permitted under PD 35: the court may direct that experts give their evidence together, with the judge putting questions and the experts commenting on each other’s answers.

title: 13  Proving the case
text:
13.4 Disclosure and inspection

13.4.1 The concepts
Disclosure is stating that a document exists or has existed (CPR 31.2). Inspection is the separate right to look at it and take a copy (CPR 31.3). A party may disclose a document but withhold inspection — on grounds of privilege, or because inspection would be disproportionate, or because the party no longer has it.
A document is “anything in which information of any description is recorded” (CPR 31.4) — which plainly includes emails, text messages, metadata, databases and voicemails.
A party discloses documents which are or have been in its control (CPR 31.8): documents which it has or has had physical possession of, or has or has had a right to possession of, or has or has had a right to inspect or take copies of.


13.4.2 Standard disclosure
CPR 31.6: standard disclosure requires a party to disclose only:

the documents on which it relies;
the documents which adversely affect its own case, adversely affect another party’s case, or support another party’s case; and
the documents which it is required to disclose by a relevant practice direction.







Exam trap



Standard disclosure is not a duty to disclose “everything relevant”. It is deliberately narrower — and, crucially, it is not confined to helpful documents. A party must disclose documents that damage its own case. That is the whole point, and it is the source of most of the questions: the client who says “I’m not producing that email, it’s fatal” must be told that they have no choice.


The search (CPR 31.7). A party must make a reasonable search. What is reasonable depends on the number of documents involved, the nature and complexity of the proceedings, the ease and expense of retrieval, and the significance of any document likely to be located. A party who has not searched a category or class of document on the ground that to do so would be unreasonable must say so in the disclosure statement.
The list and the statement (CPR 31.10). Disclosure is made by serving a list of documents in form N265, in three parts: documents in the party’s control which it does not object to the other side inspecting; documents in its control which it objects to producing (privileged documents, described by class); and documents which are no longer in its control, with an explanation of what became of them. The list includes a disclosure statement setting out the extent of the search, certifying that the party understands the duty to disclose, and stating that to the best of their knowledge they have carried it out.
The continuing duty (CPR 31.11). The duty of disclosure continues until the proceedings are concluded. A party who later comes into possession of a disclosable document must notify the other parties immediately.


13.4.3 Orders for disclosure

Specific disclosure (CPR 31.12): an order requiring a party to disclose specified documents or classes of documents, to carry out a search to the extent stated, or to disclose any documents located as a result. It is used where the applicant believes standard disclosure has been inadequate, and must be supported by evidence.
Pre-action disclosure (s.33 Senior Courts Act 1981, s.52 County Courts Act 1984, CPR 31.16). The court may order disclosure before proceedings where the applicant and respondent are likely to be parties to subsequent proceedings, the documents fall within standard disclosure, and disclosure is desirable in order to dispose fairly of the anticipated proceedings, to assist the dispute to be resolved without proceedings, or to save costs. The applicant normally pays the costs.
Non-party disclosure (s.34 Senior Courts Act 1981, CPR 31.17). Available only after proceedings have started. The documents must be likely to support the applicant’s case or adversely affect the case of one of the other parties, and disclosure must be necessary to dispose fairly of the claim or to save costs. Again, the applicant normally pays.
A Norwich Pharmacal order is a distinct jurisdiction, compelling a person mixed up in wrongdoing (however innocently) to disclose information identifying the wrongdoer, so that the applicant can bring a claim.



13.4.4 Electronic disclosure
Practice Direction 31B applies to electronic documents. The parties must discuss the scope of electronic disclosure before the first case management conference — the categories of documents, the date ranges, the custodians, the search terms and the format of exchange — and may be required to complete an Electronic Documents Questionnaire. Keyword searching, de-duplication and technology-assisted review are expressly contemplated. The overriding consideration is proportionality.






PD 57AD — Disclosure in the Business and Property Courts



Since 1 October 2022, disclosure in the Business and Property Courts is governed by Practice Direction 57AD, which replaced the disclosure pilot in PD 51U. It is a different regime from CPR Part 31, and the differences are structural:

Initial Disclosure: key documents relied on and necessary for the other party to understand the case must be served with the statements of case, subject to limits.
Extended Disclosure requires a party to identify Issues for Disclosure and to request one of five Models:







Model
Effect




A
Disclosure confined to known adverse documents


B
Limited disclosure — key documents plus known adverse documents


C
Request-led search-based disclosure of particular documents or narrow classes


D
Narrow search-based disclosure, with or without narrative documents — the closest to standard disclosure


E
Wide search-based disclosure, including documents that may lead to a train of inquiry



A Disclosure Review Document is completed jointly, and there is a free-standing duty to disclose known adverse documents regardless of the model ordered.

Outside the Business and Property Courts — which is where most claims are — CPR Part 31 and standard disclosure still apply. Read the question carefully to see which court you are in.

title: 13  Proving the case
text:
13.5 Privilege
Privilege is a right to withhold inspection of a document that must still be disclosed (listed by class in part 2 of the list). It belongs to the client, not the solicitor, and only the client can waive it.

13.5.1 Legal advice privilege
Confidential communications between a lawyer and client, made for the dominant purpose of giving or receiving legal advice. It applies whether or not litigation is contemplated.

Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England (No 5) [2003] EWCA Civ 474 gave “client” a narrow meaning: only those employees specifically tasked with seeking and receiving legal advice on the corporation’s behalf. Communications between the lawyer and other employees are not covered.
Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England (No 6) [2004] UKHL 48 gave “legal advice” a wide meaning: it extends beyond advice on legal rights and liabilities to advice as to what should prudently and sensibly be done in the relevant legal context — including presentational advice before an inquiry.



13.5.2 Litigation privilege
Confidential communications between a lawyer and client, or between either of them and a third party, where:

litigation is in progress or in reasonable contemplation; and
the communication was made for the dominant purpose of that litigation — conducting it, obtaining evidence or advice about it.
Waugh v British Railways Board [1980] AC 521 established the dominant purpose test: an internal report prepared for two purposes of equal weight — railway safety and litigation — was not privileged.
Serious Fraud Office v Eurasian Natural Resources Corporation Ltd [2018] EWCA Civ 2006 held that a criminal investigation may make litigation reasonably in contemplation, and that documents created to obtain legal advice about how to avoid or settle contemplated litigation fall within the privilege.







Exam trap



Litigation privilege covers third party communications — an expert’s report, a witness proof, an investigator’s findings — where legal advice privilege does not. That is why a shadow expert instructed to advise rather than to give evidence is protected, and why an accident report prepared for the dominant purpose of litigation is protected while one prepared to improve safety is not.




13.5.3 Without prejudice communications
Communications made in a genuine attempt to settle an existing dispute cannot be put before the court. The rule rests on public policy and on the implied agreement of the parties.

It is the substance that matters, not the label. Writing “without prejudice” on an open assertion of claim does not protect it, and omitting the label from a genuine settlement offer does not destroy the protection.
Rush & Tompkins Ltd v Greater London Council [1989] AC 1280: the protection extends to communications with other parties to the same litigation, and survives the settlement of the dispute as against a party who was not involved in the negotiations.
Unilever plc v Procter & Gamble Co [2000] 1 WLR 2436 lists the exceptions: whether a settlement was concluded and on what terms; rectification of a settlement; estoppel; unambiguous impropriety (a threat or perjury under cover of the privilege); explaining delay; and an offer expressly made “without prejudice save as to costs”.
A “without prejudice save as to costs” (Calderbank) offer is protected until liability and quantum are decided, and may then be shown to the court on the question of costs.



13.5.4 Other privileges, and waiver

Privilege against self-incrimination: a party need not produce a document that would tend to expose them to criminal proceedings or a penalty.
Common interest privilege: a privileged document may be shared with a party having a common interest in the subject matter without loss of privilege.
Public interest immunity: documents may be withheld where disclosure would damage the public interest.

Waiver may be express or implied. Deploying part of a privileged document in the proceedings — for example, relying on part of a legal opinion to explain why a party acted as it did — will generally waive privilege in the whole of that document, and possibly in the transaction to which it relates. This is the rule against cherry-picking, and it is why partial deployment is dangerous. Privilege is not waived by an inadvertent disclosure where the mistake was obvious; CPR 31.20 provides that where a party inadvertently allows a privileged document to be inspected, the party who has inspected it may use it only with the permission of the court.






Exam trap



Privilege belongs to the client. A solicitor cannot waive it, and cannot disclose a privileged document because they think it would be fairer to do so. Equally, a solicitor who receives an obviously privileged document sent to them by mistake must stop reading it, notify the other side, and return or destroy it — and must not use it without the court’s permission.

title: 13  Proving the case
text:
13.6 The solicitor’s position
Advising on the duty of disclosure. The client must be told, in writing and at the outset, that disclosure requires production of documents that harm their case, that the duty is continuing, and that documents must be preserved. A solicitor who allows a client to destroy or withhold disclosable documents risks being party to a contempt and breaches the duty not to mislead the court.
Document preservation. As soon as litigation is contemplated, the client should be told to suspend routine document destruction — including automatic email deletion policies.
Not misleading the court. A solicitor must not make a statement to the court knowing it to be untrue, must not put forward evidence they know to be false, and must draw the court’s attention to relevant cases and statutory provisions likely to have a material effect on the outcome, even where they are against the client’s case.
Where the client’s account changes. If a client admits that a served witness statement is untrue, the solicitor cannot continue to rely on it. The client must be advised to correct it; if they refuse, the solicitor must cease to act, without disclosing the reason.
Witnesses. A solicitor must not coach a witness or rehearse evidence, and must not interfere with the evidence of any witness. Taking a proof of evidence is proper; suggesting what the witness should say is not.

title: 13  Proving the case
text:
13.7 Check yourself
Q1. A claimant wishes to rely at trial on a signed statement from a witness who has since emigrated and cannot be called. The defendant objects that the statement is hearsay.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The statement is inadmissible, because the witness cannot be cross-examined.
B. The statement is admissible: hearsay is not excluded in civil proceedings on the ground that it is hearsay. The claimant should give notice under CPR 33.2; the defendant may apply for permission to call the maker for cross-examination; and the court will assess weight under s.4 of the Civil Evidence Act 1995.
C. The statement is admissible only if the court gives permission under CPR 32.1.
D. The statement is inadmissible unless the claimant obtains a witness summons.
E. The statement is admissible only if it was made contemporaneously with the events described.
Q2. A company’s in-house legal team asks employees across the business for factual information about a transaction, in order to advise the board. Litigation is not yet in prospect. The employees’ responses are later sought on disclosure.
Are the responses protected by legal advice privilege?
A. Yes, because they were created for the purpose of obtaining legal advice.
B. Yes, because all communications within a company are privileged once lawyers are involved.
C. No, on the Three Rivers (No 5) approach: for legal advice privilege the “client” is confined to those employees tasked with seeking and receiving legal advice on the company’s behalf, and communications with other employees are not covered.
D. No, because legal advice privilege does not apply to in-house lawyers.
E. Yes, because litigation privilege applies whenever a company takes legal advice.
Q3. A party wishes to rely on the evidence of a consulting engineer. It obtained a detailed report before proceedings were issued and has now filed a directions questionnaire.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The party may rely on the report at trial, because it was obtained before proceedings began.
B. The party may rely on the report provided it serves it on the other side.
C. No party may call an expert or put in an expert’s report without the court’s permission (CPR 35.4); the party must apply, identifying the field, the issues to be addressed, the expert’s name where practicable, and an estimate of costs.
D. The report is inadmissible because it is opinion evidence.
E. Permission is required only where the party wishes to call the expert to give oral evidence.
Q4. During disclosure, a defendant’s solicitor identifies an internal email in which the defendant’s managing director admits that the goods supplied were substandard. The defendant instructs the solicitor not to include it in the list of documents.
What should the solicitor do?
A. Follow the client’s instructions, because privilege belongs to the client.
B. Include the email in part 2 of the list as a privileged document.
C. Advise the client that the email falls within standard disclosure under CPR 31.6(b) because it adversely affects the defendant’s own case, that it must be disclosed, and that if the client refuses the solicitor must cease to act.
D. Disclose the email without telling the client, because the duty to the court prevails.
E. Destroy the email, because it was created before proceedings were issued.
Q5. Two experts hold a discussion directed by the court under CPR 35.12 and reach agreement on the cost of remedial works. One party’s solicitor tells the client that the claim is now settled at that figure.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The advice is correct: an agreement between experts binds the parties.
B. The advice is incorrect: where experts reach agreement in a discussion, that agreement does not bind the parties unless they expressly agree to be bound by it.
C. The advice is correct, because the court directed the discussion.
D. The advice is incorrect, because expert discussions have no legal effect of any kind and the statement cannot be shown to the court.
E. The advice is correct, unless a party applies to set the agreement aside within 21 days.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. Section 1 Civil Evidence Act 1995 abolished the rule against hearsay in civil proceedings. The consequences are procedural and evidential rather than exclusionary: notice under s.2 and CPR 33.2, the right of the other party to apply under s.3 and CPR 33.4 to call the maker for cross-examination, and the s.4 weight factors — of which “whether it would have been reasonable and practicable to produce the maker” is the first, and emigration is a good answer to it.

A imports the criminal law instinct, which is the trap.
C confuses the court’s general power to control evidence with an admissibility requirement.
D misuses a witness summons, which compels attendance and cannot reach a person abroad.
E turns a weight factor under s.4 into an admissibility condition.

Q2 — C. Three Rivers (No 5). For the purposes of legal advice privilege the “client” is confined to those employees authorised to seek and receive legal advice for the corporation. Information gathered from other employees is not privileged on that basis. Litigation privilege would cover it — but only if litigation were in reasonable contemplation, which the facts exclude.

A and B apply an organisation-wide conception of the client that Three Rivers (No 5) rejected.
D is wrong: in-house lawyers attract legal advice privilege when acting in a legal capacity.
E invokes litigation privilege where there is no litigation in reasonable contemplation.

Q3 — C. CPR 35.4(1): no party may call an expert or put in evidence an expert’s report without the court’s permission. The application is normally made in the directions questionnaire or at the CMC, and CPR 35.4(2) prescribes what must be identified.

A and B overlook the permission requirement entirely, which is the most commonly missed point in Part 35.
D is wrong: s.3 Civil Evidence Act 1972 makes qualified expert opinion admissible.
E is the sophisticated distractor: permission is required to put in the report as well as to call the expert.

Q4 — C. CPR 31.6(b) requires disclosure of documents which adversely affect the disclosing party’s own case. That is exactly what this email does. The client has no choice, and the solicitor cannot serve a list they know to be incomplete without misleading the court. If the client will not comply, the solicitor must cease to act — without disclosing the reason, because it is confidential.

A confuses privilege, which the client owns, with the duty of disclosure, which the client cannot waive away.
B is a misuse of part 2 of the list. The email is not privileged; an internal commercial email is not a lawyer-client communication and no litigation privilege attaches to a document created in the ordinary course of business.
D breaches the duty of confidentiality and the duty to act on instructions; the answer is to advise, not to act unilaterally.
E would be destruction of evidence, a contempt, and potentially a criminal offence.

Q5 — B. CPR 35.12(5): where experts reach agreement in a discussion, that agreement does not bind the parties unless the parties expressly agree to be bound by it. The parties remain free to argue for a different figure, though doing so in the face of an agreed expert position carries obvious forensic and costs risk.

A, C and E all give the experts’ agreement a binding effect it does not have.
D overstates the point in the other direction: the content of the discussion may not be referred to at trial without the parties’ agreement (CPR 35.12(4)), but the joint statement of agreement and disagreement is produced precisely so that the court can see it.

title: 14  Trial, appeals and enforcement
text: 14.1 Preparing for trial

title: 14  Trial, appeals and enforcement
text:
14.1.1 Pre-trial checklists
Towards the end of the timetable the court sends the parties a pre-trial checklist (a listing questionnaire), to be filed by a specified date. It confirms whether the directions have been complied with, whether any further directions are needed, the witnesses to be called, whether expert evidence is to be given orally, the estimated length of trial, and the availability of witnesses, experts and advocates.
If no party files a checklist, the court will normally make an unless order — that unless a checklist is filed within seven days, the claim will be struck out. If one party files and another does not, the court will usually fix a hearing or give directions.


14.1.2 Pre-trial review
On the multi-track, and in longer or more complex cases, the court may list a pre-trial review, usually before the trial judge. Its purposes are to check that the directions have been complied with, to settle the trial timetable, to decide any outstanding applications, to determine the form and scope of the evidence, and to explore settlement one last time.


14.1.3 The trial bundle
CPR 39.5: unless the court orders otherwise, the claimant must file a trial bundle not more than 7 days and not less than 3 days before the start of the trial. Its contents are prescribed by Practice Direction 32 and typically include, in this order: the claim form and all statements of case; a case summary and chronology where useful; the court orders and directions; the witness statements to be relied on; any hearsay notices; the expert reports and joint statements; and the documents disclosed and relied on.
The bundle should be paginated and indexed, agreed with the other parties wherever possible, and accompanied by a case summary in more complex cases. The costs of preparing an unnecessarily bulky bundle may be disallowed.


14.1.4 Summoning witnesses
A witness summons (CPR 34) compels a person to attend court to give evidence or to produce documents. Key points:

It is issued by the court. The court’s permission is required where a party wishes to have a summons issued less than 7 days before the date of the trial, or where the witness is to attend on any date except the trial date, or at any hearing except the trial (CPR 34.3(2)).
It is binding if served at least seven days before the date the witness is required to attend; the court may permit shorter service.
The party serving it must offer or pay conduct money — a sum reasonably sufficient to cover the witness’s travelling expenses and compensation for loss of time.
Non-compliance is a contempt of court.

A summons should be considered even for a willing witness, since it protects an employed witness from their employer and guarantees attendance.


14.1.5 Other pre-trial steps

Skeleton arguments are required in the higher courts and are increasingly directed elsewhere.
Trial fee: the claimant must pay the hearing fee by the date specified, failing which the claim will be struck out.
The parties should keep settlement under review; a Part 36 offer may be made or accepted at any time before judgment, and the costs consequences of a late acceptance are severe.

title: 14  Trial, appeals and enforcement
text:
14.2 The trial

14.2.1 Procedure
The judge may vary the order, but the standard sequence is:

Preliminary matters — housekeeping, applications, the trial timetable.
Claimant’s opening, often abbreviated where skeleton arguments have been read.
Claimant’s evidence. Each witness is sworn; the witness statement stands as evidence in chief (CPR 32.5), sometimes with limited supplementary questions with permission; then cross-examination by the defendant; then re-examination by the claimant, confined to matters arising from cross-examination.
Defendant’s evidence, in the same way.
Expert evidence, either in the party’s case or concurrently if the court has directed hot-tubbing.
Closing submissions — normally the defendant first, then the claimant.
Judgment, delivered orally at the end of the hearing or reserved and handed down later.
Consequential matters — costs, interest, permission to appeal, any stay of execution.







Exam trap



A party who wishes to challenge a witness’s evidence must put its case to that witness in cross-examination. A defendant who does not challenge a claimant’s account in cross-examination, and then invites the judge in closing to reject it as untrue, will normally be held to have accepted it. This is the rule in Browne v Dunn, and it explains why cross-examination is where the case is actually won or lost.




14.2.2 Judgment and its effect

A judgment or order takes effect from the day it is given or made, unless the court specifies a later date (CPR 40.7).
Unless it specifies otherwise, a party must comply with a judgment for the payment of money within 14 days (CPR 40.11).
Interest before judgment is discretionary: s.35A Senior Courts Act 1981 in the High Court and s.69 County Courts Act 1984 in the County Court permit simple interest on damages for all or part of the period between the cause of action arising and judgment. A claim for interest must be pleaded.
Interest after judgment runs on High Court judgments under s.17 Judgments Act 1838 at 8%, and on County Court judgments of £5,000 or more at the same rate.
A judgment creates a res judicata: the same cause of action cannot be litigated again between the same parties, and issues decided are binding on them (issue estoppel). Relitigating a point that could and should have been raised is an abuse of process under the rule in Henderson v Henderson.
Judgments for money are registered and, for judgments not satisfied within one month, entered on the Register of Judgments, Orders and Fines.

title: 14  Trial, appeals and enforcement
text:
14.3 Appeals

14.3.1 Permission
Permission to appeal is required in almost every case (CPR 52.3). It may be sought from the lower court at the hearing at which the decision was made, or from the appeal court in the appellant’s notice. A refusal by the lower court is not an appealable decision; the appellant simply asks the appeal court.
The test (CPR 52.6): permission may be given only where:

the appeal would have a real prospect of success; or
there is some other compelling reason for the appeal to be heard.

Second appeals (CPR 52.7) — an appeal to the Court of Appeal from a decision of the County Court, the family court or the High Court which was itself made on appeal — face a higher threshold. Permission may be given only by the Court of Appeal, and only where it considers that the appeal would both have a real prospect of success and raise an important point of principle or practice, or that there is some other compelling reason for the Court of Appeal to hear it.


14.3.2 Time limits and procedure
The appellant’s notice must be filed within such period as the lower court directs, or, where it directs none, within 21 days of the date of the decision appealed against (CPR 52.12). It must be served on the respondents as soon as practicable and in any event within seven days of filing.
An appeal does not operate as a stay of the decision below unless the appeal court or the lower court orders otherwise (CPR 52.16). A successful appellant who has not obtained a stay may find the judgment has already been enforced.


14.3.3 Grounds and the nature of the appeal
CPR 52.21(1): every appeal is limited to a review of the decision of the lower court, unless a practice direction provides otherwise or the court considers that in the circumstances of the individual appeal it would be in the interests of justice to hold a re-hearing.
CPR 52.21(3): the appeal court will allow an appeal where the decision of the lower court was:

wrong; or
unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity in the proceedings in the lower court.

New evidence is admitted only in accordance with the principles in Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489: the evidence could not have been obtained with reasonable diligence for use at trial; it would probably have had an important influence on the result; and it is apparently credible.






Exam trap



An appeal is a review, not a second trial. An appellate court will not interfere with a trial judge’s findings of primary fact based on oral evidence unless they are plainly wrong, because the trial judge saw the witnesses. Nor will it interfere with a discretionary case management decision merely because it would have exercised the discretion differently — the decision must be outside the range of reasonable decisions. Options offering an appeal because “the judge should have believed the claimant” are wrong.




14.3.4 Destination of appeals
Set by the Access to Justice Act 1999 (Destination of Appeals) Order 2016:







Decision of
Appeal lies to




District judge of the County Court
Circuit judge of the County Court


Circuit judge of the County Court
High Court judge


Master or district judge of the High Court
High Court judge


High Court judge
Court of Appeal


A decision made on appeal in the County Court or High Court
Court of Appeal (a second appeal)



A “leapfrog” transfer is possible: under CPR 52.23 the court may order an appeal to be transferred to the Court of Appeal where it would raise an important point of principle or practice or there is some other compelling reason. There is a separate statutory leapfrog from the High Court to the Supreme Court under the Administration of Justice Act 1969.






Exam trap



The 2016 Order simplified the destinations by reference to the judge who made the decision. The old rule sending final decisions in multi-track Part 7 claims straight to the Court of Appeal has gone. An option routing an appeal from a circuit judge’s final multi-track decision to the Court of Appeal is stating the pre-2016 position.

title: 14  Trial, appeals and enforcement
text:
14.4 Enforcing a money judgment
A judgment is not self-executing. The judgment creditor must choose a method, and the choice depends on what the debtor has.

14.4.1 Finding out what the debtor has
Order to obtain information from a judgment debtor (CPR 71) — the “oral examination”. The creditor applies without notice; the order requires the debtor (or, for a company, an officer) to attend court, usually before a court officer, to be questioned on oath about their means and to produce documents. The order must be served personally at least 14 days before the hearing, and the debtor may request travelling expenses. Failure to attend or to answer may be referred to a judge, who may make a suspended committal order for contempt.
Other sources: Land Registry searches, Companies House filings, credit reference searches, and asset tracing agents.


14.4.2 The methods









Method
Rule
Reaches
Best where




Writ or warrant of control
CPR 83; Sch 12 Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007
Goods, which enforcement agents may take control of and sell
The debtor is a trading business with valuable goods


Third party debt order
CPR 72
Money owed to the debtor by a third party — most often a bank account, but also trade debtors
The creditor knows where the debtor banks and the account is in credit


Charging order
CPR 73
The debtor’s beneficial interest in land, securities or certain funds
The debtor owns property; slow, but secure


Attachment of earnings order
CPR 89
A deduction from an employed debtor’s wages
The debtor is employed — not available against the self-employed, and County Court only


Appointment of a receiver
CPR 69
Income or assets not reachable by other means — rent, a partnership share
Unusual assets


Insolvency
Insolvency Act 1986
Everything
Pressure, or where the debtor has assets but will not pay



Writs and warrants of control. Enforcement agents must give the debtor a notice of enforcement of at least seven clear days before taking control of goods. They may not take goods that are exempt — tools of the trade and basic domestic items up to prescribed values — or goods belonging to someone else.
Which court executes matters, and the High Court and County Courts Jurisdiction Order 1991, article 8, splits it three ways for a County Court money judgment enforced against goods:







Sum to be enforced
Where




£5,000 or more
High Court only — transfer up, and a writ of control executed by a High Court Enforcement Officer


£600 to under £5,000
Either court


Less than £600
County Court only — a warrant of control executed by a County Court enforcement agent



A judgment in proceedings arising out of an agreement regulated by the Consumer Credit Act 1974 must be enforced in the County Court, whatever the sum. High Court enforcement is generally faster, which is why creditors transfer up wherever the option exists.
Third party debt orders proceed in two stages: an interim order made without notice, which freezes the sum in the third party’s hands, followed by a hearing at which a final order is made requiring payment to the creditor. The court will not make an order that causes hardship to an individual debtor, and a joint account is generally beyond reach unless the judgment is against all the account holders.
Charging orders also proceed in two stages — interim then final — and a final charging order may be registered against the title. It secures the debt but does not produce money; the creditor must then apply for an order for sale, which is discretionary and, for a modest debt secured on a family home, frequently refused or postponed.






Exam trap



Match the method to the asset, because that is the discrimination the examiner is testing:

A debtor with a shop full of stock → writ or warrant of control.
A debtor with a healthy bank balance → third party debt order.
A debtor who owns a house but has no cash → charging order, then possibly an order for sale.
A debtor in employment with no assets → attachment of earnings.
A self-employed debtor → not attachment of earnings.

The creditor is not confined to one method and may pursue several, subject to the court’s control.




14.4.3 Enforcing abroad
Where the assets are in another country, the English judgment must be recognised there.







Route
When it applies




Hague 2019 Judgments Convention
Judgments in proceedings issued on or after 1 July 2025, as between the UK and other contracting states — the EU, Ukraine, Uruguay, Albania and Montenegro among them. Not confined to exclusive jurisdiction clauses


Hague 2005 Choice of Court Convention
Where the judgment was given by a court designated in an exclusive choice of court agreement


Administration of Justice Act 1920 and Foreign Judgments (Reciprocal Enforcement) Act 1933
Registration schemes for judgments of certain Commonwealth and other designated countries


Common law
Otherwise: the creditor brings a fresh action on the English judgment in the foreign court, treating the judgment as a debt



The same framework operates in reverse for enforcing a foreign judgment in England and Wales.






Post-Brexit position — verify against your cut-off



The Brussels Recast Regulation, which provided near-automatic enforcement across the EU, no longer applies to proceedings commenced in England and Wales after the end of the transition period. Between 1 January 2021 and 1 July 2025 the position was patchy: Hague 2005 covered only exclusive jurisdiction clauses, and everything else fell back on the 1920 and 1933 Acts or the common law. The entry into force of Hague 2019 for the UK on 1 July 2025 substantially improved matters, but it applies only to proceedings issued on or after that date.

title: 14  Trial, appeals and enforcement
text:
14.5 Check yourself
Q1. A trial is listed to begin on Monday 12 October. The claimant’s solicitor asks when the trial bundle must be filed.
Which of the following is correct?
A. At least 21 days before the start of the trial.
B. Not more than 7 days and not less than 3 days before the start of the trial.
C. On the first day of the trial.
D. At least 14 days before the start of the trial.
E. Whenever the parties agree.
Q2. A circuit judge sitting in the County Court gives a final judgment in a multi-track claim worth £300,000. The losing party wishes to appeal on the ground that the judge misapplied the law on remoteness of damage.
To which court does the appeal lie, and what must the appellant establish to obtain permission?
A. The Court of Appeal, because the claim was allocated to the multi-track and the decision was final.
B. A High Court judge, and permission may be given only where the appeal would have a real prospect of success or there is some other compelling reason for it to be heard.
C. The Supreme Court, because the point is one of law.
D. A different circuit judge, and no permission is required.
E. The Court of Appeal, and the appellant must show an important point of principle or practice.
Q3. A judgment creditor is owed £40,000 by an individual who is self-employed as a consultant, rents his home, has no significant goods, but is owed £60,000 by a single large client, payable next month.
Which method of enforcement is most likely to be effective?
A. An attachment of earnings order.
B. A charging order over his home.
C. A third party debt order against the client who owes him £60,000.
D. A warrant of control.
E. A receiver by way of equitable execution over his goods.
Q4. A defendant loses at trial. The judge found the claimant’s principal witness credible and the defendant’s witness unconvincing, having heard them both give evidence over two days. The defendant wishes to appeal on the basis that the judge should have preferred its witness.
Which of the following is correct?
A. The appeal will succeed if the appeal court, reading the transcripts, would have reached a different view.
B. Permission is likely to be refused: an appeal is a review, not a re-hearing, and an appellate court will not interfere with findings of primary fact based on oral evidence unless they are plainly wrong.
C. The appeal court will hear the witnesses again.
D. The appeal will succeed because a finding on credibility is a question of law.
E. Permission is not required where the appeal concerns findings of fact.
Q5. A claimant obtains judgment for £250,000 against a company incorporated in Uruguay, in proceedings issued in England in September 2025 under an English jurisdiction clause. The company’s assets are all in Uruguay.
What is the most likely route to enforcement?
A. The Brussels Recast Regulation.
B. There is no route; an English judgment cannot be enforced outside the United Kingdom.
C. The Hague 2019 Judgments Convention, which entered into force for the United Kingdom on 1 July 2025 and applies to judgments in proceedings issued on or after that date, Uruguay being a contracting state.
D. A fresh action on the judgment at common law in Uruguay, because no convention applies.
E. Registration under the Foreign Judgments (Reciprocal Enforcement) Act 1933.






Answers and explanations





Q1 — B. CPR 39.5(2): unless the court orders otherwise, the claimant must file the trial bundle not more than seven days and not less than three days before the start of the trial. The window is deliberately narrow so that the bundle is complete but the court has time to read it.
Q2 — B. Under the Access to Justice Act 1999 (Destination of Appeals) Order 2016, an appeal from a circuit judge in the County Court lies to a High Court judge. The permission test in CPR 52.6 is a real prospect of success or some other compelling reason.

A applies the pre-2016 rule sending final multi-track decisions to the Court of Appeal, which the 2016 Order abolished. Destination now turns on the judge who made the decision.
C ignores the appellate structure entirely.
D invents a horizontal appeal and dispenses with permission.
E applies the second appeal test in CPR 52.7, which is engaged only where the decision appealed from was itself made on appeal — and states it incompletely, since that test requires a real prospect of success as well as an important point of principle or practice, unless there is some other compelling reason.

Q3 — C. A third party debt order under CPR 72 attaches a debt owed to the judgment debtor by a third party. A single, large, identified debt falling due next month is the ideal target: the interim order freezes it in the client’s hands and the final order directs payment to the creditor.

A fails because attachment of earnings requires an employed debtor and is not available against the self-employed.
B fails because he rents; there is no beneficial interest in land to charge.
D and E fail because he has no significant goods.

Q4 — B. CPR 52.21(1): an appeal is limited to a review. An appellate court has not seen the witnesses and will not interfere with findings of primary fact drawn from oral evidence unless they are plainly wrong or unsupported by any evidence. A submission that the judge should have believed the other witness is the paradigm hopeless appeal.

A applies a re-hearing standard.
C misdescribes appellate procedure; new evidence is admitted only on the Ladd v Marshall principles, and witnesses are not recalled.
D mischaracterises a finding of fact as one of law.
E is wrong: permission is required whatever the ground.

Q5 — C. The Hague 2019 Judgments Convention entered into force for the United Kingdom on 1 July 2025 and applies to judgments given in proceedings issued on or after that date. Proceedings were issued in September 2025, and Uruguay is a contracting state, so the Convention provides the treaty route for recognition and enforcement.

A no longer applies to proceedings commenced in England and Wales.
B is simply wrong.
D is the fallback where no convention applies, which is not the case here.
E applies to designated countries under a reciprocal registration scheme, which is not the route for Uruguay.

title: 15  Who pays, and how much
text:
15.1 The general rule and the court’s discretion
CPR 44.2(1): the court has a discretion as to whether costs are payable by one party to another, the amount, and when they are to be paid.
CPR 44.2(2): if the court decides to make an order, the general rule is that the unsuccessful party will be ordered to pay the costs of the successful party — “costs follow the event” — but the court may make a different order.
CPR 44.2(4): in deciding what order to make, the court will have regard to all the circumstances, including:
